articles.title: Name and territory of the Union
articles.officialText: (1) India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States. (2) The States and the territories thereof shall be as specified in the First Schedule. (3) The territory of India shall comprise— (a) the territories of the States; (b) the Union territories specified in the First Schedule; and (c) such other territories as may be acquired.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Article 1 establishes the name and geographical definition of the nation. By declaring "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States", it emphasizes the indestructible nature of the Indian Union and that the federal structure is not the result of an agreement among states.

landmarkCase.citation: In Re: Berubari Union Case (1960)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution and that Parliament cannot cede Indian territory to a foreign power under Article 3 without a constitutional amendment under Article 368.

articles.title: Admission or establishment of new States
articles.officialText: Parliament may by law admit into the Union, or establish, new States on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article grants Parliament the power to admit new states into the Union or establish new states that were not previously part of the territory of India.

landmarkCase.citation: RC Poudyal v. Union of India (1994)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court validated the admission of Sikkim into the Indian Union, holding that Parliament has wide discretion under Article 2 but must respect basic democratic principles.

articles.title: Formation of new States and alteration of areas, boundaries or names of existing States
articles.officialText: Parliament may by law— (a) form a new State by separation of territory from any State or by uniting two or more States or parts of States or by uniting any territory to a part of any State; (b) increase the area of any State; (c) diminish the area of any State; (d) alter the boundaries of any State; (e) alter the name of any State...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Article 3 allows Parliament to reorganize internal state boundaries, merge states, split states, or change state names by passing a simple majority bill, subject to consulting the affected state legislature's views.

landmarkCase.citation: Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay (1960)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that Parliament is not bound by the views of the state legislature expressed under the proviso to Article 3; it only needs to consult them.

articles.title: Citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution
articles.officialText: At the commencement of this Constitution, every person who has his domicile in the territory of India and— (a) who was born in the territory of India; or (b) either of whose parents was born in the territory of India; or (c) who has been ordinarily resident in the territory of India for not less than five years immediately preceding such commencement, shall be a citizen of India.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Article 5 outlines who became a citizen of India at the time of the Constitution's commencement on January 26, 1950, based on domicile combined with birth, parental birth, or long-term residence.

landmarkCase.citation: Pradeep Jain v. Union of India (1984)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that there is only one domicile in India—the domicile of India. Domicile of a state is not recognized under the Indian Constitution.

articles.title: Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law
articles.officialText: Nothing in the foregoing provisions of this Part shall derogate from the power of Parliament to make any provision with respect to the acquisition and termination of citizenship and all other matters relating to citizenship.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Article 11 gives Parliament plenary powers to pass laws regarding the acquisition, termination, and all other matters of citizenship, which led to the enactment of the Citizenship Act, 1955.

landmarkCase.citation: Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India (2005)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court struck down the IMDT Act, holding that it made the detection of illegal migrants in Assam extremely difficult, violating the duty of the Union under Article 355 to protect states from external aggression.

articles.title: Definition
articles.officialText: In this Part, unless the context otherwise requires, 'the State' includes the Government and Parliament of India and the Government and the Legislature of each of the States and all local or other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Article 12 defines 'the State' for the purposes of enforcing Fundamental Rights. This definition includes central, state, and local governments, as well as statutory authorities.

landmarkCase.citation: Rajasthan Electricity Board v. Mohan Lal (1967)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that 'other authorities' under Article 12 includes all bodies created by a statute on which powers are conferred by law.

articles.title: Laws inconsistent with or in derogation of the fundamental rights
articles.officialText: (1) All laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution, in so far as they are inconsistent with the provisions of this Part, shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void. (2) The State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by this Part...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Article 13 acts as the sentinel on the qui vive by establishing judicial review. It declares that any law that violates Fundamental Rights shall be void to the extent of the inconsistency.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Madras v. V.G. Row (1952)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court declared that the court's duty in regard to fundamental rights is that of a sentinel on the qui vive (watchful guardian).

articles.title: Equality before law
articles.officialText: The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Article 14 guarantees two concepts: 'Equality before Law' (a negative concept prohibiting special privileges) and 'Equal Protection of the Laws' (a positive concept directing equal treatment under equal circumstances).

landmarkCase.citation: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court introduced the new concept of equality, holding that equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects and dimensions, and it cannot be cribbed, cabined, and confined within traditional limits. Equality is antithetical to arbitrariness.

articles.title: Protection of certain rights regarding freedom of speech, etc.
articles.officialText: (1) All citizens shall have the right— (a) to freedom of speech and expression; (b) to assemble peaceably and without arms; (c) to form associations or unions or co-operative societies; (d) to move freely throughout the territory of India; (e) to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India; and (g) to practice any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Article 19 guarantees six basic democratic freedoms to Indian citizens, subject to reasonable restrictions under clauses (2) to (6) (e.g., sovereignty, security of the state, public order).

landmarkCase.citation: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, holding that it was vague, overbroad, and directly violated the right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a).

articles.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
articles.officialText: No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Article 21 is the heart of fundamental rights, guaranteeing that life and personal liberty can only be deprived by a fair, just, and reasonable procedure established by law.

landmarkCase.citation: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court revolutionized Article 21, holding that the procedure depriving a person of life or liberty must be 'reasonable, fair and just', importing the American concept of procedural due process.

articles.title: Remedies for enforcement of rights conferred by this Part
articles.officialText: (1) The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed. (2) The Supreme Court shall have power to issue directions or orders or writs...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution. It guarantees the right to petition the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of fundamental rights using writs (Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, Certiorari).

landmarkCase.citation: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the power of judicial review vested in the Supreme Court under Article 32 and High Courts under Article 226 is an integral and essential feature of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.

articles.title: Definition
articles.officialText: In this Part, unless the context otherwise requires, 'the State' has the same meaning as in Part III.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article establishes that the definition of 'the State' for the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) is identical to the one used for Fundamental Rights in Article 12. This means 'the State' includes the Government and Parliament of India, the Government and Legislature of each of the States, and all local or other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India.

By using this comprehensive definition, the Constitution ensures that all governing bodies, from municipal corporations to the central parliament, are equally bound to consider these non-justiciable principles while framing laws and policies.

landmarkCase.citation: Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib (1981)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court expanded the horizon of 'the State', laying down a six-point test to determine whether a corporation or society acts as an instrumentality or agency of the government, thereby binding it to constitutional obligations under Parts III and IV.

articles.title: Application of the principles contained in this Part
articles.officialText: The provisions contained in this Part shall not be enforceable by any court, but the principles therein laid down are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 37 clarifies the fundamental nature of the DPSPs, explicitly stating that they are non-justiciable. This means citizens cannot approach a court of law to legally force the government to implement them if it fails to do so, distinguishing them strictly from Fundamental Rights.

However, it places an active moral and constitutional obligation on the state, declaring them 'fundamental in the governance of the country'. It establishes that a welfare state must use these principles as its guiding compass whenever it drafts legislation or executive policies.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court initially held that Directive Principles cannot override Fundamental Rights and must run as subservient to them. However, later jurisprudence shifted this toward a view of harmonious construction between the two parts.

articles.title: State to secure a social order for the promotion of welfare of the people
articles.officialText: (1) The State shall strive to promote the welfare of the people by securing and protecting as effectively as it may a social order in which justice, social, economic and political, shall inform all the institutions of the national life. (2) The State shall, in particular, strive to minimise the inequalities in income, and endeavour to eliminate inequalities in status, facilities and opportunities, not only amongst individuals but also amongst groups of people residing in different areas or engaged in different vocations.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article serves as the foundational pillar of India's vision as a welfare state rather than a mere police state. It directs the government to actively create a just social order where social, economic, and political justice prevails across all public institutions.

The second clause, added by the 44th Amendment in 1978, explicitly instructs the state to reduce inequalities in income, status, facilities, and opportunities among citizens across various regions and professions, promoting egalitarian growth.

landmarkCase.citation: Air India Statutory Corporation v. United Labour Union (1997)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that concept of social justice in Article 38 is a fundamental right for workers, ensuring that the state protects human rights, dignity, and socio-economic equity to elevate the standard of living of the working class.

articles.title: Certain principles of policy to be followed by the State
articles.officialText: The State shall, in particular, direct its policy towards securing— (a) that the citizens, men and women equally, have the right to an adequate means of livelihood; (b) that the ownership and control of the material resources of the community are so distributed as best to subserve the common good; (c) that the operation of the economic system does not result in the concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment; (d) that there is equal pay for equal work for both men and women; (e) that the health and strength of workers, men and women, and the tender age of children are not abused and that citizens are not forced by economic necessity to enter avocations unsuited to their age or strength; (f) that children are given opportunities and facilities to develop in a healthy manner and in conditions of freedom and dignity and that childhood and youth are protected against exploitation and against moral and material abandonment.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 39 maps out a detailed socioeconomic blueprint for government legislation. It mandates equal livelihood opportunities, fair distribution of community resources, prevention of dangerous wealth concentration, and equal wages for equal work regardless of gender.

It also safeguards vulnerable populations by demanding that the state protect workers from hazardous environments forced by economic necessity, and ensure that children are provided the dignity and freedom to grow away from exploitation.

landmarkCase.citation: Randhir Singh v. Union of India (1982)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that while 'Equal Pay for Equal Work' is not explicitly a fundamental right, it is a constitutional goal under Articles 14, 16, and 39(d), and can be enforced through writ petitions in cases of irrational pay discrimination.

articles.title: Equal justice and free legal aid
articles.officialText: The State shall secure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice, on a basis of equal opportunity, and shall, in particular, provide free legal aid, by suitable legislation or schemes or in any other way, to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Inserted by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, this article addresses the structural barriers that impoverished citizens face when navigating the legal ecosystem. It commands the state to provide free legal aid and counsel to ensure no individual is denied justice due to financial or physical disability.

This principle recognizes that formal legal equality is meaningless if poor litigants cannot afford competent representation to defend their life, liberty, or property in court.

landmarkCase.citation: Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court established that free legal aid is an essential ingredient of a 'reasonable, fair and just' procedure, pronouncing it a fundamental right under Article 21, which heavily relied on the mandate of Article 39A.

articles.title: Organisation of village panchayats
articles.officialText: The State shall take steps to organise village panchayats and endow them with such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to function as units of self-government.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Reflecting Mahatma Gandhi's vision of 'Gram Swaraj' or village self-governance, Article 40 directs the state to build local administrative units. It instructs governments to delegate sufficient power, financial autonomy, and authority to village panchayats.

This principle shifted governance from a top-down centralized model to a bottom-up democratic framework, empowering rural communities to manage their local affairs directly.

landmarkCase.citation: State of U.P. v. Pradhan Sangh Kshettra Samiti (1995)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court validated the legislative framework leading up to the 73rd Constitutional Amendment, noting that Article 40 emphasizes decentralization of power to make democracy meaningful at the grassroots level.

articles.title: Right to work, to education and to public assistance in certain cases
articles.officialText: The State shall, within the limits of its economic capacity and development, make effective provision for securing the right to work, to education and to public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement, and in other cases of undeserved want.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 41 acts as a charter for social security in India. It requires the state to secure employment, educational avenues, and public safety nets for individuals suffering from joblessness, aging, sickness, or physical disabilities.

The implementation of this directive is explicitly linked to the state's economic capacity, serving as the direct constitutional foundation for landmark legislation like MGNREGA and national pension schemes.

landmarkCase.citation: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court linked the right to life under Article 21 to the right to livelihood, heavily deriving support from the economic welfare directives laid down under Article 41.

articles.title: Provision for just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief
articles.officialText: The State shall make provision for securing just and humane conditions of work and for maternity relief.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article underscores that economic productivity should not come at the expense of human dignity. It commands employers and the state to maintain working conditions that are safe, healthy, and humane.

Furthermore, it explicitly requires the state to institute welfare measures for maternity relief, ensuring that women workers are physically and financially protected before and after childbirth.

landmarkCase.citation: Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Female Workers (Muster Roll) (2000)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court extended the benefits of the Maternity Benefit Act to temporary and daily-wage female workers, holding that the mandate of Article 42 applies universally to protect a woman's right to safe motherhood.

articles.title: Living wage, etc., for workers
articles.officialText: The State shall endeavour to secure, by suitable legislation or economic organisation or in any other way, to all workers, agricultural, industrial or otherwise, work, a living wage, conditions of work ensuring a decent standard of life and full enjoyment of leisure and social and cultural opportunities and, in particular, the State shall endeavour to promote cottage industries on an individual or co-operative basis in rural areas.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 43 emphasizes the concept of a 'living wage' rather than a bare minimum wage. A living wage ensures that a worker can afford food, clothing, shelter, education for children, and a basic level of social security and comfort.

It also focuses on structural rural economics by directing the state to promote local cottage and co-operative industries, ensuring sustainable decentralized livelihood opportunities.

landmarkCase.citation: Bijay Cotton Mills Ltd. v. State of Ajmer (1955)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the enactment of the Minimum Wages Act is fully constitutional and justified as it carries out the foundational obligations of state policy expressed under Article 43.

articles.title: Participation of workers in management of industries
articles.officialText: The State shall take steps, by suitable legislation or in any other way, to secure the participation of workers in the management of undertakings, establishments or other organisations engaged in any industry.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Introduced via the 42nd Amendment in 1976, this socialist directive introduces industrial democracy. It calls upon governments to ensure that labor forces are not treated as mere commodities but are granted a seat at the table in industrial decision-making processes.

By involving workers in corporate or factory management, it aims to harmonize labor-capital relations and minimize industrial exploitation.

landmarkCase.citation: National Textile Workers Union v. P.R. Ramakrishnan (1983)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that workers have a fundamental locus standi to be heard in winding-up proceedings of a company, leaning heavily on Article 43A to affirm labor's partnership status in corporate operations.

articles.title: Promotion of co-operative societies
articles.officialText: The State shall endeavour to promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control and professional management of co-operative societies.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Added by the 97th Amendment in 2011, this article focuses on strengthening economic democracy through grassroots cooperation. It urges the state to actively facilitate and insulate the functioning of cooperative societies from unwarranted external political interference.

It guarantees that these institutions maintain autonomous management, democratic internal voting structures, and a professional administrative setup to benefit agricultural and local producers.

landmarkCase.citation: Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021)
landmarkCase.summary: While striking down parts of the 97th Amendment due to procedural lapses in state ratification, the Supreme Court upheld the validity of Article 43B as a directive principle governing multi-state cooperative societies.

articles.title: Uniform civil code for the citizens
articles.officialText: The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 44 directs the state to formulate a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) that replaces personal laws based on religious scriptures with a common set of laws governing civil matters such as marriage, divorce, inheritance, and adoption for all citizens.

The objective is to foster national integration and eradicate gender discrimination embedded within various patriarchal customary or religious personal laws.

landmarkCase.citation: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court regretted that Article 44 had remained a dead letter and stated that a common civil code would help the cause of national integration by removing conflicting ideologies in personal laws.

articles.title: Provision for early childhood care and education to children below the age of six years
articles.officialText: The State shall endeavour to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete the age of six years.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Originally focused on providing free and compulsory education up to 14 years, this article was amended by the 86th Amendment in 2002. After primary education became a fundamental right under Article 21A, the scope of Article 45 shifted exclusively to early childhood care and pre-school education for toddlers under six.

It targets the vital developmental years of a child, directing the state to run nutritional and educational programs like the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS).

landmarkCase.citation: Unni Krishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court read the original Article 45 in conjunction with Article 21 to hold that the right to education is a fundamental right, which eventually compelled Parliament to pass the 86th Constitutional Amendment.

articles.title: Promotion of educational and economic interests of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other weaker sections
articles.officialText: The State shall promote with special care the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections of the people, and, in particular, of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes, and shall protect them from social injustice and all forms of exploitation.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article provides the constitutional justification for affirmative action and protective discrimination policies in India. It mandates that the state actively uplift the socio-economic status of Scheduled Castes (SCs), Scheduled Tribes (STs), and other marginalized groups.

It places an explicit duty on governance to shield these historically oppressed communities from deep-seated social prejudices, systemic injustice, and economic exploitation.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas (1976)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court clarified that preferential treatment and reservations for backward classes are not an exception to the rule of equality, but are affirmative means to achieve the social order visualized in Article 46.

articles.title: Duty of the State to raise the level of nutrition and the standard of living and to improve public health
articles.officialText: The State shall regard the raising of the level of nutrition and the standard of living of its people and the improvement of public health as among its primary duties and, in particular, the State shall endeavour to bring about prohibition of the consumption except for medicinal purposes of intoxicating drinks and of drugs which are injurious to health.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 47 sets public health and nutritional security as a primary statutory obligation of the state. It forms the constitutional basis for public distribution systems, mid-day meals, and national healthcare campaigns.

Additionally, it provides state governments with the explicit authority to enforce prohibition on alcohol consumption and narcotic substances, except for strict medicinal applications.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that restrictions imposed on the consumption and sale of liquor under state laws are completely reasonable restrictions in the public interest, directly supported by the text of Article 47.

articles.title: Organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry
articles.officialText: The State shall endeavour to organise agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines and shall, in particular, take steps for preserving and improving the breeds, and prohibiting the slaughter, of cows and calves and other milch and draught cattle.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This directive blends economic modernization with traditional pastoral preservation. It instructs the state to update farming and animal husbandry practices using scientific methods to optimize output and livestock health.

The final clause contains a directive regarding livestock preservation, calling for an explicit ban on the slaughter of cows, calves, and functional agricultural cattle to protect the agrarian economy.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat (2005)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court upheld a total ban on the slaughter of cow progeny, ruling that the restriction was valid as it furthered the scientific agrarian goals enshrined under Article 48.

articles.title: Protection and improvement of environment and safeguarding of forests and wild life
articles.officialText: The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Introduced by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, this environmental charter instructs the state to move beyond mere exploitation of natural resources toward active ecological conservation.

It obligates the government to frame environmental laws protecting air and water quality, and safeguards wildlife and thick forest cover from industrial encroachment.

landmarkCase.citation: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Taj Trapezium Case) (1997)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court applied the principles of Article 48A to issue directives stopping industrial pollution from damaging the Taj Mahal, establishing the 'polluter pays' and precautionary principles in Indian law.

articles.title: Protection of monuments and places and objects of national importance
articles.officialText: It shall be the obligation of the State to protect every monument or place or object of artistic or historic interest, declared by or under law made by Parliament to be of national importance, from spoliation, disfigurement, destruction, removal, disposal or export, as the case may be.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 49 imposes a constitutional obligation on the state to protect cultural, artistic, and historical heritage sites. It commands the state to shield monuments declared of national importance from disfigurement, destruction, or illegal smuggling.

This guarantees that India's tangible historical legacy is preserved via agencies like the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) for future generations.

landmarkCase.citation: Rajeev Mankotia v. Secretary to the President of India (1997)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that the state has a binding duty under Article 49 to maintain and preserve historical monuments, conversion of which into commercial hotels without maintaining heritage integrity is impermissible.

articles.title: Separation of judiciary from executive
articles.officialText: The State shall take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article is essential for securing the rule of law and the independence of the courts. It commands the state to structurally isolate judicial functionaries from executive or administrative control.

By ensuring magistrates and judges are not answerable to political masters or bureaucrats, it protects impartial criminal trials and administrative dispute resolutions from bias.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Bihar v. Bal Mukund Sah (2000)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court emphasized that the separation of the judiciary from the executive is part of the basic structure of the Constitution, heavily drawing authority from the design of Article 50.

articles.title: Promotion of international peace and security
articles.officialText: The State shall endeavour to— (a) promote international peace and security; (b) maintain just and honourable relations between nations; (c) foster respect for international law and treaty obligations in the dealings of organised peoples with one another; and (d) encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 51 outlines India's constitutional foreign policy goals. It directs the sovereign state to prioritize international peace, foster respectful bilateral treaties, adhere to global laws, and support international arbitration over military escalation.

While domestic laws take precedence inside Indian territory, courts frequently use Article 51 to read international human rights treaties into local jurisprudence when gaps exist.

landmarkCase.citation: Gramophone Company of India Ltd. v. Birendra Bahadur Pandey (1984)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that international law doctrines should be harmoniously incorporated into domestic law, provided they do not conflict with an Act of Parliament, fulfilling the spirit of Article 51.

articles.title: Fundamental duties
articles.officialText: It shall be the duty of every citizen of India— (a) to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem; (b) to cherish and follow the noble ideals which inspired our national struggle for freedom; (c) to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India; (d) to defend the country and render national service when called upon to do so; (e) to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India transcending religious, linguistic and regional or sectional diversities; to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women; (f) to value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture; (g) to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures; (h) to develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform; (i) to safeguard public property and to abjure violence; (j) to strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity so that the nation constantly rises to higher levels of endeavour and achievement; (k) who is a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to his child or, as the case may be, ward between the age of six and fourteen years.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Inserted by the 42nd Amendment in 1976 on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee (and updated in 2002), this single article introduces a moral code of conduct for citizens. It establishes that rights cannot exist in a vacuum without corresponding duties toward the nation and co-citizens.

While these duties are non-enforceable by direct writs, they serve as crucial interpretive tools for courts to evaluate the constitutional validity of laws restricting public actions or penalizing civic misconduct.

landmarkCase.citation: AIIMS Students Union v. AIIMS (2002)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that Fundamental Duties under Article 51A are of equal systemic weight as Fundamental Rights, and can be used to check state policies or actions that degrade national excellence or individual merit.

articles.title: The President of India
articles.officialText: There shall be a President of India.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article establishes the highest constitutional office in the Republic of India. It marks the President as the structural head of state and the symbol of national unity, continuity, and sovereignty.

The use of the mandatory term 'shall' means this office can never remain vacant, guaranteeing a continuous constitutional head for the Union.

landmarkCase.citation: Rai Sahib Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court clarified that the Indian Constitution adopts the British Parliamentary system, making the President the formal or nominal executive head, while real executive power rests with the Cabinet.

articles.title: Executive power of the Union
articles.officialText: (1) The executive power of the Union shall be vested in the President and shall be exercised by him either directly or through officers subordinate to him in accordance with this Constitution. (2) Without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing provision, the supreme command of the Defence Forces of the Union shall be vested in the President and the exercise thereof shall be regulated by law. (3) Nothing in this article shall— (a) be deemed to transfer to the President any functions conferred by any existing law on the Government of any State or other authority; or (b) prevent Parliament from conferring by law functions on authorities other than the President.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 53 vests all formal executive authority of the Union of India in the President. It also proclaims the President as the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces.

Crucially, it mandates that this power must be exercised 'in accordance with this Constitution', meaning it is bounded by parliamentary checks and ministerial advice.

landmarkCase.citation: Samsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974)
landmarkCase.summary: A seven-judge bench held that the President must exercise executive powers only on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, except in highly limited, exceptional situations requiring personal discretion.

articles.title: Election of President
articles.officialText: The President shall be elected by the members of an electoral college consisting of— (a) the elected members of both Houses of Parliament; and (b) the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article defines the democratic basis of the presidency. Instead of a direct popular vote, the President is chosen by an Electoral College representing both federal houses and state legislatures.

By excluding nominated members, it ensures the office represents only elected democratic representatives across the Union and the States.

landmarkCase.citation: In re Presidential Election (1974)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court delivered an advisory opinion stating that the presidential election must be completed before the term expires, even if a state legislative assembly stands dissolved at that time.

articles.title: Manner of election of President
articles.officialText: (1) As far as practicable, there shall be uniformity in the scale of representation of the different States at the election of the President... (3) The election of the President shall be held in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote and the voting at such election shall be by secret ballot.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 55 provides complex mathematical formulas to ensure parity between states and the Union in presidential voting power. It mandates the system of proportional representation with a single transferable vote.

This design prevents populous states from dominating the election, preserving federal balance within the electoral process.

landmarkCase.citation: Babu Rao Pragatu v. A.B. Vajpayee (1977)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court validated the rigorous procedural conditions under the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, confirming they fulfill the constitutional framework of Article 55.

articles.title: Term of office of President
articles.officialText: (1) The President shall hold office for a term of five years from the date on which he enters upon his office: Provided that— (a) the President may, by writing under his hand addressed to the Vice-President, resign his office; (b) the President may, for violation of the Constitution, be removed from office by impeachment in the manner provided in article 61; (c) the President shall, notwithstanding the expiration of his term, continue to hold office until his successor enters upon his office.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article fixes the standard tenure of the President at five years. It also details early exit scenarios: voluntary resignation via a letter to the Vice-President, or removal via constitutional impeachment.

Clause (c) acts as a continuity mechanism, preventing a constitutional vacuum by extending the incumbent's term until the next president takes the oath.

landmarkCase.citation: Union of India v. V. Sriharan (2016)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that specific tenures fixed by constitutional offices like Article 56 demonstrate the continuous nature of sovereign executive authorities in parliamentary frameworks.

articles.title: Eligibility for re-election
articles.officialText: A person who holds, or who has held, office as President shall, subject to the other provisions of this Constitution, be eligible for re-election to that office.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Unlike some republics that impose hard term limits, Article 57 permits an individual to stand for re-election to the office of President multiple times.

While constitutionally permissible, Indian political conventions have generally limited presidents to serving a maximum of two terms.

landmarkCase.citation: Dr. Narayan Bhaskar Khare v. Election Commission of India (1957)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court examined the legal parameters of presidential candidature, confirming that eligibility under Article 57 is subject to the conditions laid down in subsequent qualification articles.

articles.title: Qualifications for election as President
articles.officialText: (1) No person shall be eligible for election as President unless he— (a) is a citizen of India, (b) has completed the age of thirty-five years, and (c) is qualified for election as a member of the House of the People. (2) A person shall not be eligible for election as President if he holds any office of profit under the Government of India or the Government of any State or under any local or other authority subject to the control of any of the said Governments.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 58 sets the minimum eligibility requirements for a presidential candidate. They must be an Indian citizen, at least 35 years old, and qualified to sit in the Lok Sabha.

It also bars anyone holding an 'office of profit' from contesting, preventing executive conflicts of interest and ensuring the candidate's independence.

landmarkCase.citation: Jaya Bachchan v. Union of India (2006)
landmarkCase.summary: Though dealing directly with Parliament membership, the Supreme Court clarified that an 'office of profit' is determined by whether the office is capable of yielding financial profit or benefit, relevant to Article 58(2).

articles.title: Conditions of President's office
articles.officialText: (1) The President shall not be a member of either House of Parliament or of a House of the Legislature of any State... (3) The President shall be entitled without payment of rent to the use of his official residences and shall be also entitled to such emoluments, allowances and privileges as may be determined by Parliament by law...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article protects the neutrality of the head of state. If a member of Parliament or a state assembly is elected President, their legislative seat automatically becomes vacant on the day they take office.

It also guarantees official housing (Rashtrapati Bhavan) and protects presidential salaries from being reduced during their term of office.

landmarkCase.citation: Satwant Singh Sawhney v. Assistant Passport Officer (1967)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court noted that constitutional privileges and protections under provisions like Article 59 ensure that high institutional offices operate without financial or executive vulnerability.

articles.title: Oath or affirmation by the President
articles.officialText: Every President and every person acting as President or discharging the functions of the President shall, before entering upon his office, make and subscribe before the Chief Justice of India or, in his absence, the most senior Judge of the Supreme Court available, an oath or affirmation...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 60 prescribes the exact text of the oath or affirmation taken by the President before the Chief Justice of India. The wording explicitly charges the President to 'preserve, protect and defend the Constitution'.

This links the office directly to constitutional defense, making the President a guardian of the supreme law rather than a political administration.

landmarkCase.citation: N. Radhakrishna v. Union of India (2007)
landmarkCase.summary: The court reiterated that the unique phrasing of the President's oath highlights their role as an anchor of constitutionalism, distinct from standard legislative or ministerial oaths.

articles.title: Procedure for impeachment of the President
articles.officialText: (1) When a President is to be impeached for violation of the Constitution, the charge shall be preferred by either House of Parliament... (4) If as a result of the investigation a resolution is passed by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the total membership of the House... such resolution shall have the effect of removing the President from his office...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article sets out a strict quasi-judicial process for removing a President from office. The sole ground for impeachment is a 'violation of the Constitution'.

The process requires a high threshold: a fourteen-day written notice, investigation by one house of Parliament, and a final vote passed by a two-thirds majority of the total membership of both houses.

landmarkCase.citation: K. Anandan Nambiar v. Chief Secretary (1966)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court noted that the exceptional nature of the two-thirds total majority requirement under Article 61 demonstrates the high level of institutional stability given to the Head of State.

articles.title: Time of holding election to fill vacancy in the office of President and the term of office of person elected to fill casual vacancy
articles.officialText: (1) An election to fill a vacancy caused by the expiration of the term of office of President shall be completed before the expiration of the term. (2) An election to fill a vacancy in the office of President occurring by reason of his death, resignation or removal... shall be held as soon as possible after, and in no case later than six months from, the date of occurrence of the vacancy...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 62 sets mandatory timelines for filling presidential vacancies. Regular elections must be completed before the incumbent's five-year term ends.

In cases of sudden vacancies due to death, resignation, or impeachment, the election must occur within six months, ensuring governance remains stable.

landmarkCase.citation: In re Presidential Poll Reference Case (1974)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court re-emphasized that the timeline in Article 62(1) is absolute, and administrative or political difficulties cannot be used to delay a presidential election past the expiration date.

articles.title: The Vice-President of India
articles.officialText: There shall be a Vice-President of India.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article establishes the second-highest constitutional office in the country. The Vice-President occupies a dual role, acting as the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and standing next in line to the presidency.

This office provides constitutional continuity, ensuring an immediate temporary successor is available if the presidency is suddenly vacated.

landmarkCase.citation: Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955)
landmarkCase.summary: The structural reading of the executive framework under Articles 52 and 63 shows how the framers established structural contingencies to prevent executive breakdown.

articles.title: The Vice-President to be ex-officio Chairman of the Council of States
articles.officialText: The Vice-President shall be ex-officio Chairman of the Council of States and shall not hold any other office of profit...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 64 links the executive role of the Vice-President with a legislative role, appointing them as the presiding officer of the Rajya Sabha. It prevents the Vice-President from holding any other office of profit during their tenure.

While performing these legislative duties, the Vice-President receives a salary fixed for the Chairman of the Council of States, rather than as Vice-President.

landmarkCase.citation: Union of India v. Shrikant Yaduvanshi (2019)
landmarkCase.summary: The court detailed the functioning of ex-officio authorities under constitutional provisions, holding that such offices carry independent structural responsibilities defined across legislative arenas.

articles.title: The Vice-President to act as President or to discharge his functions during casual vacancies in the office, or during the absence, of President
articles.officialText: (1) In the event of the occurrence of any vacancy in the office of the President by reason of his death, resignation or removal... the Vice-President shall act as President until the date on which a new President elected... enters upon his office...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article empowers the Vice-President to assume the powers, immunities, and emoluments of the President during temporary absences or casual vacancies. While acting as President, they vacate their legislative seat as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

This mechanism prevents administrative paralysis when a President is unable to discharge their duties due to illness, travel, or sudden vacancy.

landmarkCase.citation: Election Commission of India v. Shivaji (1988)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court noted that when the Vice-President acts as President under Article 65, they temporarily step into an entirely separate institutional role governed by presidential norms.

articles.title: Election of Vice-President
articles.officialText: (1) The Vice-President shall be elected by the members of an electoral college consisting of the members of both Houses of Parliament... in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article establishes the electoral process for the Vice-President. Unlike the presidential electoral college, the vice-presidential college consists solely of members of both houses of Parliament, omitting state assemblies.

It includes both elected and nominated MPs, reflecting the Vice-President's primary role as the presiding officer of the central Parliament's upper house.

landmarkCase.citation: Charan Lal Sahu v. Giani Zail Singh (1984)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that election disputes concerning the President or Vice-President can only be raised after the completion of the election process, ensuring the timelines under Articles 55 and 66 are maintained.

articles.title: Term of office of Vice-President
articles.officialText: The Vice-President shall hold office for a term of five years from the date on which he enters upon his office: Provided that— (a) a Vice-President may, by writing under his hand addressed to the President, resign his office; (b) a Vice-President may be removed from his office by a resolution of the Council of States passed by a majority of all the then members...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 67 sets the Vice-President's tenure at five years and outlines the procedures for resignation or removal. To resign, they must submit a handwritten letter to the President.

The removal process differs from presidential impeachment: it begins with a resolution passed by a majority of all the then-members of the Rajya Sabha, which must then be agreed to by the Lok Sabha.

landmarkCase.citation: K.A. Nambiar v. Chief Secretary (1966)
landmarkCase.summary: The court highlighted that the simplified removal process for the Vice-President under Article 67 reflects their distinct functional responsibilities within the legislature compared to the Head of State.

articles.title: Time of holding election to fill vacancy in the office of Vice-President and the term of office of person elected to fill casual vacancy
articles.officialText: (1) An election to fill a vacancy caused by the expiration of the term of office of Vice-President shall be completed before the expiration of the term. (2) An election to fill a vacancy in the office of Vice-President occurring by reason of his death, resignation or removal... shall be held as soon as possible after the occurrence of the vacancy...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article sets out timelines for vice-presidential elections. Regular elections must be concluded before the incumbent's five-year term expires.

In the event of an unexpected vacancy due to death, resignation, or removal, the election must take place 'as soon as possible', though it does not specify a strict six-month limit like the presidential article.

landmarkCase.citation: In re Presidential Election (1974)
landmarkCase.summary: The court observed that constitutional provisions governing structural successions require prompt compliance to maintain institutional stability within both the executive and legislative branches.

articles.title: Oath or affirmation by the Vice-President
articles.officialText: Every Vice-President shall, before entering upon his office, make and subscribe before the President, or some person appointed in that behalf by him, an oath or affirmation...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 69 requires the Vice-President to take an oath or affirmation before entering office, administered by the President or a designated representative.

Unlike the President's oath to 'preserve, protect and defend the Constitution', the Vice-President swears to 'bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution' and to faithfully discharge their duties.

landmarkCase.citation: N. Radhakrishna v. Union of India (2007)
landmarkCase.summary: The ruling noted that the textual variations across administrative oaths emphasize the specific constitutional obligations assigned to each respective office.

articles.title: Discharge of President's functions in other contingencies
articles.officialText: Parliament may make such provision as it thinks fit for the discharge of the functions of the President in any contingency not provided for in this Chapter.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 70 is a safety clause that grants Parliament the authority to handle unexpected situations where both the President and Vice-President are simultaneously unavailable.

This power enabled Parliament to pass the President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969, which provides that the Chief Justice of India will discharge presidential duties if both offices fall vacant.

landmarkCase.citation: In re Presidential Poll Reference (1974)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court recognized Parliament's residual power under Article 70 to pass laws addressing extraordinary situations, ensuring constitutional governance is maintained.

articles.title: Matters relating to, or connected with, the election of a President or Vice-President
articles.officialText: (1) All doubts and disputes arising out of or in connection with the election of a President or Vice-President shall be inquired into and decided by the Supreme Court whose decision shall be final...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article vests the exclusive jurisdiction to handle disputes regarding presidential or vice-presidential elections in the Supreme Court of India. Its rulings on these matters are final.

It also protects stability of governance by providing that if an election is declared void by the Court, any official acts performed by the President prior to that decision remain valid.

landmarkCase.citation: Dr. Khare v. Election Commission (1957)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court clarified that it can only hear a challenge to a presidential election after the final results are declared, refusing to pause an ongoing electoral process.

articles.title: Power of President to grant pardons, etc., and to suspend, remit or commute sentences in certain cases
articles.officialText: (1) The President shall have the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment or to suspend, remit or commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offence— (a) in all cases where the punishment or sentence is by a Court Martial; (b) in all cases where the punishment or sentence is for an offence against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the Union extends; (c) in all cases where the sentence is a sentence of death.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 72 vests the President with executive clemency powers, allowing them to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remissions of punishment, or to suspend, remit, or commute sentences. This applies to all death penalties, court-martial convictions, and offenses under Union laws.

This power acts as an executive check on the judiciary, providing a mechanism to correct potential judicial errors or offer relief on humanitarian grounds.

landmarkCase.citation: Maru Ram v. Union of India (1980)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that the President's power under Article 72 must be exercised on the advice of the Central Government, and is subject to limited judicial review against arbitrariness or bad faith.

articles.title: Extent of executive power of the Union
articles.officialText: (1) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, the executive power of the Union shall extend— (a) to the matters with respect to which Parliament has power to make laws; and (b) to the exercise of such rights, authority and jurisdiction as are exercisable by the Government of India by virtue of any treaty or agreement...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article defines the boundaries of the Union's executive authority, aligning it with Parliament's legislative powers under the Seventh Schedule. It allows the Union executive to act on matters within the Union and Concurrent Lists.

It also establishes that the Union's executive authority can extend beyond existing statutes to implement international treaties or agreements, provided it does not infringe upon individual rights.

landmarkCase.citation: Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the executive power of the government is not confined to implementing laws passed by the legislature; the executive can act even without specific prior legislation, provided it does not violate constitutional provisions or private rights.

articles.title: Council of Ministers to aid and advise President
articles.officialText: (1) There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President who shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice: Provided that the President may require the Council of Ministers to reconsider such advice... (2) The question whether any, and if so what, advice was tendered by Ministers to the President shall not be inquired into in any court.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 74 defines the core of India's parliamentary democracy. It establishes the Council of Ministers, led by the Prime Minister, to aid and advise the President, who must act in accordance with that advice.

The 44th Amendment added a check allowing the President to send advice back once for reconsideration, but they must accept the resubmitted advice. Clause (2) insulates this process by barring courts from examining the specific advice given.

landmarkCase.citation: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court clarified that while Article 74(2) bars courts from inquiring into the advice given to the President, it does not prevent judicial review of the objective material on which that advice was based.

articles.title: Other provisions as to Ministers
articles.officialText: (1) The Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President and the other Ministers shall be appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister... (3) The Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the House of the People...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article sets out the rules governing the appointment, tenure, and responsibility of Ministers. It establishes the principle of collective responsibility, meaning the Cabinet is jointly accountable to the Lok Sabha and must resign if it loses a vote of no-confidence.

Amendments to this article have capped the total number of ministers at 15% of the Lok Sabha's strength and require any minister who is not an MP to secure a seat within six months of appointment.

landmarkCase.citation: U.N.R. Rao v. Indira Gandhi (1971)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the Council of Ministers does not dissolve when the Lok Sabha is dissolved, as the President cannot exercise executive power under Article 74(1) without a Council of Ministers to provide advice.

articles.title: Attorney-General for India
articles.officialText: (1) The President shall appoint a person who is qualified to be appointed a Judge of the Supreme Court to be Attorney-General for India... (4) The Attorney-General shall hold office during the pleasure of the President, and shall receive such remuneration as the President may determine.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 76 creates the office of the Attorney-General for India, the chief legal advisor to the Union Government. The appointee must possess the qualifications required to serve as a Supreme Court judge.

The Attorney-General represents the government in major litigation and holds office during the pleasure of the President, conventionally resigning when the appointing administration changes.

landmarkCase.citation: P.N. Duda v. P. Shiv Shanker (1988)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court noted that the Attorney-General plays a distinct role in guiding the court on matters of public interest and maintaining the administration of justice.

articles.title: Conduct of business of the Government of India
articles.officialText: (1) All executive action of the Government of India shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the President... (3) The President shall make rules for the more convenient transaction of the business of the Government of India, and for the allocation among Ministers of the said business.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article dictates how the Union Government conducts its administrative business. It requires all official executive actions to be executed in the name of the President of India.

It also empowers the President to frame the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, which distribute portfolios and administrative duties among various ministries and departments.

landmarkCase.citation: Samsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court affirmed that executive business rules made under Article 77 are essential to the practical delegation of administrative power in a modern parliamentary government.

articles.title: Duties of Prime Minister as respects the furnishing of information to the President, etc.
articles.officialText: It shall be the duty of the Prime Minister— (a) to communicate to the President all decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to the administration of the affairs of the Union and proposals for legislation; (b) to furnish such information... as the President may call for; and (c) if the President so requires, to submit for the consideration of the Council of Ministers any matter on which a decision has been taken by a Minister but which has not been considered by the Council.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 78 acts as an information link between the active executive (the Prime Minister) and the nominal head of state (the President). It obligates the Prime Minister to report all cabinet decisions regarding administration and legislative proposals to the President.

This mechanism ensures the President can monitor governance, ask for information, and ensure individual ministerial decisions are reviewed by the full Cabinet if necessary.

landmarkCase.citation: B.R. Kapur v. State of Tamil Nadu (2001)
landmarkCase.summary: The court emphasized that information sharing under constitutional routes like Article 78 is vital to maintaining institutional harmony between the Head of State and the Head of Government.

articles.title: Constitution of Parliament
articles.officialText: There shall be a Parliament for the Union which shall consist of the President and two Houses to be known respectively as the Council of States and the House of the People.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article establishes the structure of India's bicameral federal legislature. It defines Parliament as consisting of three parts: the President, the Council of States (Rajya Sabha), and the House of the People (Lok Sabha).

Including the President as an integral part of Parliament, despite not sitting in either house, ensures they are involved in the legislative process, as no bill can become law without presidential assent.

landmarkCase.citation: Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2006)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court reviewed the structural design of Parliament, confirming that the bicameral system is structured to balance federal state representation with popular democracy.

articles.title: Composition of the Council of States
articles.officialText: (1) The Council of States shall consist of— (a) twelve members to be nominated by the President in accordance with the provisions of clause (3); and (b) not more than two hundred and thirty-eight representatives of the States and of the Union territories...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 80 outlines the composition of the Rajya Sabha, limiting its membership to 250. This includes 12 members nominated by the President for their contributions to literature, science, art, or social service, with the remainder elected by state and territorial legislatures.

This structure ensures the upper house acts as a permanent federal body representing state interests, balancing the directly elected lower house.

landmarkCase.citation: Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2006)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court upheld amendments that removed the domicile requirement for Rajya Sabha candidates and introduced open ballots, ruling these changes did not violate federal principles.

articles.title: Composition of the House of the People
articles.officialText: (1) Subject to the provisions of article 331, the House of the People shall consist of— (a) not more than five hundred and thirty members chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies in the States, and (b) not more than twenty members to represent the Union territories...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article defines the composition of the Lok Sabha, which represents the population of India through direct elections based on universal adult suffrage. It sets caps on representation for states and Union Territories.

It mandates that seats must be allocated to states in proportion to their population, ensuring equal voting representation across the country. These allocations have been temporarily frozen by amendments to prevent penalizing states that successfully manage population growth.

landmarkCase.citation: R.C. Poudyal v. Union of India (1994)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that while Article 81 emphasizes equal representation, some historical adjustments or protections for minor states do not undermine democratic principles.

articles.title: Readjustment after each census
articles.officialText: Upon the completion of each census, the allocation of seats in the House of the People to the States and the division of each State into territorial constituencies shall be readjusted by such authority and in such manner as Parliament may by law determine...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 82 requires electoral boundaries to be adjusted after each national census. This process is handled by an independent Delimitation Commission to ensure constituencies reflect shifting population patterns.

Constitutional amendments have frozen the reallocation of seats among states based on older census data to ensure states implementing family planning policies are not disadvantaged by a loss of legislative representation.

landmarkCase.citation: Meghraj Khandelwal v. Delimitation Commission (1967)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that once a Delimitation Commission publishes its boundary orders under parliamentary law, courts cannot intervene to disrupt election timelines.

articles.title: Duration of Houses of Parliament
articles.officialText: (1) The Council of States shall not be subject to dissolution, but as nearly as possible one-third of the members thereof shall retire as soon as may be on the expiration of every second year... (2) The House of the People, unless sooner dissolved, shall continue for five years...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article establishes the lifespans of both houses of Parliament. The Rajya Sabha is a permanent body not subject to dissolution; its members serve staggered six-year terms, with one-third retiring every two years to ensure continuity.

In contrast, the Lok Sabha has a fixed five-year term from its first meeting, unless it is dissolved earlier by the President or extended during a declared National Emergency.

landmarkCase.citation: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court analyzed legislative tenures, holding that the legal extension of a house during a valid emergency complies with constitutional provisions.

articles.title: Qualification for membership of Parliament
articles.officialText: A person shall not be qualified to be chosen to fill a seat in Parliament unless he— (a) is a citizen of India... (b) is, in the case of a seat in the Council of States, not less than thirty years of age and, in the case of a seat in the House of the People, not less than twenty-five years of age; and (c) possesses such other qualifications as may be prescribed...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 84 outlines the basic criteria for becoming a Member of Parliament. Candidates must be Indian citizens, take a formal constitutional oath, and meet minimum age requirements: 25 for the Lok Sabha and 30 for the Rajya Sabha.

It also gives Parliament the authority to establish additional qualifications or disqualifications by law, which it did through the Representation of the People Act, 1951.

landmarkCase.citation: Mann Lal Shukla v. State of M.P. (1971)
landmarkCase.summary: The court affirmed that satisfying the age and citizenship criteria under Article 84 is mandatory at the time of scrutiny of nomination papers for an election to be valid.

articles.title: Sessions of Parliament, prorogation and dissolution
articles.officialText: (1) The President shall from time to time summon each House of Parliament to meet at such time and place as he thinks fit, but six months shall not intervene between their last sitting in one session and the date appointed for their first sitting in the next session...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article governs the scheduling of parliamentary sessions. It requires the President to summon Parliament regularly, mandating that the gap between two consecutive sessions cannot exceed six months, ensuring legislative oversight of the executive.

It also empowers the President to prorogue (end) a session of either house and to dissolve the Lok Sabha on the advice of the Prime Minister.

landmarkCase.citation: Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court noted that the power to dissolve a legislative body must be exercised based on valid, objective material, and cannot be used for partisan political advantage.

articles.title: Right of President to address and send messages to Houses
articles.officialText: (1) The President may address either House of Parliament or both Houses assembled together, and for that purpose require the attendance of members. (2) The President may send messages to either House of Parliament, whether with respect to a Bill then pending in Parliament or otherwise...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 86 grants the President the right to address either house of Parliament or a joint sitting, and to compel the attendance of members for this purpose.

It also allows the President to send formal messages to Parliament regarding pending bills or other matters, which the legislature is required to consider promptly.

landmarkCase.citation: Ram Das v. State of U.P. (1995)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that the President's power to address and send messages underscores their role as an institutional link between executive policy and legislative action.

articles.title: Special address by the President
articles.officialText: (1) At the commencement of the first session after each general election to the House of the People and at the commencement of the first session of each year the President shall address both Houses of Parliament assembled together and inform Parliament of the causes of its summons.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article mandates a special presidential address at two specific times: at the start of a new Parliament after a general election, and at the beginning of each year's first session (the Budget Session).

This address outlines the government's policy agenda and legislative priorities for the coming year. It is followed by a debate and vote on the Motion of Thanks in both houses.

landmarkCase.citation: Yogendra Narain v. Union of India (2001)
landmarkCase.summary: The court observed that the special address under Article 87 outlines the executive administration's policy vision, and the subsequent parliamentary debate is an essential part of legislative oversight.

articles.title: Rights of Ministers and Attorney-General as respects Houses
articles.officialText: Every Minister and the Attorney-General for India shall have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, either House, any joint sitting of the Houses, and any committee of Parliament of which he may be named a member, but shall not by virtue of this article be entitled to vote.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 88 allows Union Ministers and the Attorney-General to speak and participate in the proceedings of either house of Parliament, joint sittings, or parliamentary committees.

This ensures that ministers can defend policies in a house where they are not members, and allows the Attorney-General to provide legal counsel, though neither can vote under this provision.

landmarkCase.citation: A.K. Roy v. Union of India (1982)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court noted that Article 88 ensures full participation of the government's chief legal officer and executive ministers in legislative deliberations, enhancing accountability.

articles.title: The Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Council of States
articles.officialText: (1) The Vice-President of India shall be ex-officio Chairman of the Council of States. (2) The Council of States shall, as soon as may be, choose a member of the Council to be Deputy Chairman thereof...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article establishes the leadership structure of the Rajya Sabha. It reinforces that the Vice-President serves as the ex-officio Chairman, and mandates that the house elect a member to serve as Deputy Chairman.

The Deputy Chairman presides over sessions and manages house business when the Chairman is absent or acting as President.

landmarkCase.citation: Ramachandra Rao v. Council of States (2011)
landmarkCase.summary: The court affirmed that the officers of the Rajya Sabha derive their authority directly from constitutional provisions, ensuring their independence in managing legislative business.

articles.title: Vacation and resignation of, and removal from, the office of Deputy Chairman
articles.officialText: A member holding office as Deputy Chairman of the Council of States— (a) shall vacate his office if he ceases to be a member of the Council; (b) may at any time, by writing under his hand addressed to the Chairman, resign his office; and (c) may be removed from his office by a resolution of the Council passed by a majority of all the then members...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 90 details how the office of the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha may be vacated. The office becomes vacant if they lose their seat in the house, if they submit a resignation to the Chairman, or if they are removed by a majority vote of the house.

A fourteen-day notice period is required before a removal resolution can be moved, protecting the office from sudden partisan actions.

landmarkCase.citation: K.A. Nambiar v. Union of India (1966)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that procedural requirements for removing legislative officers protect these positions from sudden political maneuvers, ensuring stable house management.

articles.title: Power of the Deputy Chairman or other person to perform the duties of the office of, or to act as, Chairman
articles.officialText: (1) While the office of Chairman is vacant, or during any period when the Vice-President is acting as, or discharging the functions of, President, the duties of the office shall be performed by the Deputy Chairman...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article ensures the Rajya Sabha always has a presiding officer. It directs the Deputy Chairman to assume the Chairman's duties if the office is vacant or if the Vice-President is acting as President.

If both offices are vacant, the President can appoint a member of the house to temporarily discharge these duties.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Goa v. Amit Palekar (2020)
landmarkCase.summary: The court highlighted that provisions governing deputy officers maintain institutional continuity, preventing a breakdown in legislative leadership.

articles.title: The Chairman or the Deputy Chairman not to preside while a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration
articles.officialText: (1) At any sitting of the Council of States, while any resolution for the removal of the Vice-President from his office is under consideration, the Chairman, or while any resolution for the removal of the Deputy Chairman... is under consideration, the Deputy Chairman, shall not, though he is present, preside...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 92 applies the principle that no one should be a judge in their own cause to parliamentary proceedings. It prevents the Chairman or Deputy Chairman from presiding over a session while a resolution for their removal is being considered.

The targeted officer can still attend and speak during the debate to defend themselves, but they cannot vote or preside over the proceedings.

landmarkCase.citation: Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016)
landmarkCase.summary: While dealing with a state assembly speaker, the Supreme Court applied this constitutional principle, holding that a presiding officer cannot bypass removal resolutions by using their official powers.

articles.title: The Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People
articles.officialText: The House of the People shall, as soon as may be, choose two members of the House to be respectively Speaker and Deputy Speaker thereof and, so often as the office of Speaker or Deputy Speaker becomes vacant, the House shall choose another member to be Speaker or Deputy Speaker...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
