This article requires the Lok Sabha to elect two of its members to serve as Speaker and Deputy Speaker. The Speaker manages the proceedings, maintains order, and represents the collective authority of the house.

The phrase 'as soon as may be' directs the house to fill these positions promptly after a general election to ensure proper legislative administration.

landmarkCase.citation: Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court recognized the high status of the Speaker's office, holding that the Speaker acts as an independent tribunal when deciding disqualification cases under the Tenth Schedule.

articles.title: Vacation and resignation of, and removal from, the offices of Speaker and Deputy Speaker
articles.officialText: A member holding office as Speaker or Deputy Speaker of the House of the People— (a) shall vacate his office if he ceases to be a member of the House of the People; (b) may at any time, by writing under his hand addressed, if such member is the Speaker, to the Deputy Speaker, and if such member is the Deputy Speaker, to the Speaker, resign his office; and (c) may be removed from his office by a resolution of the House of the People passed by a majority of all the then members...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 94 details the terms of office for the Speaker and Deputy Speaker. It requires them to vacate their office if they lose their seat in Parliament. The Speaker resigns by writing to the Deputy Speaker, and vice versa.

It also establishes a removal process requiring a 14-day notice and a majority vote of the house. Crucially, the Speaker does not vacate their office upon a dissolution of the Lok Sabha; they remain in office until the first meeting of the next Parliament.

landmarkCase.citation: Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court emphasized that constitutional protections for presiding officers ensure they can operate neutrally without fearing sudden removal by shifting political majorities.

articles.title: Power of the Deputy Speaker or other person to perform the duties of the office of, or to act as, Speaker
articles.officialText: (1) While the office of Speaker is vacant, the duties of the office shall be performed by the Deputy Speaker...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article governs leadership transitions in the Lok Sabha. It directs the Deputy Speaker to perform the Speaker's duties if the office becomes vacant.

If both offices are vacant, the President can appoint a member of the house to act as Speaker until formal elections can be held.

landmarkCase.citation: G.V. Mavalankar v. State (1952)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that provisions for deputy officers ensure the lower house can continue its legislative functions without administrative interruptions.

articles.title: The Speaker or the Deputy Speaker not to preside while a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration
articles.officialText: (1) At any sitting of the House of the People, while any resolution for the removal of the Speaker from his office is under consideration, the Speaker, or while any resolution for the removal of the Deputy Speaker... is under consideration, the Deputy Speaker, shall not, though he is present, preside...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 96 prevents the Speaker or Deputy Speaker from presiding over the Lok Sabha while a resolution for their removal is being debated.

The officer has the right to attend, speak, and vote on the resolution in the first instance, but cannot exercise a casting vote in the event of a tie.

landmarkCase.citation: Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that a presiding officer cannot entertain or act on disqualification petitions against other members while a resolution for their own removal is pending.

articles.title: Salaries and allowances of the Chairman and Deputy Chairman and the Speaker and Deputy Speaker
articles.officialText: There shall be paid to the Chairman and the Deputy Chairman of the Council of States, and to the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the House of the People, such salaries and allowances as may be respectively fixed by Parliament by law...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article requires the salaries and allowances of the presiding officers of both houses to be fixed by parliamentary law.

These expenses are charged directly to the Consolidated Fund of India, protecting them from annual parliamentary votes and helping ensure the financial independence of these offices.

landmarkCase.citation: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997)
landmarkCase.summary: The court observed that charging salaries of major constitutional functionaries directly to the Consolidated Fund insulates them from political influence.

articles.title: Secretariat of Parliament
articles.officialText: (1) Each House of Parliament shall have a separate secretarial staff: Provided that nothing in this clause shall be construed as preventing the creation of posts common to both Houses of Parliament...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 98 requires both the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha to maintain independent secretarial staffs. This ensures that the administration of Parliament is separate from the government civil service.

It empowers Parliament to regulate the recruitment and service conditions of its secretarial staff, reinforcing the structural independence of the legislative branch.

landmarkCase.citation: MSM Sharma v. Sri Krishna Sinha (1959)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court noted that the independent administrative structure of legislative secretariats protects the internal operations of Parliament from executive interference.

articles.title: Oath or affirmation by members
articles.officialText: Every member of either House of Parliament shall, before taking his seat, make and subscribe before the President, or some person appointed in that behalf by him, an oath or affirmation according to the form set out for the purpose in the Third Schedule.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article mandates that every newly elected or nominated Member of Parliament must take a formal oath or affirmation before the President or a designated representative before they can take their seat.

Taking this oath is a mandatory prerequisite; members cannot participate in debates or vote in parliamentary proceedings until they have complied.

landmarkCase.citation: Pashupati Nath Sukul v. Nem Chandra Jain (1984)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court clarified that an elected candidate becomes a member of the house immediately upon election, but cannot take their seat or perform legislative duties until they take the oath under Article 99.

articles.title: Voting in Houses, power of Houses to act notwithstanding vacancies and quorum
articles.officialText: (1) Save as otherwise provided in this Constitution, all questions at any sitting of the Houses or joint sitting of the Houses shall be determined by a majority of votes of the members present and voting, other than the Speaker or person acting as Chairman or Speaker... (3) Until Parliament by law otherwise provides, the quorum to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament shall be one-tenth of the total number of members of the House.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 100 governs the rules for voting and decision-making in Parliament. It establishes that decisions are made by a simple majority of members present and voting. The presiding officer cannot vote initially, but holds a casting vote in the event of a tie.

Clause (3) sets the standard quorum at 10% of the house's total membership. If a session lacks a quorum, the presiding officer must adjourn or suspend the meeting until enough members are present.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1978)
landmarkCase.summary: The court affirmed that parliamentary voting and internal proceedings are guided by constitutional rules, which protect the validity of laws passed in accordance with these procedures.

articles.title: Vacation of seats
articles.officialText: (1) No person shall be a member of both Houses of Parliament and provision shall be made by Parliament by law for the vacation by a person who is chosen a member of both Houses of his seat in one or the other House...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article outlines the rules against dual membership in Parliament. A person cannot simultaneously hold a seat in both houses of Parliament, or in a house of Parliament and a state legislature.

It details how seats become vacant through dual election, resignation, or unexcused absence from the house for more than 60 consecutive days.

landmarkCase.citation: P.V. Narasimha Rao v. State (1998)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court analyzed the rules governing membership and vacancies, noting that these provisions ensure legislators hold only one active mandate at a time.

articles.title: Disqualifications for membership
articles.officialText: (1) A person shall be disqualified for being chosen as, and for being, a member of either House of Parliament— (a) if he holds any office of profit... (b) if he is of unsound mind... (c) if he is an undischarged insolvent; (d) if he is not a citizen of India... (e) if he is so disqualified by or under any law made by Parliament...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 102 details the grounds for disqualifying an individual from holding a seat in Parliament. These include holding an office of profit, being declared of unsound mind, being an undischarged insolvent, or voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship.

Clause (2) incorporates the Anti-Defection Law, disqualifying members who switch political parties or violate party whips, as detailed in the Tenth Schedule.

landmarkCase.citation: Jaya Bachchan v. Union of India (2006)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that whether an office constitutes an 'office of profit' depends on whether it carries the potential for financial gain, regardless of whether the individual actually receives it.

articles.title: Decision on questions as to disqualifications of members
articles.officialText: (1) If any question arises as to whether a member of either House of Parliament has become subject to any of the disqualifications mentioned in clause (1) of article 102, the question shall be referred for the decision of the President and his decision shall be final...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article establishes the procedure for deciding disqualification cases under Article 102(1). Such questions are referred to the President for a final decision.

However, the President is constitutionally required to obtain and follow the opinion of the Election Commission of India, making the process objective and binding.

landmarkCase.citation: Brundaban Nayak v. Election Commission of India (1965)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the President must act in accordance with the Election Commission's opinion on disqualification matters under this provision.

articles.title: Penalty for sitting and voting before making oath or affirmation under article 99 or when not qualified or when disqualified
articles.officialText: If a person sits or votes as a member of either House of Parliament before he has complied with the requirements of article 99... he shall be liable in respect of each day on which he so sits or votes to a penalty of five hundred rupees to be recovered as a debt due to the Union.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 104 imposes a financial penalty on anyone who sits or votes in Parliament before taking the mandatory oath or while knowing they are disqualified.

The fixed penalty is 500 rupees per day, which can be recovered as a debt to the Union, reinforcing the requirement for all legislators to maintain valid credentials.

landmarkCase.citation: Pashupati Nath Sukul v. Nem Chandra Jain (1984)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that this penalty enforces compliance with the oath requirement, preventing unqualified or disqualified individuals from participating in legislative votes.

articles.title: Powers, privileges, etc., of the Houses of Parliament and of the members and committees thereof
articles.officialText: (1) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution and to the rules and standing orders of Parliament, there shall be freedom of speech in Parliament. (2) No member of Parliament shall be liable to any proceedings in any court in respect of anything said or any vote given by him in Parliament or any committee thereof...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article establishes parliamentary privileges, guaranteeing freedom of speech within the legislature. It protects MPs from legal liability or court proceedings for anything said or any vote cast inside Parliament or its committees.

This protection allows legislators to debate and perform their duties without fearing legal retaliation, though their speech remains subject to internal house rules.

landmarkCase.citation: P.V. Narasimha Rao v. State (1998)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the constitutional immunity under Article 105(2) protects MPs from prosecution for bribery tied to speech or voting inside the house, a position that has since faced significant refinement regarding corruption boundaries.

articles.title: Salaries and allowances of members
articles.officialText: Members of either House of Parliament shall be entitled to receive such salaries and allowances as may from time to time be determined by Parliament by law...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 106 gives Parliament the authority to determine the salaries, allowances, and pensions of its members through legislation.

This financial support is designed to ensure that individuals can serve as full-time legislators regardless of their personal financial background.

landmarkCase.citation: Lok Prahari v. Union of India (2018)
landmarkCase.summary: The court examined the mechanisms for determining legislative salaries, recommending independent frameworks to avoid conflicts of interest when legislators vote on their own compensation.

articles.title: Provisions as to introduction and passing of Bills
articles.officialText: (1) Subject to the provisions of articles 109 and 117 with respect to Money Bills and other financial Bills, a Bill may originate in either House of Parliament... (3) A Bill pending in Parliament shall not lapse by reason of the prorogation of the Houses...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article defines the standard procedure for introducing and passing regular legislation. Ordinary bills can originate in either house and must be approved by both houses in identical terms to proceed.

It also notes that pending bills do not lapse when a parliamentary session is prorogued, but bills pending in the Lok Sabha generally lapse when that house is dissolved.

landmarkCase.citation: Purushothaman Nambudiri v. State of Kerala (1962)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court clarified how the dissolution of a house affects pending legislation, confirming that bills pending before the Rajya Sabha which have not passed the Lok Sabha do not lapse.

articles.title: Joint sitting of both Houses in certain cases
articles.officialText: (1) If after a Bill has been passed by one House and transmitted to the other House— (a) the Bill is rejected by the other House; or (b) the Houses have finally disagreed as to the amendments... the President may... notify to the Houses his intention to summon them to a joint sitting...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 108 provides a mechanism to resolve legislative deadlocks between the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha over ordinary bills. If a bill is rejected by one house or delayed for over six months, the President can summon a joint sitting.

Decisions at a joint sitting are made by a simple majority of all members present. This process does not apply to Money Bills or Constitutional Amendment Bills.

landmarkCase.citation: Pesara Pushpamala Reddy v. G.S.S. Anjaneya Murthy (2009)
landmarkCase.summary: The court reviewed the rare use of joint sittings, confirming it is an exceptional constitutional tool designed to resolve persistent legislative disagreements between the two houses.

articles.title: Special procedure in respect of Money Bills
articles.officialText: (1) A Money Bill shall not be introduced in the Council of States. (2) After a Money Bill has been passed by the House of the People it shall be transmitted to the Council of States for its recommendations and the Council of States shall within a period of fourteen days return the Bill to the House of the People...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article establishes the Lok Sabha's primacy over financial legislation. It prohibits the introduction of Money Bills in the Rajya Sabha.

Once the Lok Sabha passes a Money Bill, the Rajya Sabha has 14 days to review it and offer recommendations. The Lok Sabha can accept or reject these suggestions, and if the Rajya Sabha does not return the bill within 14 days, it is deemed passed by both houses.

landmarkCase.citation: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (Aadhaar Judgment) (2018)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court examined the definition of Money Bills, holding that classifying legislation under this category is subject to judicial review to ensure it meets the requirements of Article 110.

articles.title: Definition of "Money Bill"
articles.officialText: (1) For the purposes of this Chapter, a Bill shall be deemed to be a Money Bill if it contains only provisions dealing with all or any of the following matters, namely:— (a) the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax; (b) the regulation of the borrowing of money... (c) the custody of the Consolidated Fund or the Contingency Fund of India... (3) If any question arises whether a Bill is a Money Bill or not, the decision of the Speaker of the House of the People thereon shall be final.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 110 defines a Money Bill as legislation dealing exclusively with financial matters like taxation, government borrowing, or expenditures from the Consolidated Fund of India.

Clause (3) grants the Speaker of the Lok Sabha the final authority to certify whether a piece of legislation qualifies as a Money Bill, protecting the process from procedural delays.

landmarkCase.citation: Rojer Mathew v. South Indian Bank Ltd. (2020)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court referred the issue of certifying non-financial legislation as Money Bills to a larger bench, emphasizing the need for compliance with the definition in Article 110.

articles.title: Assent to Bills
articles.officialText: When a Bill has been passed by the Houses of Parliament, it shall be presented to the President, and the President shall declare either that he assents to the Bill, or that he withholds assent therefrom: Provided that the President may... return the Bill to the Houses with a message requesting that they will reconsider the Bill...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article details the final stage of the lawmaking process. After a bill passes both houses, it must be presented to the President for their assent to become law.

The President can grant assent, withhold it, or return non-money bills for reconsideration. However, if both houses pass the bill again with or without amendments, the President is constitutionally required to grant assent.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Telangana v. Governor (2023)
landmarkCase.summary: Though concerning a state Governor, the Supreme Court emphasized that constitutional heads must process bills presented for assent promptly, as holding bills indefinitely undermines legislative authority.

articles.title: Annual financial statement
articles.officialText: (1) The President shall in respect of every financial year cause to be laid before both the Houses of Parliament a statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India for that year... referred to as the 'annual financial statement'.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 112 mandates the presentation of the Annual Financial Statement, commonly known as the Union Budget. The President must ensure this detailed accounting of estimated receipts and expenditures is laid before both houses each financial year.

The budget separates expenses into sums charged directly to the Consolidated Fund of India (non-votable) and sums required for other government expenditures (votable), ensuring structural transparency.

landmarkCase.citation: Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court noted that the formal budgetary process under Article 112 ensures democratic control over public finances by requiring legislative approval for executive spending.

articles.title: Procedure in Parliament with respect to estimates
articles.officialText: (1) So much of the estimates as relates to expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India shall not be submitted to the vote of Parliament... (2) So much of the said estimates as relates to other expenditure shall be submitted in the form of demands for grants to the House of the People...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article details the voting rules for budget estimates. Expenditures charged directly to the Consolidated Fund, such as judicial salaries, cannot be voted on by Parliament, though they can be debated.

All other spending requests must be presented to the Lok Sabha as Demands for Grants, giving the lower house the power to approve, reject, or reduce proposed expenditures.

landmarkCase.citation: Bhim Singh v. Union of India (2010)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the power to review demands for grants under Article 113 allows the legislature to monitor and regulate public welfare expenditures.

articles.title: Appropriation Bills
articles.officialText: (1) As soon as may be after the grants under article 113 have been made by the House, there shall be introduced a Bill to provide for the appropriation out of the Consolidated Fund of India of all moneys required to meet— (a) the grants so made by the House; and (b) the expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 114 requires an Appropriation Bill to be passed before any money can be legally withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India. This bill legalizes the spending grants approved under Article 113.

This rule ensures the executive cannot spend public funds without explicit statutory authorization from Parliament.

landmarkCase.citation: State of U.P. v. Attar Singh (1955)
landmarkCase.summary: The court confirmed that no executive department can withdraw funds from the public treasury without an Appropriation Act passed in accordance with Article 114.

articles.title: Supplementary, additional or excess grants
articles.officialText: (1) The President shall cause to be laid before both the Houses of Parliament if— (a) the amount authorised by any law... is found to be insufficient... or (b) any money has been spent on any service during a financial year in excess of the amount granted for that service...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article provides financial flexibility for handling unexpected expenses during a fiscal year. It allows the government to request supplementary, additional, or excess grants if authorized funds prove insufficient or if a department overspends its budget.

These mid-year funding adjustments must be presented to Parliament and passed using the same legislative process as the primary budget.

landmarkCase.citation: Bhim Singh v. Union of India (2010)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that supplementary grants provide the necessary flexibility to respond to changing administrative needs while maintaining legislative oversight.

articles.title: Votes on account, votes of credit and exceptional grants
articles.officialText: (1) Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Chapter, the House of the People shall have power— (a) to make any grant in advance in respect of the estimated expenditure for a part of any financial year pending the completion of the procedure prescribed in article 113...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 116 allows the Lok Sabha to authorize short-term funding measures to keep the government running while the full budget is being debated. This includes a 'Vote on Account', which provides advance funding for routine expenses at the start of a financial year.

It also allows for 'Votes of Credit' to cover unexpected expenditures during national emergencies, acting as a financial safety valve for the state.

landmarkCase.citation: Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955)
landmarkCase.summary: The court observed that interim financial mechanisms like a Vote on Account prevent administrative shutdowns during lengthy budget review processes.

articles.title: Special provisions as to financial Bills
articles.officialText: (1) A Bill or amendment making provision for any of the matters specified in sub-clauses (a) to (f) of clause (1) of article 110 shall not be introduced or moved except on the recommendation of the President and a Bill making such provision shall not be introduced in the Council of States...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article outlines the rules for broader Financial Bills that contain fiscal provisions but do not qualify as strict Money Bills. Like Money Bills, they require the President's prior recommendation and cannot be introduced in the Rajya Sabha.

However, once introduced, ordinary financial bills require the approval of both houses, meaning the Rajya Sabha enjoys its standard voting powers rather than the restricted 14-day advisory role applied to Money Bills.

landmarkCase.citation: Rojer Mathew v. South Indian Bank Ltd. (2020)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court analyzed the distinctions between Money Bills under Article 110 and Financial Bills under Article 117, emphasizing that procedural requirements must be strictly followed.

articles.title: Rules of procedure
articles.officialText: (1) Each House of Parliament may make rules for regulating, subject to the provisions of this Constitution, its procedure and the conduct of its business.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 118 empowers both the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha to frame their own independent rules of procedure and conduct of business. This ensures that Parliament can organize its daily operations, debates, and committees without external interference.

These rules must comply with constitutional provisions, but they grant each house internal autonomy over its legislative affairs.

landmarkCase.citation: Pandit MSM Sharma v. Sri Krishna Sinha (1959)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court confirmed that the internal rules framed by a legislative house under this article generally override general statutory provisions regarding internal business management.

articles.title: Regulation by law in Parliament in relation to financial business
articles.officialText: Parliament may, for the purpose of the timely completion of financial business, regulate by law the procedure of, and the conduct of business in, each House of Parliament in relation to any financial matter...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article allows Parliament to pass laws regulating its own procedures for processing financial business and budgets. This helps ensure that financial measures are passed before the start of the new fiscal year.

If an internal procedural rule conflicts with a statutory law passed under this article, the statutory law takes precedence to avoid financial delays.

landmarkCase.citation: Bhim Singh v. Union of India (2010)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that statutory regulations governing financial business are designed to ensure timely budget implementation while maintaining accountability.

articles.title: Language to be used in Parliament
articles.officialText: (1) Notwithstanding anything in Part XVII, but subject to the provisions of article 348, business in Parliament shall be transacted in Hindi or in English: Provided that the Chairman of the Council of States or Speaker of the House of the People... may permit any member who cannot adequately express himself in Hindi or in English to address the House in his mother-tongue.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 120 establishes Hindi and English as the primary languages for conducting business in Parliament. This ensures that legislative debates and records are accessible across different regions.

It also contains an inclusivity clause, allowing the presiding officer to permit any member who cannot express themselves effectively in Hindi or English to address the house in their mother tongue.

landmarkCase.citation: Union of India v. Murasoli Maran (1977)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court analyzed the constitutional status of languages in official business, confirming that provisions like Article 120 are designed to balance accessibility with regional representation.

articles.title: Restriction on discussion in Parliament
articles.officialText: No discussion shall take place in Parliament with respect to the conduct of any Judge of the Supreme Court or of a High Court in the discharge of his duties except upon a motion for presenting an address to the President praying for the removal of the Judge...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article protects judicial independence by barring Parliament from debating the conduct or rulings of Supreme Court or High Court judges during regular sessions.

The sole exception to this rule is when Parliament is actively considering a formal removal motion against a judge, ensuring that judicial decisions are protected from political pressure.

landmarkCase.citation: Subcommittee on Judicial Accountability v. Union of India (1991)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the restriction under Article 121 protects the judiciary from political debates, ensuring judges can perform their duties without fear of partisan criticism.

articles.title: Courts not to inquire into proceedings of Parliament
articles.officialText: (1) The validity of any proceedings in Parliament shall not be called in question on the ground of any alleged irregularity of procedure. (2) No officer or member of Parliament in whom powers are vested by or under this Constitution for regulating procedure... shall be subject to the jurisdiction of any court in respect of the exercise by him of those powers.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 122 protects the separation of powers by prohibiting courts from challenging the validity of parliamentary proceedings based on alleged procedural irregularities. This gives Parliament final authority over its internal operations.

It also insulates presiding officers and MPs from lawsuits regarding how they exercise their powers to manage internal house business.

landmarkCase.citation: Raja Ram Pal v. Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha (2007)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that while procedural irregularities are protected from judicial review under Article 122, courts can intervene if a parliamentary proceeding suffers from a substantive illegality or violates constitutional rights.

articles.title: Power of President to legislate during recess of Parliament
articles.officialText: (1) If at any time, except when both Houses of Parliament are in session, the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article grants the President the executive authority to promulgate Ordinances when Parliament is in recess. These ordinances carry the same legal weight as an Act of Parliament and are designed to allow immediate action during emergencies.

This power is subject to strict democratic limits: any ordinance must be laid before both houses of Parliament once they reconvene, and it will automatically expire six weeks after the start of the session unless formally approved.

landmarkCase.citation: D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that re-promulgating ordinances repeatedly without presenting them to the legislature is a subversion of the democratic process and a fraud on the Constitution.

articles.title: Establishment and constitution of Supreme Court
articles.officialText: (1) There shall be a Supreme Court of India consisting of a Chief Justice of India and, until Parliament by law prescribes a larger number, of not more than seven other Judges...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 124 establishes the Supreme Court of India as the highest judicial body in the country. It details the composition of the court, the qualifications required for judges, and the rules governing their appointments.

It also sets the mandatory retirement age for Supreme Court judges at 65 and outlines the removal process, which requires a special majority vote in both houses of Parliament on grounds of proven misbehavior or incapacity.

landmarkCase.citation: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (NJAC Case) (2015)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court struck down the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) Act, holding that the selection of judges by a body containing executive members compromised judicial independence, which is part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

articles.title: National Judicial Appointments Commission
articles.officialText: (1) There shall be a Commission to be known as the National Judicial Appointments Commission consisting of— (a) the Chief Justice of India, Chairperson, ex-officio; (b) two other senior Judges of the Supreme Court... (c) the Union Minister in charge of Law and Justice... (d) two eminent persons to be nominated...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Inserted by the 99th Amendment in 2014, this article attempted to replace the judicial Collegium system with a broader National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) for appointing judges. The proposed body included judicial, executive, and independent members.

The provision aimed to introduce civil society and executive oversight into judicial appointments, but it was challenged as an encroachment on the independence of the judiciary.

landmarkCase.citation: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court declared the 99th Constitutional Amendment and Article 124A unconstitutional and void, restoring the pre-existing Collegium system for judicial appointments.

articles.title: Functions of Commission
articles.officialText: It shall be the duty of the National Judicial Appointments Commission to— (a) recommend persons for appointment as Chief Justice of India, Judges of the Supreme Court, Chief Justices of High Courts and other Judges of High Courts; (b) recommend transfer of Chief Justices and other Judges of High Courts...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article outlined the intended functions of the NJAC, which included recommending candidates for judicial appointments to the Supreme Court and High Courts, and managing the transfers of High Court judges.

Because the Supreme Court struck down the 99th Amendment, this article is no longer operational, and these functions remain under the control of the judicial Collegium system.

landmarkCase.citation: NJAC Judgment (2015)
landmarkCase.summary: The striking down of the entire 99th Amendment rendered the functional mandates under Article 124B legally inoperative, maintaining the judiciary's control over appointments and transfers.

articles.title: Power of Parliament to make law
articles.officialText: Parliament may, by law, regulate the procedure for the appointment of Chief Justice of India and other Judges of the Supreme Court and Chief Justices and other Judges of High Courts and empower the Commission to lay down by regulations... the procedure for the discharge of its functions...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 124C aimed to give Parliament the statutory authority to pass laws regulating the procedures for judicial appointments and transfers under the NJAC framework.

Like Articles 124A and 124B, this provision was invalidated by the Supreme Court in 2015 to protect the independence of the judiciary from legislative changes.

landmarkCase.citation: NJAC Judgment (2015)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court invalidated Article 124C along with the rest of the 99th Amendment, ruling that allowing Parliament to regulate appointment procedures could compromise judicial independence.

articles.title: Salaries, etc., of Judges
articles.officialText: (1) There shall be paid to the Judges of the Supreme Court such salaries and allowances as may be determined by Parliament by law and, until provision in that behalf is so made, such salaries and allowances as are specified in the Second Schedule...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 125 requires the salaries, allowances, and pensions of Supreme Court judges to be fixed by parliamentary law. These financial provisions are protected by the Constitution.

It explicitly states that a judge's salary and privileges cannot be reduced to their disadvantage during their term of office, protecting them from financial pressure from the executive or legislature.

landmarkCase.citation: Union of India v. Sankalchand Himatlal Sheth (1977)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court observed that financial protections for judges are essential to maintaining an independent judiciary capable of ruling without fear of economic retaliation.

articles.title: Appointment of acting Chief Justice
articles.officialText: When the office of Chief Justice of India is vacant or when the Chief Justice is, by reason of absence or otherwise, unable to perform the duties of his office, the duties of the office shall be performed by such one of the other Judges of the Court as the President may appoint for the purpose.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article provides a continuity mechanism for the judiciary. It empowers the President to appoint a senior Supreme Court judge to serve as the acting Chief Justice if the office falls vacant or if the incumbent is unable to perform their duties due to illness or absence.

This ensures that the administrative and judicial leadership of the highest court continues without interruption.

landmarkCase.citation: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (1993)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that appointments of acting officials under Article 126 are temporary measures meant to maintain institutional leadership until a permanent appointment is made.

articles.title: Appointment of ad hoc Judges
articles.officialText: (1) If at any time there should not be a quorum of the Judges of the Supreme Court available to hold or continue any session of the Court, the National Judicial Appointments Commission on a reference made to it by the Chief Justice of India, may with the previous consent of the President... request in writing the attendance at the sittings of the Court, as an ad hoc Judge, of a Judge of a High Court...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 127 allows for the appointment of ad hoc judges to the Supreme Court if a session lacks a quorum of permanent judges. The Chief Justice of India can request a qualified High Court judge to temporarily serve on the Supreme Court, subject to the consent of the President.

This allows the court to continue its judicial work and handle sudden backlogs or quorum issues without delaying cases.

landmarkCase.citation: Ashok Tanwar v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2005)
landmarkCase.summary: The court clarified that ad hoc judicial appointments are exceptional measures designed to resolve temporary quorum issues and ensure the continuous administration of justice.

articles.title: Attendance of retired Judges at sittings of the Supreme Court
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding anything in this Chapter, the National Judicial Appointments Commission may at any time, with the previous consent of the President, request any person who has held the office of a Judge of the Supreme Court or of a High Court... to sit and act as a Judge of the Supreme Court...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article allows the Chief Justice of India to invite retired Supreme Court or High Court judges to temporarily sit and hear cases, subject to the consent of the President and the consent of the retired judge themselves.

While acting in this capacity, the retired judge enjoys the jurisdiction and privileges of a Supreme Court judge, helping the court manage complex or long-pending cases.

landmarkCase.citation: Lok Prahari v. Union of India (2021)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court activated the guidelines for using Article 128 to bring back retired judges to help clear severe case backlogs, emphasizing its value as a tool for judicial efficiency.

articles.title: Supreme Court to be a court of record
articles.officialText: The Supreme Court shall be a court of record and shall have all the powers of such a court including the power to punish for contempt of itself.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 129 declares the Supreme Court to be a 'court of record', meaning its judgments, proceedings, and acts are recorded for permanent testimony and serve as binding legal precedents for all lower courts.

Crucially, it grants the court the inherent power to punish for contempt of itself. This authority allows the court to penalize actions that disrespect, disobey, or lower the authority of the judiciary, protecting its institutional integrity.

landmarkCase.citation: In re Arundhati Roy (2002)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that its power to punish for contempt under Article 129 is an inherent constitutional authority that cannot be abridged or limited by statutory ordinary laws.

articles.title: Seat of Supreme Court
articles.officialText: The Supreme Court shall sit in Delhi or in such other place or places as the Chief Justice of India may, with the approval of the President, from time to time, appoint.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article designates New Delhi as the official seat of the Supreme Court of India. It establishes a central physical location for the nation's highest appellate court.

It also provides flexibility by allowing the Chief Justice, with the prior approval of the President, to hold sittings in other regional locations to improve access to justice, though this power has rarely been exercised for permanent regional benches.

landmarkCase.citation: Union of India v. S.P. Anand (2008)
landmarkCase.summary: The court held that deciding whether to establish regional benches of the Supreme Court away from Delhi is a matter of administrative policy for the Chief Justice and the President, and cannot be compelled by a writ of mandamus.

articles.title: Original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
articles.officialText: Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, the Supreme Court shall, to the exclusion of any other court, have original jurisdiction in any dispute— (a) between the Government of India and one or more States; or (b) between the Government of India and any State or States on one side and one or more other States on the other; or (c) between two or more States...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 131 grants the Supreme Court exclusive original jurisdiction to hear federal disputes. This means the court acts as the first and final forum for resolving legal conflicts between the central government and the states, or between different states.

This provision excludes lower courts from handling interstate or federal-state disputes, ensuring a single, authoritative judicial resolution for structural federal conflicts.

landmarkCase.citation: State of West Bengal v. Union of India (1963)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court confirmed that a suit under Article 131 must involve a legal right or constitutional boundary dispute between federal units, rather than political disagreements.

articles.title: Exclusive jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in regard to questions as to constitutional validity of Central laws
articles.officialText: [Repealed by the Constitution (Forty-third Amendment) Act, 1977.]
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Inserted by the 42nd Amendment during the Emergency, this article stripped High Courts of their power to review the constitutional validity of Central laws, vesting that authority exclusively in the Supreme Court.

This measure concentrated judicial review power at the central level, but it was quickly repealed by the 43rd Amendment in 1977 to restore the traditional judicial review powers of the High Courts.

landmarkCase.citation: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997)
landmarkCase.summary: Though analyzing later amendments, the Supreme Court reaffirmed that the judicial review power of High Courts over all laws is part of the basic structure and cannot be eliminated.

articles.title: Appellate jurisdiction of Supreme Court in appeals from High Courts in certain cases
articles.officialText: (1) An appeal shall lie to the Supreme Court from any judgment, decree or final order of a High Court... whether in a civil, criminal or other proceeding, if the High Court certifies under article 134A that the case involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of this Constitution.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 132 establishes the Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction for cases involving constitutional interpretation. It allows appeals from High Court rulings in civil, criminal, or other proceedings if the case involves a substantial question of law regarding the Constitution.

This requires a certificate from the High Court under Article 134A, ensuring that major constitutional issues can be brought to the highest court for a definitive ruling.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Jammu & Kashmir v. Ganga Singh (1960)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court clarified that an appeal under Article 132 is meant exclusively to resolve substantial questions regarding constitutional interpretation rather than factual disputes.

articles.title: Appellate jurisdiction of Supreme Court in appeals from High Courts in regard to civil matters
articles.officialText: (1) An appeal shall lie to the Supreme Court from any judgment, decree or final order in a civil proceeding of a High Court... if the High Court certifies under article 134A— (a) that the case involves a substantial question of law of general importance; and (b) that in the opinion of the High Court the said question needs to be decided by the Supreme Court.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article governs appeals to the Supreme Court in civil matters. It allows a party to appeal a High Court civil judgment if the case involves a substantial question of law of general importance that requires a resolution by the Supreme Court.

This mechanism screens out routine civil disputes, ensuring the Supreme Court can focus on civil matters with broader legal or policy implications.

landmarkCase.citation: State Bank of India v. S.B.I. Staff Association (2004)
landmarkCase.summary: The court held that a certificate for civil appeal under Article 133 should only be granted if the legal question has wider impact and lacks clear precedent.

articles.title: Appellate jurisdiction of Supreme Court in regard to criminal matters
articles.officialText: (1) An appeal shall lie to the Supreme Court from any judgment, final order or sentence in a criminal proceeding of a High Court... if the High Court— (a) has on appeal reversed an order of acquittal of an accused person and sentenced him to death; or (b) has withdrawn for trial before itself any case from any court subordinate to its authority and has in such trial convicted the accused person and sentenced him to death...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 134 governs criminal appeals to the Supreme Court. It grants an absolute right of appeal without requiring a certificate in cases where a High Court reverses an acquittal and sentences an individual to death, or takes a case from a lower court to impose a death sentence.

For other criminal matters, an appeal requires a certificate from the High Court stating that the case is fit for review by the Supreme Court, providing an extra safeguard where life and liberty are at stake.

landmarkCase.citation: Babu v. State of Kerala (2010)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court clarified its duty under Article 134, holding that when a High Court reverses an acquittal to impose a death sentence, the Supreme Court must independently re-evaluate the entire evidence.

articles.title: Certificate for appeal to the Supreme Court
articles.officialText: Every High Court, passing or making a judgment, decree, final order, or sentence, referred to in clause (1) of article 132 or clause (1) of article 133 or clause (1) of article 134— (a) may, if it thinks fit so to do, on its own motion; and (b) shall, if an oral application is made, by or on behalf of the party aggrieved... determine immediately after the passing or making of such judgment... whether a certificate... may be given in respect of that case.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Inserted by the 44th Amendment in 1978, this article simplifies the process for obtaining an appeal certificate from a High Court. It allows the High Court to grant a certificate on its own motion or based on an oral application made immediately after its ruling.

This streamlined procedure avoids the need for separate written petitions, helping speed up the transition of eligible cases to the Supreme Court.

landmarkCase.citation: State Bank of India v. S.B.I. Staff Association (2004)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court noted that Article 134A requires High Courts to quickly assess whether a case meets the high standards required for a Supreme Court appeal.

articles.title: Jurisdiction and powers of the Federal Court under existing law to be exercisable by the Supreme Court
articles.officialText: Until Parliament by law otherwise provides, the Supreme Court shall also have jurisdiction and powers in relation to any matter to which the provisions of article 133 or article 134 do not apply if jurisdiction and powers in relation to that matter were exercisable by the Federal Court immediately before the commencement of this Constitution.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This transitional article transferred the jurisdiction and powers of the pre-independence Federal Court of India to the newly established Supreme Court.

This ensured legal continuity when the Constitution took effect, allowing the Supreme Court to handle matters that fell under the Federal Court's jurisdiction but were not explicitly covered by Articles 133 or 134.

landmarkCase.citation: Garikapati Veeraya v. N. Subbiah Choudhry (1957)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the right of appeal is a vested right that arises at the date of the suit, and pre-existing rights to appeal to the Federal Court were preserved and transferred to the Supreme Court under Article 135.

articles.title: Special leave to appeal by the Supreme Court
articles.officialText: (1) Notwithstanding anything in this Chapter, the Supreme Court may, in its discretion, grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, determination, sentence or order in any cause or matter passed or made by any court or tribunal in the territory of India.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 136 grants the Supreme Court broad discretionary power to hear appeals through Special Leave Petitions (SLPs). This allows the court to intervene against any judgment, decree, or order passed by any court or tribunal in the country, with the exception of military courts.

This acts as a residual safety net, allowing the Supreme Court to step in and correct gross injustices or procedural failures even when standard appeal routes are unavailable.

landmarkCase.citation: Lallubhai Jogibhai Patel v. Union of India (1981)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court emphasized that while Article 136 grants broad discretionary power, it should be exercised sparingly and only in exceptional cases involving grave injustices or substantial questions of law.

articles.title: Review of judgments or orders by the Supreme Court
articles.officialText: Subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament or any rules made under article 145, the Supreme Court shall have power to review any judgment pronounced or order made by it.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article gives the Supreme Court the authority to review its own previously pronounced judgments or orders. This allows the court to correct patent errors, factual mistakes, or clear injustices in its own rulings.

This power provides a mechanism to rectify judicial errors without requiring a formal constitutional amendment, helping maintain the accuracy of legal precedents.

landmarkCase.citation: Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court established the concept of a 'Curative Petition' as a final remedy under its inherent powers to prevent an abuse of process and cure gross miscarriages of justice even after a review petition has been dismissed.

articles.title: Enlargement of the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
articles.officialText: (1) The Supreme Court shall have such further jurisdiction and powers with respect to any of the matters in the Union List as Parliament may by law confer...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 138 allows Parliament to expand the jurisdiction and powers of the Supreme Court through legislation. This can apply to matters within the Union List or other legal areas authorized by special agreements.

This allows the legislature to grant the highest court extra responsibilities as needed to handle changing national legal requirements.

landmarkCase.citation: In re Special Courts Bill (1979)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court noted that Parliament's power to expand its jurisdiction allows for the creation of specialized legal pathways to handle urgent issues of public importance.

articles.title: Conferment on the Supreme Court of powers to issue certain writs
articles.officialText: Parliament may by law confer on the Supreme Court power to issue directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them, for any purposes other than those mentioned in clause (2) of article 32.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
While Article 32 empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs exclusively for enforcing Fundamental Rights, Article 139 allows Parliament to pass laws giving the court the authority to issue writs for other legal purposes.

This allows Parliament to expand the court's writ jurisdiction into broader administrative or statutory areas if necessary.

landmarkCase.citation: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997)
landmarkCase.summary: The court discussed the structural framework of writ jurisdictions, noting that expansions under Article 139 run alongside the established powers of the High Courts.

articles.title: Transfer of certain cases
articles.officialText: (1) Where cases involving the same or substantially the same questions of law are pending before the Supreme Court and one or more High Courts... the Supreme Court may withdraw the case or cases pending before the High Court or the High Courts and dispose of all the cases itself...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Inserted by the 42nd Amendment and updated by the 44th, this article allows the Supreme Court to withdraw cases from High Courts and consolidate them before itself if they involve substantially identical questions of law of general importance.

It also allows the Supreme Court to transfer a case from one High Court to another to ensure a fair trial, prevent conflicting judgments, and improve judicial efficiency.

landmarkCase.citation: Union of India v. Shiromani Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee (2000)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court exercised its power under Article 139A to transfer cases across jurisdictions to prevent conflicting rulings from different High Courts on identical statutory interpretations.

articles.title: Ancillary powers of Supreme Court
articles.officialText: Parliament may by law make provision for conferring upon the Supreme Court such supplemental powers not inconsistent with any of the provisions of this Constitution as may appear to be necessary or desirable for the purpose of enabling the Court more effectively to exercise the jurisdiction conferred upon it by or under this Constitution.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 140 allows Parliament to grant the Supreme Court supplemental or ancillary powers to help it exercise its jurisdiction more effectively.

These extra powers must be consistent with the Constitution and are designed to ensure the court has the practical tools needed to enforce its decisions.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1978)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that ancillary powers ensure that the Supreme Court's jurisdictional declarations can be backed by practical enforcement orders.

articles.title: Law declared by Supreme Court to be binding on all courts
articles.officialText: The law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within the territory of India.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article establishes the principle of stare decisis at the national level, declaring that any law established by the Supreme Court is strictly binding on all other courts within India.

This makes the Supreme Court the final authority on legal interpretation, ensuring uniformity and consistency across the country's entire judicial system. The Supreme Court itself is not bound by its own past decisions and can overrule them if necessary.

landmarkCase.citation: Bengal Immunity Co. v. State of Bihar (1955)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that while its rulings are binding on all other Indian courts under Article 141, the Supreme Court is not bound by its own decisions and can overrule them to correct errors.

articles.title: Enforcement of decrees and orders of Supreme Court and orders as to discovery, etc.
articles.officialText: (1) The Supreme Court in the exercise of its jurisdiction may pass such decree or make such order as is necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it, and any decree so passed or order so made shall be enforceable throughout the territory of India...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 142 grants the Supreme Court equitable power to issue decrees or orders necessary for doing 'complete justice' in any matter before it. This allows the court to transcend statutory lacunae or procedural hurdles to fashion unique remedies when a strict application of written law would result in an unjust outcome.

These orders are enforceable across the entire country, making this provision a powerful tool for judicial equity and public interest interventions.

landmarkCase.citation: Union Carbide Corporation v. Union of India (Bhopal Gas Leak Case) (1991)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that its expansive power under Article 142 to do complete justice cannot be limited by statutory laws, allowing it to bypass procedural rules to award an immediate $470 million settlement to victims.

articles.title: Power of President to consult Supreme Court
articles.officialText: (1) If at any time it appears to the President that a question of law or fact has arisen, or is likely to arise, which is of such a nature and of such public importance that it is expedient to obtain the opinion of the Supreme Court upon it, he may refer the question to that Court for consideration and the Court may, after such hearing as it thinks fit, report to the President its opinion thereon.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article establishes the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. It empowers the President to refer important questions of law or fact to the court for its formal opinion.

The Supreme Court can decline to answer certain references under clause (1). Rulings under this advisory jurisdiction are not binding judgments, but they carry significant legal weight and guide government actions.

landmarkCase.citation: In re Special Courts Bill (1979)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court clarified that while its advisory opinions under Article 143 are not binding judgments, they are highly persuasive and entitled to great respect from all authorities.

articles.title: Civil and judicial authorities to act in aid of the Supreme Court
articles.officialText: All authorities, civil and judicial, in the territory of India shall act in aid of the Supreme Court.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 144 requires all civil and judicial authorities across India to actively assist and enforce the orders and decrees of the Supreme Court.

This leaves no room for administrative or local resistance, ensuring that the highest court's rulings are carried out by executive and judicial officers nationwide.

landmarkCase.citation: In re Vinay Chandra Mishra (1995)
landmarkCase.summary: The court emphasized that Article 144 ensures the executive administration must fully implement the directives of the Supreme Court, reinforcing the rule of law.

articles.title: Special provisions as to disposal of questions relating to constitutional validity of laws
articles.officialText: [Repealed by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976 - subsequently removed by Forty-third Amendment Act, 1977.]
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article was inserted during the Emergency to require a minimum of seven judges to determine the constitutional validity of a central law, requiring a two-thirds majority to strike it down.

This restriction on judicial operations was repealed by the 43rd Amendment in 1977, restoring standard judicial voting and bench sizes.

landmarkCase.citation: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997)
landmarkCase.summary: The historical review of these short-lived provisions confirmed that attempts to restrict the mechanics of judicial review are contrary to the traditional balance of powers.

articles.title: Rules of Court, etc.
articles.officialText: (1) Subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament, the Supreme Court may from time to time, with the approval of the President, make rules for regulating generally the practice and procedure of the Court... (3) The minimum number of Judges who are to sit for the purpose of deciding any case involving a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of this Constitution... shall be five...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 145 empowers the Supreme Court to frame its own rules to regulate its internal practices and procedures, subject to the approval of the President. This includes setting rules for handling appeals, bail applications, and review petitions.

Crucially, clause (3) mandates that a minimum of five judges must sit to decide any case involving a substantial question of law regarding constitutional interpretation, establishing the framework for Constitutional Benches.

landmarkCase.citation: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that procedural rules made under Article 145 help organize the administration of justice while maintaining the court's core constitutional structures.

articles.title: Officers and servants and the expenses of the Supreme Court
articles.officialText: (1) Appointments of officers and servants of the Supreme Court shall be made by the Chief Justice of India or such other Judge or officer of the Court as he may direct... (3) The administrative expenses of the Supreme Court, including all salaries, allowances and pensions payable to or in respect of the officers and servants of the Court, shall be charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article protects the administrative independence of the Supreme Court. It gives the Chief Justice of India exclusive authority over appointing and regulating the service conditions of the court's officers and staff, free from executive civil service rules.

It also mandates that all administrative expenses of the court, including salaries and pensions, are charged directly to the Consolidated Fund of India, insulating the judiciary from political funding changes.

landmarkCase.citation: Union of India v. S.B. Vohra (2004)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the Chief Justice's independence under Article 146 in managing court staff cannot be easily overridden by executive budget departments.

articles.title: Interpretation
articles.officialText: In this Chapter and in Chapter V of Part VI, references to any substantial question of law as to the interpretation of this Constitution shall be construed as including references to any substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Government of India Act, 1935...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 147 is an interpretive clause that clarifies what constitutes a substantial question of law regarding constitutional interpretation.

It states that this definition includes legal questions regarding older constitutional documents like the Government of India Act, 1935, or subsequent Orders in Council, allowing the Supreme Court to interpret historical statutory lineages that affect modern constitutional rights.

landmarkCase.citation: Garikapati Veeraya v. N. Subbiah Choudhry (1957)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court used this interpretation clause to clarify how legal rights derived from pre-constitutional statutes continue under the current constitutional framework.

articles.title: Comptroller and Auditor-General of India
articles.officialText: (1) There shall be a Comptroller and Auditor-General of India who shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal and shall only be removed from office in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article establishes the office of the Comptroller and Auditor-General (CAG) of India, the independent guardian of the public purse. The CAG monitors public expenditures and audits the accounts of the Union and the States.

To protect this office from political pressure, the Constitution grants the CAG security of tenure; they can only be removed through the same rigorous process applied to a Supreme Court judge, and they are barred from holding further government office after retirement.

landmarkCase.citation: Arvind Gupta v. Union of India (2013)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court dismissed challenges to the CAG's authority, confirming that the CAG has the mandate to run performance audits to ensure public funds are spent efficiently.

articles.title: Duties and powers of the Comptroller and Auditor-General
articles.officialText: The Comptroller and Auditor-General shall perform such duties and exercise such powers in relation to the accounts of the Union and of the States and of any other authority or body as may be prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 149 outlines the primary duties and powers of the CAG, authorizing them to audit the financial transactions and accounts of the Union, the States, and other public bodies.

It leaves the specific details of these powers to be defined by parliamentary law, which was done through the CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, giving the office broad access to financial records.

landmarkCase.citation: Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2G Spectrum Case) (2012)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court relied heavily on the CAG's audit findings regarding financial losses to public funds, demonstrating the office's importance in maintaining accountability.

articles.title: Form of accounts of the Union and of the States
articles.officialText: The accounts of the Union and of the States shall be kept in such form as the President may, on the advice of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, prescribe.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article governs how public accounts are maintained across the country. It requires the financial accounts of the Union and State governments to be kept in a uniform format prescribed by the President.

Crucially, this format must be based on the expert advice of the CAG, ensuring that financial data is standardized and verifiable nationwide.

landmarkCase.citation: Arvind Gupta v. Union of India (2013)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that standardized accounting under Article 150 is essential for enabling accurate national audits and maintaining financial transparency.

articles.title: Audit reports
articles.officialText: (1) The reports of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India relating to the accounts of the Union shall be submitted to the President, who shall cause them to be laid before each House of Parliament...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
Article 151 details the reporting process for national audits. It requires the CAG to submit their formal audit reports on Union accounts to the President, who must then ensure they are laid before both houses of Parliament.

For state accounts, the CAG submits the reports to the respective Governor to be laid before the state legislature. This ensures that audit findings are made public and can be scrutinized by legislative Public Accounts Committees.

landmarkCase.citation: Ramdas Athawale v. Union of India (2010)
landmarkCase.summary: The court affirmed that presenting audit reports under Article 151 triggers legislative oversight, allowing Parliament to review and hold the executive accountable for public expenditures.

articles.title: Definition
articles.officialText: In this Part, unless the context otherwise requires, the expression 'State' does not include the State of Jammu and Kashmir.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article sets the geographic and political scope for Part VI of the Constitution, which establishes the governance structure for Indian States.
  • Historically, it explicitly excluded the State of Jammu and Kashmir due to its special status under Article 370. Following the 2019 constitutional reforms and the formal statutory reorganization, this historical exception has been functionally superseded, making the state-level machinery uniform across the territory of India.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Jammu & Kashmir v. Dr. Mohammad Aslam (2001)
landmarkCase.summary: The court examined the scope of Article 152 in relation to federal asymmetry, clarifying how the structural layout of Part VI applied strictly to standard states while skipping regions with distinct constitutional exemptions.

articles.title: Governors of States
articles.officialText: There shall be a Governor for each State: Provided that nothing in this article shall prevent the appointment of the same person as Governor for two or more States.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article creates the constitutional post of the Governor, who serves as the formal or nominal executive head of a State, mirroring the President's position at the Union level.
  • The proviso, added by the 7th Constitutional Amendment in 1956, offers administrative flexibility by permitting a single individual to be appointed as the Governor of two or more states simultaneously.

landmarkCase.citation: Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that the Governor's office is an independent constitutional post that is not under the control or subordinate to the Government of India, requiring a neutral and non-partisan discharge of duties.

articles.title: Executive power of State
articles.officialText: (1) The executive power of the State shall be vested in the Governor and shall be exercised by him either directly or through officers subordinate to him in accordance with this Constitution.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article vests all executive authority of a state government in the Governor, declaring that every official executive action taken by the state must be made in their name.
  • It establishes that the Governor can exercise this power either directly or via subordinate administrative bodies, but explicitly mandates that all such actions must strictly follow constitutional boundaries.

landmarkCase.citation: Samsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974)
landmarkCase.summary: A seven-judge bench firmly established that the Governor is a formal, constitutional head of state who must exercise their executive powers almost exclusively on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers.

articles.title: Appointment of Governor
articles.officialText: The Governor of a State shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article details the appointment process for the Governor, steering away from an elected model to prevent local political rivalries with the State's Chief Minister.
  • By vesting the appointment power directly in the President, the Constitution allows the Union executive to select the formal head of each state, emphasizing a strong centralized federal system.

landmarkCase.citation: B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court observed that while the President appoints the Governor on the advice of the Prime Minister, the Governor cannot be removed arbitrarily or for partisan political reasons without valid justification.

articles.title: Term of office of Governor
articles.officialText: (1) The Governor shall hold office during the pleasure of the President... (3) Subject to the foregoing provisions, a Governor shall hold office for a term of five years from the date on which he enters upon his office.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article sets the baseline tenure of a Governor at five years from the date they assume office, but subjects it entirely to the 'pleasure of the President'.
  • It provides that a Governor can resign early by addressing a letter to the President, and includes a continuity clause stating they will remain in office past five years until a successor takes over.

landmarkCase.citation: B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010)
landmarkCase.summary: The court held that 'the pleasure of the President' under Article 156(1) is not absolute or arbitrary; the removal of a Governor can be judicially reviewed if it is found to be based on bad faith or irrelevant political considerations.

articles.title: Qualifications for appointment as Governor
articles.officialText: No person shall be eligible for appointment as Governor unless he is a citizen of India and has completed the age of thirty-five years.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article establishes the two simple, baseline constitutional qualifications required for a candidate to be appointed as a State Governor.
  • The candidate must be an absolute citizen of India and must have completed a minimum age of thirty-five years, avoiding complex legislative or judicial prerequisites.

landmarkCase.citation: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
landmarkCase.summary: The court reviewed the role of the Governor, noting that satisfying the basic criteria of Article 157 qualifies an individual for an office that requires impartiality and high statesmanship in federal relations.

articles.title: Conditions of Governor's office
articles.officialText: (1) The Governor shall not be a member of either House of Parliament or of a House of the Legislature of any State... (2) The Governor shall not hold any other office of profit.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article guards the neutrality of the Governor's office by barring them from holding a seat in Parliament or any state legislature. If an active lawmaker is appointed, their seat automatically becomes vacant.
  • It explicitly prohibits the Governor from holding any other office of profit and ensures that their official emoluments, allowances, and residential privileges cannot be reduced during their tenure.

landmarkCase.citation: G.S. Dhillon v. State of Punjab (1976)
landmarkCase.summary: The court held that the operational conditions attached to the Governor's office under Article 158 protect it from commercial conflicts of interest and ensure complete independence from political ministries.

articles.title: Oath or affirmation by the Governor
articles.officialText: Every Governor and every person discharging the functions of the Governor shall, before entering upon his office, make and subscribe before the Chief Justice of the High Court... an oath or affirmation...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article outlines the constitutional oath or affirmation that a Governor must take, administered by the Chief Justice of the state's High Court.
  • The text binds the Governor to 'preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law' and to devote themselves to the service and welfare of the people of that State.

landmarkCase.citation: Hardwari Lal v. Bhajan Lal (1993)
landmarkCase.summary: The court highlighted that the Governor's oath under Article 159 mirrors the President's oath under Article 60, emphasizing their primary duty to preserve the rule of law over shifting regional political interests.

articles.title: Discharge of the functions of the Governor in certain contingencies
articles.officialText: The President may make such provision as he thinks fit for the discharge of the functions of the Governor of a State in any contingency not provided for in this Chapter.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article serves as a constitutional safety valve, giving the President the power to make temporary arrangements for running a state executive during unforeseen events.
  • For example, if a Governor passes away suddenly or is incapacitated and there is no active Vice-Governor, the President can authorize a neighboring Governor or the Chief Justice of the state High Court to temporarily step into the role.

landmarkCase.citation: In re Presidential Reference (1999)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court noted that Article 160 grants the Union executive the constitutional power to handle administrative emergencies at the state level without causing a breakdown of law and order.

articles.title: Power of Governor to grant pardons, etc., and to suspend, remit or commute sentences in certain cases
articles.officialText: The Governor of a State shall have the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment or to suspend, remit or commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offence against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the State extends.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article vests the Governor with executive clemency powers at the state level, allowing them to grant pardons, reprieves, remissions, or commutations of sentences.
  • This power applies strictly to offenses against laws that fall within the executive authority of the State (State List and Concurrent List), providing an administrative check on judicial errors.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Haryana v. Rajkumar (2021)
