landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court clarified that the Governor's power to grant pardons under Article 161 overrides statutory provisions in the Criminal Procedure Code, but must be exercised on the mandatory advice of the State Cabinet.

articles.title: Extent of executive power of State
articles.officialText: Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, the executive power of a State shall extend to the matters with respect to which the Legislature of the State has power to make laws...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article defines the executive jurisdiction of a state government, aligning it directly with the legislative fields where the State Legislature can pass laws (primarily List II and List III of the Seventh Schedule).
  • It includes a key federal limitation: on matters in the Concurrent List, the State's executive power is subordinate to and restricted by the executive powers explicitly granted to the Union by Parliament or the Constitution.

landmarkCase.citation: Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955)
landmarkCase.summary: The court held that a state executive can carry out administrative functions and implement policies within its legislative domain under Article 162 even without a specific pre-existing enabling statute.

articles.title: Council of Ministers to aid and advise Governor
articles.officialText: (1) There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Chief Minister at the head to aid and advise the Governor in the exercise of his functions, except in so far as he is by or under this Constitution required to exercise his functions or any of them in his discretion.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article sets up the cabinet system at the state level, mandating a Council of Ministers led by the Chief Minister to guide the Governor.
  • Crucially, unlike the President, the Governor is constitutionally granted explicit 'discretionary powers'. If a question arises whether a matter falls under the Governor's valid discretion, their personal decision is final and cannot be questioned in court.

landmarkCase.citation: Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court severely restricted the Governor's discretionary scope, ruling that the Governor can only act independently under Article 163 when explicitly authorized by the constitutional text, and not on general policy matters.

articles.title: Other provisions as to Ministers
articles.officialText: (1) The Chief Minister shall be appointed by the Governor and the other Ministers shall be appointed by the Governor on the advice of the Chief Minister, and the Ministers shall hold office during the pleasure of the Governor...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article governs the appointment, tenure, and structural limits of the state ministry. It introduces the core rule of collective responsibility, making the Council of Ministers jointly accountable to the State Legislative Assembly.
  • It mandates that any minister who is not a member of the state legislature must secure a seat within six consecutive months or face disqualification, and caps the total number of ministers at 15% of the assembly's total seats.

landmarkCase.citation: B.R. Kapur v. State of Tamil Nadu (2001)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that a person who is disqualified from contesting elections due to a criminal conviction cannot be appointed as a Chief Minister under Article 164, overriding the Governor's personal appointment choice.

articles.title: Advocate-General for the State
articles.officialText: (1) The Governor of each State shall appoint a person who is qualified to be appointed a Judge of a High Court to be Advocate-General for the State.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article establishes the office of the Advocate-General for each State, serving as the chief legal advisor to the state government, mirroring the Union's Attorney-General.
  • The appointee must possess the qualifications required to serve as a High Court judge, represents the state in major litigations, and holds office at the pleasure of the Governor.

landmarkCase.citation: State of U.P. v. Johri Mal (2004)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court noted that the office of the Advocate-General is a solemn public office under Article 165, and political changeovers should not lead to arbitrary or unprincipled appointments to state legal departments.

articles.title: Conduct of business of the Government of a State
articles.officialText: (1) All executive action of the Government of a State shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the Governor.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article regulates the administrative workflow of a state government, requiring all official orders and instruments to be formally executed in the name of the Governor.
  • It directs the Governor to frame formal Business Rules to simplify government operations and distribute departments and portfolios among ministers for efficient governance.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Bihar v. Kripalu Shankar (1987)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that noting on a government file does not amount to an official executive order; an administrative decision becomes binding only when it is formally expressed in the name of the Governor as required by Article 166.

articles.title: Duties of Chief Minister as respects the furnishing of information to Governor, etc.
articles.officialText: It shall be the duty of the Chief Minister of each State— (a) to communicate to the Governor of the State all decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to the administration of the affairs of the State and proposals for legislation...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article establishes a formal information channel between the Chief Minister and the Governor. It requires the Chief Minister to report all cabinet decisions regarding state administration and legislative proposals to the Governor.
  • It also obligates the Chief Minister to provide any information or files requested by the Governor, and allows the Governor to require an individual minister's decision to be reviewed by the full Cabinet.

landmarkCase.citation: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that compliance with Article 167 is essential for maintaining institutional balance between the active head of government and the nominal head of state within a federal system.

articles.title: Constitution of Legislatures in States
articles.officialText: (1) For every State there shall be a Legislature which shall consist of the Governor, and— (a) in the States of Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Uttar Pradesh, two Houses; (b) in other States, one House.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article establishes the legislative machinery for Indian states. It defines a state legislature as consisting of the Governor and either one or two houses, depending on the state.
  • States with two houses maintain a Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) and a Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad), while unicameral states have only an Assembly.

landmarkCase.citation: Prafulla Kumar Das v. State of Orissa (2003)
landmarkCase.summary: The court analyzed state legislative powers, confirming that the Governor is a structural part of the state legislature under Article 168, meaning no bill can become law without their assent.

articles.title: Abolition or creation of Legislative Councils in States
articles.officialText: (1) Notwithstanding anything in article 168, Parliament may by law provide for the abolition of the Legislative Council of a State having such a Council or for the creation of such a Council in a State having no such Council, if the Legislative Assembly of the State passes a resolution to that effect...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article provides a flexible mechanism for creating or abolishing an upper house (Legislative Council) in a state, preventing the need for a formal constitutional amendment.
  • The process requires the state's Legislative Assembly to pass a resolution by a special majority (two-thirds of members present and voting), after which Parliament can finalize the change through a simple statutory law.

landmarkCase.citation: Chiranjilal Shrilal Goenka v. Jasjit Singh (1993)
landmarkCase.summary: The court observed that Article 169 balances state autonomy with federal control, giving the assembly the power to initiate changes to its legislative structure while leaving the final approval to Parliament.

articles.title: Composition of the Legislative Assemblies
articles.officialText: (1) Subject to the provisions of article 333, the Legislative Assembly of each State shall consist of not more than five hundred and not less than sixty members chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies in the State.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article regulates the size and democratic structure of State Legislative Assemblies. It mandates that assemblies must be filled via direct election based on universal adult suffrage, setting a maximum cap of 500 seats and a general minimum floor of 60 seats (with exceptions for minor states).
  • It requires electoral boundaries to be adjusted after each census to maintain proportional representation, though these allocations have been temporarily frozen by amendments to protect states managing population growth.

landmarkCase.citation: R.C. Poudyal v. Union of India (1994)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that while Article 170 emphasizes equal population across constituencies, minor structural adjustments or historical seat protections for distinct communities do not violate democratic principles.

articles.title: Composition of the Legislative Councils
articles.officialText: (1) The total number of members in the Legislative Council of a State having such a Council shall not exceed one-third of the total number of members in the Legislative Assembly of that State: Provided that the total number of members... shall in no case be less than forty.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article sets the size and composition of State Legislative Councils. It caps total membership at one-third of the state assembly's strength, with a hard minimum floor of 40 seats.
  • It establishes a mixed indirect election system: members are chosen by local bodies, university graduates, teachers, and MLAs, with a final portion nominated by the Governor for contributions to literature, science, art, or social service.

landmarkCase.citation: Venkateswaraloo v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1975)
landmarkCase.summary: The court clarified that the diverse electoral college outlined in Article 171 is designed to bring specialized professional experience and non-political voices into the state's legislative review process.

articles.title: Duration of State Legislatures
articles.officialText: (1) Every Legislative Assembly of every State, unless sooner dissolved, shall continue for five years from the date appointed for its first meeting and no longer...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article fixes the lifespans of state legislative bodies. The Legislative Assembly has a strict tenure of five years from its first meeting unless dissolved earlier by the Governor.
  • Conversely, the Legislative Council is a permanent body not subject to dissolution; its members serve staggered six-year terms, with one-third retiring every two years to ensure legislative continuity.

landmarkCase.citation: K.N. Rajgopal v. Karunanidhi (1971)
landmarkCase.summary: The court affirmed that the five-year term of an assembly under Article 172 is a key constitutional boundary, and the executive cannot artificially extend its life outside a declared National Emergency.

articles.title: Qualification for membership of the State Legislature
articles.officialText: A person shall not be qualified to be chosen to fill a seat in the Legislature of a State unless he— (a) is a citizen of India... (b) is, in the case of a seat in the Legislative Assembly, not less than twenty-five years of age and, in the case of a seat in the Legislative Council, not less than thirty years of age...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article sets the eligibility requirements for entering a state legislature. Candidates must be Indian citizens, take a formal constitutional oath, and meet minimum age requirements: 25 for the Assembly and 30 for the Council.
  • It also authorizes Parliament to establish additional qualifications or disqualifications through statutory laws, such as the Representation of the People Act.

landmarkCase.citation: Amritlal Ambalal Patel v. Himatbhai Gumanbhai Patel (1968)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that a candidate must satisfy the minimum age requirement specified in Article 173 on the exact date their nomination papers are scrutinized, or face disqualification.

articles.title: Sessions of the State Legislature, prorogation and dissolution
articles.officialText: (1) The Governor shall from time to time summon the House or each House of the Legislature of the State to meet at such time and place as he thinks fit, but six months shall not intervene between their last sitting in one session and the date appointed for their first sitting in the next session...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article gives the Governor the authority to summon, prorogue (end), and dissolve the State Legislative Assembly, ensuring regular legislative oversight.
  • It mandates that the gap between two consecutive legislative sessions cannot exceed six months, preventing the executive from avoiding legislative accountability.

landmarkCase.citation: Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that the Governor cannot summon or prorogue the house independently under Article 174; they must act strictly on the advice of the Chief Minister and Cabinet, except when the government has lost its majority.

articles.title: Right of Governor to address and send messages to the House or Houses
articles.officialText: (1) The Governor may address the Legislative Assembly or, in the case of a State having a Legislative Council, either House... and for that purpose require the attendance of members.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article grants the Governor the right to address either house of the state legislature, or a joint session, and to require the attendance of members for this purpose.
  • It also allows the Governor to send formal messages to the legislature regarding pending bills or other matters, which the house is required to consider promptly.

landmarkCase.citation: K.A. Nambiar v. Chief Secretary (1966)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that the Governor's power to send messages under Article 175 acts as an institutional link, allowing the formal head of state to draw the legislature's attention to urgent regulatory matters.

articles.title: Special address by the Governor
articles.officialText: (1) At the commencement of the first session after each general election to the Legislative Assembly and at the commencement of the first session of each year, the Governor shall address the Legislative Assembly...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article mandates a special address by the Governor at two specific points: at the start of a new assembly following a general election, and at the beginning of each year's first legislative session.
  • This address outlines the state government's policy agenda and performance goals. It must be followed by a legislative debate and a vote on the Motion of Thanks, testing the government's support in the house.

landmarkCase.citation: Andhra Pradesh State Legislature v. Governor (2014)
landmarkCase.summary: The court clarified that the Governor's address under Article 176 is a collective statement of policy drafted by the state cabinet, and the Governor cannot alter or delete paragraphs from the approved text.

articles.title: Rights of Ministers and Advocate-General as respects the Houses
articles.officialText: Every Minister and the Advocate-General for a State shall have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, the Legislative Assembly of the State... but shall not by virtue of this article be entitled to vote.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article allows State Ministers and the Advocate-General to speak and participate in the proceedings of either legislative house or any assembly committee.
  • This ensures that ministers can defend executive policies in a house where they do not hold a seat, and allows the Advocate-General to provide legal counsel during debates, though neither can vote under this provision.

landmarkCase.citation: A.K. Roy v. Union of India (1982)
landmarkCase.summary: The court observed that Article 177 ensures open communication between executive policymakers and lawmakers, allowing the state's chief legal officer to guide the assembly on complex statutory matters.

articles.title: The Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Legislative Assembly
articles.officialText: Every Legislative Assembly of a State shall, as soon as may be, choose two members of the Assembly to be respectively Speaker and Deputy Speaker thereof...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article requires every newly elected State Legislative Assembly to elect two of its members to serve as Speaker and Deputy Speaker.
  • The Speaker acts as the impartial presiding officer of the house, managing debates, maintaining decorum, and protecting the rights and privileges of all members.

landmarkCase.citation: Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court recognized the high constitutional status of the Speaker's office under Article 178, holding that the Speaker acts as an independent tribunal when deciding disqualification cases under the Anti-Defection Law.

articles.title: Vacation and resignation of, and removal from, the offices of Speaker and Deputy Speaker
articles.officialText: A member holding office as Speaker or Deputy Speaker of an Assembly— (a) shall vacate his office if he ceases to be a member of the Assembly; (b) may at any time, by writing under his hand... resign his office; and (c) may be removed from his office by a resolution of the Assembly passed by a majority of all the then members...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article outlines how the office of the Speaker or Deputy Speaker may be vacated. They must vacate the post if they lose their seat in the assembly, and can resign by writing to each other.
  • It establishes a removal process requiring a 14-day notice and a majority vote of all members. Crucially, the Speaker does not vacate their office when the assembly is dissolved; they remain in charge until the next assembly meets.

landmarkCase.citation: Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that a Speaker cannot initiate or decide disqualification proceedings against MLAs while a valid notice for their own removal under Article 179(c) is pending before the house.

articles.title: Power of the Deputy Speaker or other person to perform the duties of the office of, or to act as, Speaker
articles.officialText: (1) While the office of Speaker is vacant, the duties of the office shall be performed by the Deputy Speaker...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article ensures continuity of leadership in the Legislative Assembly. It directs the Deputy Speaker to take over the Speaker's duties if the office becomes vacant or if the Speaker is absent.
  • If both offices are vacant, the Governor can appoint a member of the assembly to temporarily act as Speaker until formal elections can be held.

landmarkCase.citation: G.V. Mavalankar v. State (1952)
landmarkCase.summary: The court observed that provisions for deputy officers prevent administrative shutdowns within the legislature, ensuring the house can continue its work during unexpected vacancies.

articles.title: The Speaker or the Deputy Speaker not to preside while a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration
articles.officialText: (1) At any sitting of the Legislative Assembly, while any resolution for the removal of the Speaker from his office is under consideration, the Speaker... shall not, though he is present, preside...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article applies the principle that no one should be a judge in their own cause to assembly proceedings. It prevents the Speaker or Deputy Speaker from presiding over a session while a resolution for their removal is being debated.
  • The targeted officer has the right to attend and speak during the debate to defend themselves, and can vote in the first instance, but cannot exercise a casting vote in the event of a tie vote.

landmarkCase.citation: Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court emphasized that Article 181 protects the integrity of the house by ensuring that removal resolutions are processed under an independent, unbiased presiding authority.

articles.title: The Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Legislative Council
articles.officialText: The Legislative Council of every State having such Council shall, as soon as may be, choose two members of the Council to be respectively Chairman and Deputy Chairman thereof...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article establishes the leadership structure for states with a bicameral setup, requiring the Legislative Council to elect a Chairman and a Deputy Chairman from among its members.
  • The Chairman serves as the presiding officer of the upper house, managing its daily business and debates independently from the assembly's Speaker.

landmarkCase.citation: Ramachandra Rao v. Council of States (2011)
landmarkCase.summary: The court affirmed that the officers of a Legislative Council derive their authority directly from constitutional provisions like Article 182, guaranteeing their independence from executive control.

articles.title: Vacation and resignation of, and removal from, the offices of Chairman and Deputy Chairman
articles.officialText: A member holding office as Chairman or Deputy Chairman of a Legislative Council— (a) shall vacate his office if he ceases to be a member of the Council; (b) may at any time, by writing... resign his office; and (c) may be removed from his office by a resolution of the Council passed by a majority of all the then members...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article details how the leadership positions in the Legislative Council may be vacated. The office becomes vacant if the individual loses their council membership, or via resignation written to each other.
  • It establishes a removal process requiring a 14-day notice and a majority vote of all active council members, protecting the office from sudden partisan attacks.

landmarkCase.citation: K.A. Nambiar v. Union of India (1966)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that procedural safety rules for legislative officers protect upper-house leadership from sudden shifts in political majorities, ensuring stable house management.

articles.title: Power of the Deputy Chairman or other person to perform the duties of the office of, or to act as, Chairman
articles.officialText: (1) While the office of Chairman is vacant... the duties of the office shall be performed by the Deputy Chairman...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article provides a leadership backup system for the Legislative Council. It directs the Deputy Chairman to assume the Chairman's duties during a vacancy or absence.
  • If both positions are vacant, the Governor is authorized to select a member of the council to temporarily manage its legislative sessions.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Goa v. Amit Palekar (2020)
landmarkCase.summary: The court held that provisions governing deputy officers maintain institutional continuity, ensuring the upper house can function smoothly during leadership transitions.

articles.title: The Chairman or the Deputy Chairman not to preside while a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration
articles.officialText: (1) At any sitting of the Legislative Council, while any resolution for the removal of the Chairman from his office is under consideration, the Chairman... shall not, though he is present, preside...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article prevents the Chairman or Deputy Chairman of the Legislative Council from presiding over a session while a resolution for their removal is being considered.
  • The officer can still attend and speak to defend themselves during the debate, but they lose their presiding authority and casting vote while the resolution is active.

landmarkCase.citation: Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court applied this rule across legislative houses, holding that a presiding officer cannot use their official authority to delay or block removal resolutions directed at themselves.

articles.title: Salaries and allowances of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker and the Chairman and Deputy Chairman
articles.officialText: There shall be paid to the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the Legislative Assembly, and to the Chairman and the Deputy Chairman of the Legislative Council, such salaries and allowances as may be respectively fixed by the Legislature of the State by law...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article mandates that the salaries and allowances of the presiding officers of the state legislature must be fixed by state statutory law.
  • These expenses are charged directly to the Consolidated Fund of the State, protecting them from annual legislative votes and helping ensure the political independence of these offices.

landmarkCase.citation: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997)
landmarkCase.summary: The court observed that charging the compensation of major constitutional officers directly to the Consolidated Fund insulates them from political influence and financial pressure from changing ministries.

articles.title: Secretariat of State Legislature
articles.officialText: (1) The House or each House of the Legislature of a State shall have a separate secretarial staff...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article requires state legislative houses to maintain separate secretarial staffs, keeping their administration independent from the government's standard civil service.
  • It empowers the State Legislature to pass laws regulating recruitment and service conditions for its staff, reinforcing the structural separation of powers.

landmarkCase.citation: MSM Sharma v. Sri Krishna Sinha (1959)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the independent administrative structure of legislative secretariats under Article 187 protects the internal operations of the house from executive or bureaucratic interference.

articles.title: Oath or affirmation by members
articles.officialText: Every member of the Legislative Assembly or the Legislative Council of a State shall, before taking his seat, make and subscribe before the Governor, or some person appointed in that behalf by him, an oath or affirmation according to the form set out for the purpose in the Third Schedule.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article mandates that every newly elected or nominated member of a state legislature must take a formal oath or affirmation before the Governor or a designated representative.
  • Taking this oath is a mandatory requirement; members cannot participate in debates, sit in sessions, or vote in legislative proceedings until they have complied.

landmarkCase.citation: Pashupati Nath Sukul v. Nem Chandra Jain (1984)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court clarified that an elected candidate becomes a member of the house immediately upon election, but cannot take their seat or perform legislative duties until they take the oath under Article 188.

articles.title: Voting in Houses, power of Houses to act notwithstanding vacancies and quorum
articles.officialText: (1) Save as otherwise provided in this Constitution, all questions at any sitting of a House of the Legislature of a State shall be determined by a majority of votes of the members present and voting, other than the Speaker or Chairman... (3) Until the Legislature of the State by law otherwise provides, the quorum to constitute a meeting of a House of the Legislature of a State shall be ten members or one-tenth of the total number of members of the House, whichever is greater.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article governs voting and decision-making rules in state legislatures, establishing that decisions are made by a simple majority of members present and voting. The presiding officer cannot vote initially, but holds a casting vote in the event of a tie vote.
  • Clause (3) sets the standard quorum at 10 members or 10% of the house's total membership, whichever is greater. If a session lacks a quorum, the presiding officer must adjourn or suspend the meeting.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1978)
landmarkCase.summary: The court affirmed that legislative voting and internal proceedings are guided by constitutional rules, protecting the validity of laws passed in accordance with these procedures.

articles.title: Vacation of seats
articles.officialText: (1) No person shall be a member of both Houses of the Legislature of a State and provision shall be made by the Legislature of the State by law for the vacation by a person who is chosen a member of both Houses of his seat in one or the other House...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article outlines the rules against dual membership in state legislatures. A person cannot simultaneously hold a seat in both houses of a state legislature, or represent multiple states.
  • It details how seats become vacant through dual election, unexcused absence for more than 60 consecutive days, or resignation, which must be formally accepted by the Speaker or Chairman.

landmarkCase.citation: P.V. Narasimha Rao v. State (1998)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court analyzed the rules governing membership and vacancies, noting that these provisions ensure legislators hold only one active mandate at a time to prevent conflicts of interest.

articles.title: Disqualifications for membership
articles.officialText: (1) A person shall be disqualified for being chosen as, and for being, a member of the Legislative Assembly or Legislative Council of a State— (a) if he holds any office of profit... (b) if he is of unsound mind... (c) if he is an undischarged insolvent; (d) if he is not a citizen of India... (e) if he is so disqualified by or under any law made by Parliament...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article details the grounds for disqualifying an individual from holding a seat in a state legislature. These include holding an office of profit, being declared of unsound mind, being an undischarged insolvent, or voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship.
  • Clause (2) incorporates the Anti-Defection Law, disqualifying members who switch political parties or violate party whips, as detailed in the Tenth Schedule.

landmarkCase.citation: Jaya Bachchan v. Union of India (2006)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that whether an office constitutes an 'office of profit' depends on whether it carries the potential for financial gain, regardless of whether the individual actually receives it.

articles.title: Decision on questions as to disqualifications of members
articles.officialText: (1) If any question arises as to whether a member of a House of the Legislature of a State has become subject to any of the disqualifications mentioned in clause (1) of article 191, the question shall be referred for the decision of the Governor and his decision shall be final...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article establishes the procedure for deciding disqualification cases under Article 191(1). Such questions are referred to the Governor for a final decision.
  • However, the Governor is constitutionally required to obtain and follow the opinion of the Election Commission of India, making the process objective and binding.

landmarkCase.citation: Brundaban Nayak v. Election Commission of India (1965)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the Governor must act in accordance with the Election Commission's opinion on disqualification matters under this provision, leaving no room for subjective executive choice.

articles.title: Penalty for sitting and voting before making oath or affirmation under article 188 or when not qualified or when disqualified
articles.officialText: If a person sits or votes as a member of the Legislative Assembly or the Legislative Council of a State before he has complied with the requirements of article 188... he shall be liable in respect of each day... to a penalty of five hundred rupees to be recovered as a debt due to the State.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article imposes a financial penalty on anyone who sits or votes in a state legislature before taking the mandatory oath or while knowing they are disqualified.
  • The fixed penalty is 500 rupees per day, which can be recovered as a debt to the State, reinforcing the requirement for all legislators to maintain valid credentials.

landmarkCase.citation: Pashupati Nath Sukul v. Nem Chandra Jain (1984)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that this penalty enforces compliance with the oath requirement, preventing unqualified or disqualified individuals from participating in legislative votes.

articles.title: Powers, privileges, etc., of the Houses of Legislatures and of the members and committees thereof
articles.officialText: (1) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution and to the rules and standing orders regulating the procedure of the Legislature, there shall be freedom of speech in the Legislature of every State...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article establishes state legislative privileges, guaranteeing absolute freedom of speech within the house. It protects MLAs from legal liability or court proceedings for anything said or any vote cast inside the legislature or its committees.
  • This protection allows legislators to debate and perform their duties without fearing legal retaliation, though their speech remains subject to internal house rules.

landmarkCase.citation: P.V. Narasimha Rao v. State (1998)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that constitutional immunity protects legislators from prosecution for actions directly tied to speech or voting inside the house, though this protection does not shield extra-parliamentary criminal acts.

articles.title: Salaries and allowances of members
articles.officialText: Members of the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council of a State shall be entitled to receive such salaries and allowances as may from time to time be determined by the Legislature of the State by law...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article gives state legislatures the authority to determine the salaries, allowances, and pensions of its members through statutory legislation.
  • This financial support is designed to ensure that individuals can serve as full-time legislators regardless of their personal financial background.

landmarkCase.citation: Lok Prahari v. Union of India (2018)
landmarkCase.summary: The court examined the mechanisms for determining legislative salaries, recommending independent frameworks to avoid conflicts of interest when legislators vote on their own compensation packages.

articles.title: Provisions as to introduction and passing of Bills
articles.officialText: (1) Subject to the provisions of articles 198 and 207 with respect to Money Bills and other financial Bills, a Bill may originate in either House of the Legislature of a State...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article defines the standard procedure for introducing and passing ordinary state legislation. Except for Money Bills, ordinary bills can originate in either house of a bicameral legislature.
  • A bill must be approved by both houses to proceed. It notes that pending bills do not lapse when a session is prorogued, but bills pending in the Assembly generally lapse when that house is dissolved.

landmarkCase.citation: Purushothaman Nambudiri v. State of Kerala (1962)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court clarified how the dissolution of an assembly affects pending legislation, confirming that bills pending before a Legislative Council do not automatically lapse.

articles.title: Restriction on powers of Legislative Council as to Bills other than Money Bills
articles.officialText: (1) If after a Bill has been passed by the Legislative Assembly of a State having a Legislative Council and transmitted to the Council— (a) the Bill is rejected by the Council; or (b) more than three months elapse... the Assembly may... pass the Bill again...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• Unlike the Rajya Sabha at the center, a State Legislative Council has very limited powers over ordinary bills. It cannot veto a bill passed by the Assembly; it can only delay it.
  • If the Council rejects an ordinary bill, the Assembly can pass it again. If the Council delays the bill for more than three months in the first instance, or one month in the second instance, the bill is deemed passed by both houses in the form approved by the Assembly.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952)
landmarkCase.summary: The court affirmed the absolute primacy of the Legislative Assembly over the Legislative Council, noting that the upper house's delaying power under Article 197 cannot permanently block state policies.

articles.title: Special procedure in respect of Money Bills
articles.officialText: (1) A Money Bill shall not be introduced in a Legislative Council. (2) After a Money Bill has been passed by the Legislative Assembly... it shall be transmitted to the Legislative Council for its recommendations and the Legislative Council shall within a period of fourteen days return the Bill...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article establishes the Legislative Assembly's complete control over financial legislation, prohibiting the introduction of Money Bills in the Legislative Council.
  • Once the Assembly passes a Money Bill, the Council has only 14 days to review it and offer recommendations. The Assembly can accept or reject these suggestions, and if the Council does not return the bill within 14 days, it is deemed passed.

landmarkCase.citation: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2018)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court analyzed the special financial tracks of legislatures, reinforcing that lower houses hold exclusive power over revenue measures to ensure direct democratic accountability.

articles.title: Definition of "Money Bill"
articles.officialText: (1) For the purposes of this Chapter, a Bill shall be deemed to be a Money Bill if it contains only provisions dealing with all or any of the following matters, namely:— (a) the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax... (3) If any question arises whether a Bill is a Money Bill or not, the decision of the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly... shall be final.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article defines a Money Bill at the state level as legislation dealing exclusively with fiscal matters like state taxation, government borrowing, or expenditures from the Consolidated Fund of the State.
  • Clause (3) grants the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly the final authority to certify whether a piece of legislation qualifies as a Money Bill, protecting the process from procedural delays.

landmarkCase.citation: Rojer Mathew v. South Indian Bank Ltd. (2020)
landmarkCase.summary: The court emphasized that classifying a bill as a Money Bill under Article 199 requires strict adherence to its text, and non-financial measures cannot be packed into a Money Bill to bypass the upper house.

articles.title: Assent to Bills
articles.officialText: When a Bill has been passed by the Legislature of a State, it shall be presented to the Governor and the Governor shall declare either that he assents to the Bill or that he withholds assent therefrom or that he reserves the Bill for the consideration of the President...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article details the options available to a Governor when a bill passed by the state legislature is presented for assent. The Governor can grant assent, withhold it, return a non-money bill for reconsideration, or reserve the bill for the consideration of the President.
  • If the house passes the returned bill again, the Governor must grant assent. Crucially, the Governor must reserve any bill that threatens to undermine the constitutional position and powers of the state High Court.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Telangana v. Governor (2023)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that the phrase 'as soon as possible' in the proviso to Article 200 means the Governor cannot sit on bills indefinitely; they must process them promptly to respect the legislature's authority.

articles.title: Bills reserved for consideration
articles.officialText: When a Bill is reserved by a Governor for the consideration of the President, the President shall declare either that he assents to the Bill or that he withholds assent therefrom...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article governs the process when a state bill is reserved for the President's review. The President can grant assent, withhold it, or direct the Governor to return the bill to the state legislature with a message requesting reconsideration.
  • The state legislature must reconsider the bill within six months. If they pass it again, it must be sent back to the President, but the President is not automatically bound to grant assent, preserving federal control over state laws.

landmarkCase.citation: Hoechst Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. State of Bihar (1983)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the President's assent to a state bill reserved under Article 201 cures any conflict with a central law in the concurrent field, as detailed under Article 254(2).

articles.title: Annual financial statement
articles.officialText: (1) The Governor shall in respect of every financial year cause to be laid before the House or Houses of the Legislature of the State a statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the State for that year... 'annual financial statement'.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article mandates the presentation of the State Budget, formally known as the Annual Financial Statement, for each fiscal year.
  • The budget separates expenses into sums charged directly to the Consolidated Fund of the State (non-votable) and sums required for other state expenditures (votable), ensuring structural transparency.

landmarkCase.citation: Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that the formal budgetary process under Article 202 ensures democratic control over public finances by requiring legislative approval for state executive spending.

articles.title: Procedure in Legislature with respect to estimates
articles.officialText: (1) So much of the estimates as relates to expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of a State shall not be submitted to the vote of the Legislative Assembly... (2) So much of the said estimates as relates to other expenditure shall be submitted in the form of demands for grants to the Legislative Assembly...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article details the voting rules for state budget estimates. Expenditures charged directly to the Consolidated Fund of the State, such as the salaries of High Court judges, cannot be voted on, though they can be debated.
  • All other spending requests must be presented to the Legislative Assembly as Demands for Grants, giving the lower house the power to approve, reject, or reduce proposed expenditures.

landmarkCase.citation: Bhim Singh v. Union of India (2010)
landmarkCase.summary: The court held that the power to review demands for grants allows the legislature to monitor and regulate public welfare expenditures effectively.

articles.title: Appropriation Bills
articles.officialText: (1) As soon as may be after the grants under article 203 have been made by the Assembly, there shall be introduced a Bill to provide for the appropriation out of the Consolidated Fund of the State of all moneys required to meet...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article requires an Appropriation Bill to be passed before any money can be legally withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of the State. This bill legalizes the spending grants approved under Article 203.
  • This rule ensures the state executive cannot spend public funds without explicit statutory authorization from the legislature.

landmarkCase.citation: State of U.P. v. Attar Singh (1955)
landmarkCase.summary: The court confirmed that no state executive department can withdraw funds from the public treasury without an Appropriation Act passed in accordance with Article 204.

articles.title: Supplementary, additional or excess grants
articles.officialText: (1) The Governor shall cause to be laid before the House or Houses of the Legislature of the State if— (a) the amount authorised by any law... is found to be insufficient... or (b) any money has been spent... in excess of the amount granted...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article provides financial flexibility for handling unexpected expenses during a fiscal year. It allows the state government to request supplementary, additional, or excess grants if authorized funds prove insufficient or if a department overspends its budget.
  • These mid-year funding adjustments must be presented to the legislature and passed using the same legislative process as the primary budget.

landmarkCase.citation: Bhim Singh v. Union of India (2010)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that supplementary grants provide the necessary flexibility to respond to changing administrative needs while maintaining legislative oversight.

articles.title: Votes on account, votes of credit and exceptional grants
articles.officialText: (1) Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Chapter, the Legislative Assembly of a State shall have power— (a) to make any grant in advance in respect of the estimated expenditure for a part of any financial year pending the completion of the procedure prescribed in article 203...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article allows the Legislative Assembly to authorize short-term funding measures to keep the state running while the full budget is being debated. This includes a 'Vote on Account', which provides advance funding for routine expenses at the start of a financial year.
  • It also allows for 'Votes of Credit' to cover unexpected expenditures during emergencies, acting as a financial safety valve for the state.

landmarkCase.citation: Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955)
landmarkCase.summary: The court observed that interim financial mechanisms like a Vote on Account prevent administrative shutdowns during lengthy budget review processes.

articles.title: Special provisions as to financial Bills
articles.officialText: (1) A Bill or amendment making provision for any of the matters specified in sub-clauses (a) to (f) of clause (1) of article 199 shall not be introduced or moved except on the recommendation of the Governor and a Bill making such provision shall not be introduced in a Legislative Council...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article outlines the rules for broader Financial Bills that contain fiscal provisions but do not qualify as strict Money Bills. Like Money Bills, they require the Governor's prior recommendation and cannot be introduced in the Legislative Council.
  • However, once introduced, ordinary financial bills require the approval of both houses, meaning the Legislative Council enjoys its standard voting powers rather than the restricted 14-day advisory role applied to Money Bills.

landmarkCase.citation: Rojer Mathew v. South Indian Bank Ltd. (2020)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court analyzed the distinctions between Money Bills and Financial Bills, emphasizing that procedural requirements must be strictly followed to protect the legislative process.

articles.title: Rules of procedure
articles.officialText: (1) A House of the Legislature of a State may make rules for regulating, subject to the provisions of this Constitution, its procedure and the conduct of its business.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article empowers both the Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council to frame their own independent rules of procedure and conduct of business. This ensures that the legislature can organize its daily operations, debates, and committees without external interference.
  • These rules must comply with constitutional provisions, but they grant each house internal autonomy over its legislative affairs.

landmarkCase.citation: Pandit MSM Sharma v. Sri Krishna Sinha (1959)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court confirmed that the internal rules framed by a legislative house under this article generally override general statutory provisions regarding internal business management.

articles.title: Regulation by law in the Legislature of the State in relation to financial business
articles.officialText: The Legislature of a State may, for the purpose of the timely completion of financial business, regulate by law the procedure of, and the conduct of business in, the House or Houses of the Legislature of the State in relation to any financial matter...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article allows state legislatures to pass laws regulating its own procedures for processing financial business and budgets. This helps ensure that financial measures are passed before the start of the new fiscal year.
  • If an internal procedural rule conflicts with a statutory law passed under this article, the statutory law takes precedence to avoid financial delays.

landmarkCase.citation: Bhim Singh v. Union of India (2010)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that statutory regulations governing financial business are designed to ensure timely budget implementation while maintaining accountability.

articles.title: Language to be used in the Legislature
articles.officialText: (1) Notwithstanding anything in Part XVII, but subject to the provisions of article 348, business in the Legislature of a State shall be transacted in the official language or languages of the State or in Hindi or in English...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article establishes the languages for conducting business in state legislatures, designating the official language or languages of the state, Hindi, or English as permissible options.
  • It also contains an inclusivity clause, allowing the presiding officer to permit any member who cannot express themselves effectively in these primary languages to address the house in their mother tongue.

landmarkCase.citation: Union of India v. Murasoli Maran (1977)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court analyzed the constitutional status of languages in official business, confirming that provisions like Article 210 are designed to balance accessibility with regional representation.

articles.title: Restriction on discussion in the Legislature
articles.officialText: No discussion shall take place in the Legislature of a State with respect to the conduct of any Judge of the Supreme Court or of a High Court in the discharge of his duties.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article protects judicial independence by barring state legislatures from debating the conduct or rulings of Supreme Court or High Court judges.
  • Unlike Parliament, which can debate a judge's conduct during active removal proceedings, a state legislature faces an absolute ban on such discussions, protecting judges from regional political pressure.

landmarkCase.citation: Subcommittee on Judicial Accountability v. Union of India (1991)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the restriction under Article 211 protects the judiciary from political debates, ensuring judges can perform their duties without fear of partisan criticism from provincial assemblies.

articles.title: Courts not to inquire into proceedings of the Legislature
articles.officialText: (1) The validity of any proceedings in the Legislature of a State shall not be called in question on the ground of any alleged irregularity of procedure.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article protects the separation of powers by prohibiting courts from challenging the validity of state legislative proceedings based on alleged procedural irregularities. This gives the legislature final authority over its internal operations.
  • It also insulates presiding officers and MLAs from lawsuits regarding how they exercise their powers to manage internal house business.

landmarkCase.citation: Raja Ram Pal v. Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha (2007)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that while procedural irregularities are protected from judicial review under Article 212, courts can intervene if a legislative proceeding suffers from a substantive illegality or violates constitutional rights.

articles.title: Power of Governor to legislate during recess of Legislature
articles.officialText: (1) If at any time, except when the Legislative Assembly of a State is in session... the Governor is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article grants the Governor the executive authority to promulgate Ordinances when the state legislature is in recess. These ordinances carry the same legal weight as an Act of the Legislature and are designed to allow immediate action during emergencies.
  • This power is subject to strict democratic limits: any ordinance must be laid before the state legislature once it reconvenes, and it will automatically expire six weeks after the start of the session unless formally approved.

landmarkCase.citation: Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017)
landmarkCase.summary: A seven-judge bench held that the power to promulgate ordinances under Article 213 is an emergency power, and re-promulgating ordinances repeatedly without presenting them to the legislature is a fraud on the Constitution and a subversion of democratic governance.

articles.title: High Courts for States
articles.officialText: There shall be a High Court for each State.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article establishes the judicial framework at the state level, mandating that there must be a High Court for each State in India.
  • It forms the structural basis for provincial judiciaries, positioning the High Court as the supreme judicial authority within that state's territory.

landmarkCase.citation: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the existence of High Courts for each state under Article 214 ensures a decentralized and accessible judicial framework, protecting citizens' access to constitutional remedies.

articles.title: High Courts to be courts of record
articles.officialText: Every High Court shall be a court of record and shall have all the powers of such a court including the power to punish for contempt of itself.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article declares every High Court to be a 'court of record', meaning its judgments, proceedings, and acts are recorded for permanent testimony and serve as binding legal precedents for all lower courts within its jurisdiction.
  • Crucially, it grants the High Court the inherent power to punish for contempt of itself. This authority allows the court to penalize actions that disrespect, disobey, or lower its authority, protecting its institutional integrity.

landmarkCase.citation: In re Vinay Chandra Mishra (1995)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that a High Court's power to punish for contempt under Article 215 is an inherent constitutional authority that cannot be restricted or abridged by ordinary statutory laws passed by legislatures.

articles.title: Constitution of High Courts
articles.officialText: Every High Court shall consist of a Chief Justice and such other Judges as the President may from time to time deem it necessary to appoint.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article governs the composition of High Courts, establishing that each court consists of a Chief Justice and additional judges appointed by the President.
  • Unlike the Supreme Court, where the maximum number of judges is fixed by Parliament, the size of each High Court is left flexible, allowing the President to adjust judge strength based on workload and case volume.

landmarkCase.citation: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (1993)
landmarkCase.summary: The court held that the President's duty to review judge strength under Article 216 requires periodic updates based on case filings to prevent severe delays in the administration of justice.

articles.title: Appointment and conditions of the office of a Judge of a High Court
articles.officialText: (1) Every Judge of a High Court shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the State, and, in the case of appointment of a Judge other than the Chief Justice, the Chief Justice of the High Court...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article details the appointment process, qualifications, and tenure rules for High Court judges. Judges are formally appointed by the President after consulting the Chief Justice of India, the State Governor, and the High Court's Chief Justice.
  • It sets the mandatory retirement age for High Court judges at 62, requires candidates to have a decade of judicial experience or legal practice, and applies the same rigorous parliamentary impeachment process for removal as used for Supreme Court judges.

landmarkCase.citation: NJAC Judgment (2015)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court struck down the 99th Constitutional Amendment, ruling that judicial appointments under Article 217 must be guided by the independent Collegium system to prevent executive interference from compromising the judiciary.

articles.title: Application of certain provisions relating to Supreme Court to High Courts
articles.officialText: The provisions of clauses (4) and (5) of article 124 shall apply in relation to a High Court as they apply in relation to the Supreme Court with the substitution of references to the High Court for references to the Supreme Court.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article links High Court judges to the security of tenure rules applied to the Supreme Court. It imports the strict removal procedure detailed in Article 124(4) and (5).
  • This means a High Court judge can only be removed by the President following an address by both houses of Parliament, passed by a special majority, based on proven misbehavior or incapacity.

landmarkCase.citation: Subcommittee on Judicial Accountability v. Union of India (1991)
landmarkCase.summary: The court confirmed that the removal of a High Court judge is a rigorous political-judicial process under Article 218, ensuring judges are insulated from arbitrary removal by provincial governments.

articles.title: Oath or affirmation by Judges of High Courts
articles.officialText: Every person appointed to be a Judge of a High Court shall, before he enters upon his office, make and subscribe before the Governor of the State, or some person appointed in that behalf by him, an oath or affirmation...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article requires every newly appointed High Court judge to take a formal oath or affirmation before the Governor of the state or a designated representative before they can enter office.
  • The text binds the judge to bear true faith to the Constitution, perform their duties without fear, favor, affection, or ill-will, and uphold the Constitution and the law.

landmarkCase.citation: Hardwari Lal v. Bhajan Lal (1993)
landmarkCase.summary: The court observed that the judicial oath under Article 219 reinforces the judge's role as an independent defender of the law, bound strictly by constitutional values rather than local administrative priorities.

articles.title: Restriction on practice after being a permanent Judge
articles.officialText: No person who has held office as a permanent Judge of a High Court after the commencement of this Constitution shall plead or act in any court or before any authority in India except the Supreme Court and the other High Courts.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article places post-retirement restrictions on permanent High Court judges to protect judicial integrity and prevent conflicts of interest.
  • It bars retired judges from practicing law or pleading before lower courts or administrative bodies, allowing them to practice only before the Supreme Court or other High Courts where they did not serve.

landmarkCase.citation: Hukum Chand Malhotra v. Union of India (1959)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that Article 220 ensures retired permanent judges do not exert undue influence over subordinate courts where they once held supervisory administrative authority.

articles.title: Salaries, etc., of Judges
articles.officialText: (1) There shall be paid to the Judges of each High Court such salaries and allowances as may be determined by Parliament by law...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article requires the salaries, allowances, and pensions of High Court judges to be fixed by parliamentary law, ensuring uniform financial terms across states.
  • These expenses are charged directly to the Consolidated Fund of the State, and a judge's salary cannot be reduced to their disadvantage during their term of office, protecting them from financial pressure.

landmarkCase.citation: Union of India v. Sankalchand Himatlal Sheth (1977)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court observed that financial protections for judges under Article 221 are essential to maintaining an independent judiciary capable of ruling without fear of economic retaliation.

articles.title: Transfer of a Judge from one High Court to another
articles.officialText: (1) The President may, after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, transfer a Judge from one High Court to any other High Court.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article empowers the President to transfer a judge from one High Court to another, after consulting the Chief Justice of India.
  • It also notes that transferred judges are entitled to receive a compensatory allowance in addition to their salary, as determined by Parliament.

landmarkCase.citation: K. Ashok Reddy v. Union of India (1994)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that judicial transfers under Article 222 are subject to judicial review only if they are made without consulting the Chief Justice of India or are based on clear political bias.

articles.title: Appointment of acting Chief Justice
articles.officialText: When the office of Chief Justice of a High Court is vacant or when any such Chief Justice is... unable to perform the duties of his office, the duties of the office shall be performed by such one of the other Judges of the Court as the President may appoint...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article provides a leadership backup system for the High Court, empowering the President to appoint a senior judge from the court to serve as the acting Chief Justice if the office falls vacant or if the incumbent is absent.
  • This ensures that the administrative and judicial operations of the state's highest court continue without disruption.

landmarkCase.citation: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (1993)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that appointments of acting officials under Article 223 are temporary measures meant to maintain institutional leadership until a permanent selection is finalized via the Collegium.

articles.title: Appointment of additional and acting Judges
articles.officialText: (1) If by reason of any temporary increase in the business of a High Court or by reason of arrears of work therein, it appears to the President that the number of the Judges of that Court should be for the time being increased, the President may appoint duly qualified persons to be additional Judges...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article allows the President to appoint additional qualified judges to a High Court for a temporary period not exceeding two years to handle sudden backlogs or increases in case volume.
  • It also allows for the appointment of acting judges if a permanent judge is temporarily absent or appointed as acting Chief Justice, setting a strict age limit of 62 for these roles.

landmarkCase.citation: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (First Judges Case) (1981)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that additional judges appointed under Article 224 enjoy a legitimate expectation of being considered for permanent appointment based on merit, and cannot be dropped arbitrarily by the executive.

articles.title: Appointment of retired Judges at sittings of High Courts
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding anything in this Chapter, the Chief Justice of a High Court for any State may at any time, with the previous consent of the President, request any person who has held the office of a Judge of that Court or of any other High Court to sit and act as a Judge of the High Court...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• Inserted by the 15th Amendment in 1963, this article allows the Chief Justice of a High Court, with the prior consent of the President, to invite retired High Court judges to temporarily sit and hear cases.
  • The retired judge must consent to the request, and while serving, they enjoy the jurisdiction and privileges of a High Court judge, helping the court manage severe case backlogs.

landmarkCase.citation: Lok Prahari v. Union of India (2021)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court activated detailed guidelines for using Article 224A to bring back retired judges to tackle long-pending cases, emphasizing its value as an efficient tool for judicial management.

articles.title: Jurisdiction of existing High Courts
articles.officialText: Subject to the provisions of this Constitution and to the provisions of any law of the appropriate Legislature... the jurisdiction of, and the law administered in, any existing High Court... shall be the same as immediately before the commencement of this Constitution...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This transitional article preserved the pre-constitutional jurisdictions, legal powers, and administrative rules of existing High Courts when the Constitution took effect.
  • It ensured structural continuity, allowing High Courts to maintain their established civil, criminal, and appellate workflows while subjecting them to subsequent legislative changes.

landmarkCase.citation: Garikapati Veeraya v. N. Subbiah Choudhry (1957)
landmarkCase.summary: The court confirmed that pre-existing legal powers and appellate routes were structurally preserved and transferred under provisions like Article 225, maintaining continuity across the legal system.

articles.title: Power of High Courts to issue certain writs
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding anything in Article 32 every High Court shall have power, throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction, to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases any Government, within those territories directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article vests High Courts with expansive writ jurisdiction, allowing them to issue orders and writs to protect individual rights and enforce the rule of law. It covers five core writs:
  • Habeas Corpus: An order to produce a detained individual in court to evaluate the legal validity of their confinement, protecting personal liberty.
  • Mandamus: A command directing a public official, court, or statutory body to perform a mandatory public duty that they have failed to carry out.
  • Quo Warranto: A judicial review challenging an individual's legal authority to hold a public office, preventing illegal usurpation of public posts.
  • Prohibition: A preventive writ issued to a lower court or tribunal to stop it from exceeding its legal jurisdiction or violating natural justice principles.
  • Certiorari: A curative writ used to quash an order already passed by a lower court or administrative body due to a jurisdictional error or illegality.
  • Crucially, the phrase 'and for any other purpose' makes the High Court's writ power broader than the Supreme Court's under Article 32, allowing them to issue writs for enforcing standard statutory legal rights as well as Fundamental Rights.

landmarkCase.citation: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court firmly established that the writ jurisdiction vested in High Courts under Article 226 is an essential part of the basic structure of the Constitution, and cannot be excluded or diluted by constitutional amendments or statutory exclusions.

articles.title: Constitutional validity of Central laws not to be considered in proceedings under article 226
articles.officialText: [Repealed by the Constitution (Forty-third Amendment) Act, 1977.]
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• Inserted during the Emergency via the 42nd Amendment, this article stripped High Courts of their power to review the constitutional validity of Central laws during writ proceedings.
  • This measure concentrated judicial review power at the central level, but it was quickly repealed by the 43rd Amendment in 1977 to restore the traditional judicial review powers of the High Courts.

landmarkCase.citation: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997)
landmarkCase.summary: The court reviewed this historical interlude, confirming that the power of judicial review over all laws is an unalterable part of the basic structure, validating High Court oversight under Article 226.

articles.title: Power of superintendence over all courts by the High Court
articles.officialText: (1) Every High Court shall have superintendence over all courts and tribunals throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article grants each High Court administrative and judicial superintendence over all lower courts and tribunals operating within its territorial jurisdiction, with the exception of military courts.
  • It empowers the High Court to call for returns, frame operational rules, regulate record-keeping, and correct jurisdictional errors made by subordinate judicial bodies, ensuring uniform judicial administration.

landmarkCase.citation: Shalini Shyam Shetty v. Rajendra Shankar Patil (2010)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court clarified that the power of superintendence under Article 227 is a discretionary, supervisory power that must be used sparingly to correct gross miscarriages of justice, and cannot be used as a routine second appeal.

articles.title: Transfer of certain cases to High Court
articles.officialText: If the High Court is satisfied that a case pending in a court subordinate to it involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of this Constitution the determination of which is necessary for the disposal of the case, it shall withdraw the case and may— (a) either dispose of the case itself, or (b) determine the said question of law and return the case...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article empowers a High Court to withdraw a case from a lower court if it involves a substantial question of law regarding the interpretation of the Constitution.
  • The High Court can either dispose of the entire case itself or resolve the constitutional question and return the file to the lower court, ensuring that constitutional interpretations are handled by senior judiciaries.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Jammu & Kashmir v. Ganga Singh (1960)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that Article 228 ensures uniform constitutional interpretation within a state, preventing lower courts from delivering conflicting or erroneous constitutional rulings.

articles.title: Special provisions as to disposal of questions relating to constitutional validity of State laws
articles.officialText: [Repealed by the Constitution (Forty-third Amendment) Act, 1977.]
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• Inserted by the 42nd Amendment, this short-lived article placed restrictions on how High Courts could determine the constitutional validity of state laws, requiring minimum bench sizes and large voting majorities.
  • It was repealed by the 43rd Amendment in 1977, restoring standard judicial management and voting rules for High Courts.

landmarkCase.citation: NJAC Judgment (2015)
landmarkCase.summary: The court observed that historical restrictions like Article 228A failed because attempts to dictate judicial voting thresholds compromise independent judicial operations.

articles.title: Officers and servants and the expenses of High Courts
articles.officialText: (1) Appointments of officers and servants of a High Court shall be made by the Chief Justice of the Court or such other Judge or officer of the Court as he may direct...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article protects the administrative independence of the High Court. It gives the Chief Justice exclusive authority over appointing and regulating the service conditions of the court's staff, free from executive civil service controls.
  • It also mandates that all administrative expenses of the High Court, including salaries and pensions, are charged directly to the Consolidated Fund of the State, protecting it from annual political budget votes.

landmarkCase.citation: Union of India v. S.B. Vohra (2004)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the Chief Justice's administrative independence under Article 229 in managing court staff cannot be easily overridden by executive state budget departments.

articles.title: Extension of jurisdiction of High Courts to Union territories
articles.officialText: (1) Parliament may by law extend the jurisdiction of a High Court to, or exclude the jurisdiction of a High Court from, any Union territory.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article grants Parliament the authority to extend a state High Court's jurisdiction over an adjacent Union Territory, or to exclude it.
  • For example, Parliament used this power to place the Union Territory of Chandigarh under the jurisdiction of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, optimizing judicial resources across regions.

landmarkCase.citation: P.I.O., High Court of Madras v. B. Bharathi (2014)
landmarkCase.summary: The court analyzed territorial extensions under Article 230, confirming that when a High Court's jurisdiction is extended over a Union Territory, its constitutional authority applies uniformly across that region.

articles.title: Establishment of a common High Court for two or more States
articles.officialText: (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in the preceding provisions of this Chapter, Parliament may by law establish a common High Court for two or more States or for two or more States and a Union territory.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article empowers Parliament to establish a common High Court for two or more states, or for multiple states and a Union Territory.
  • This provides structural flexibility and cost efficiency, as seen in the creation of the Gauhati High Court, which historically served multiple northeastern states, and the common Bombay High Court serving Maharashtra and Goa.

landmarkCase.citation: K. Thomas Eladhi v. Legislative Assembly (1998)
landmarkCase.summary: The court validated the establishment of common High Courts under Article 231, holding that a shared judicial structure does not dilute the court's sovereign power over each respective state.

articles.title: Interpretation
articles.officialText: [Repealed/Substituted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956.]
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article originally contained specific interpretive provisions regarding High Courts serving multiple states.
  • It was amended and reorganized by the 7th Constitutional Amendment in 1956 to streamline definitions following the reorganization of states into uniform categories.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951)
landmarkCase.summary: The early structural modifications leading up to the 1956 amendments were noted by courts as necessary steps to normalize provincial judicial terms across the country.

articles.title: Appointment of district judges
articles.officialText: (1) Appointments of persons to be, and the posting and promotion of, district judges in any State shall be made by the Governor of the State in consultation with the High Court exercising jurisdiction in relation to such State.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article governs the appointment, posting, and promotion of District Judges. These appointments are made by the State Governor, but require consultation with the High Court.
  • It sets minimum eligibility requirements for direct candidates from the legal profession, requiring a minimum of seven years of active practice as an advocate, alongside a recommendation from the High Court.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Bihar v. Bal Mukund Sah (2000)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the High Court's consultation under Article 233 is mandatory, and the state government cannot bypass judicial input by introducing separate administrative service quotas for district appointments.

articles.title: Validation of appointments of, and judgments, etc., delivered by, certain district judges
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding any judgment, decree or order of any court, no appointment of any person... to be a district judge in any State... shall be deemed to be illegal or void or ever to have become illegal or void by reason only of the fact that such appointment, posting or promotion was not made in accordance with the provisions of article 233...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• Inserted by the 20th Amendment in 1966, this retrospective article validated certain appointments and postings of district judges that had been declared invalid by courts due to procedural lapses under Article 233.
  • It also protected the validity of all judgments, decrees, and sentences delivered by these judges prior to the amendment, preventing structural disruption across the trial court ecosystem.

landmarkCase.citation: Chandra Mohan v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1966)
landmarkCase.summary: Following this ruling, which invalidated certain judicial appointments due to executive interference, Parliament passed Article 233A to cure the procedural defects while preserving trial court judgments.

articles.title: Recruitment of persons other than district judges to the judicial service
