articles.officialText: Appointments of persons other than district judges to the judicial service of a State shall be made by the Governor of the State in accordance with rules made by him in that behalf after consultation with the State Public Service Commission and with the High Court...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article governs the recruitment of the subordinate judiciary below the rank of a district judge, such as civil judges and judicial magistrates.
  • These appointments are made by the Governor following rules drafted in consultation with the State Public Service Commission and the state High Court, ensuring standardized competitive examinations and merit-based selection.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Bihar v. Bal Mukund Sah (2000)
landmarkCase.summary: The court emphasized that rules framed under Article 234 must respect the primary role of the High Court in managing judicial selections to preserve the separation of powers at the grassroots level.

articles.title: Control over subordinate courts
articles.officialText: The control over district courts and courts subordinate thereto including the posting and promotion of, and the grant of leave to, persons belonging to the judicial service of a State... shall be vested in the High Court...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article establishes the principle of judicial independence by vesting absolute administrative control over all subordinate trial courts and judicial officers directly in the High Court.
  • This control covers postings, promotions, leaves, transfers, and internal disciplinary proceedings, ensuring that trial judges are completely insulated from bureaucratic or political pressure.

landmarkCase.citation: Chief Justice of Andhra Pradesh v. L.V.A. Dixitulu (1979)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the word 'control' in Article 235 is comprehensive and exclusive, vesting full disciplinary authority over the subordinate judiciary in the High Court to keep trial courts free from executive influence.

articles.title: Interpretation
articles.officialText: In this Chapter— (a) the expression 'district judge' includes judge of a city civil court, additional district judge, joint district judge, assistant district judge, chief judge of a small cause court, chief presidency magistrate... (b) the expression 'judicial service' means a service consisting exclusively of persons intended to fill the post of district judge and other civil judicial posts inferior to the post of district judge.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article is a definition clause that clarifies the terminology used for the subordinate judiciary. It defines 'district judge' expansively to cover various designations like city civil court judges, additional district judges, and chief presidency magistrates.
  • It also defines 'judicial service' strictly as a career path consisting exclusively of officers dedicated to civil and criminal judicial roles, separating them from administrative civil services.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Bihar v. Bal Mukund Sah (2000)
landmarkCase.summary: The court used the precise definition of 'judicial service' in Article 236 to reinforce that the judiciary is a distinct constitutional organ that cannot be merged with general executive services.

articles.title: Application of the provisions of this Chapter to certain class or classes of magistrates
articles.officialText: The Governor may by public notification direct that the foregoing provisions of this Chapter and any rules made thereunder shall with effect from such date as may be fixed by him in that behalf apply in relation to any class or classes of magistrates in the State as they apply in relation to persons belonging to the judicial service...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article allows the Governor to extend the judicial selection and control rules of this chapter to other classes of magistrates within the state, such as executive or revenue magistrates.
  • This provides a mechanism to bring administrative officials under the supervisory control of the High Court, helping separate judicial functions from executive duties across various local authorities.

landmarkCase.citation: State of U.P. v. Mohammad Naim (1964)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that notifications under Article 237 serve as important steps toward fulfilling the directive principle in Article 50 by separating judicial magistracies from executive control.

partTitle: Relations between the Union and the States

articles.title: Extent of laws made by Parliament and by the Legislatures of States
articles.officialText: (1) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India, and the Legislature of a State may make laws for the whole or any part of the State...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article defines the territorial limits of legislative powers, establishing that Parliament can pass laws for the entire territory of India, while a State Legislature can pass laws strictly for its own state.
  • Clause (2) clarifies that an Act of Parliament cannot be declared invalid simply because it has 'extra-territorial operation', meaning it affects Indian citizens or property located outside the country's physical borders.

landmarkCase.citation: GVK Industries Ltd. v. Income Tax Officer (2011)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that Parliament's power to pass extra-territorial laws under Article 245 is valid as long as there is a real, identifiable connection or relationship to interests within India.

articles.title: Subject-matter of laws made by Parliament and by the Legislatures of States
articles.officialText: (1) Notwithstanding anything in clauses (2) and (3), Parliament has exclusive power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List I in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the 'Union List')...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article distributes legislative powers across three distinct fields detailed in the Seventh Schedule, forming the foundation of Indian federalism:
  • Union List (List I): Subject areas under the exclusive legislative control of Parliament (e.g., defense, foreign affairs, banking).
  • State List (List II): Subject areas under the standard legislative control of State Legislatures (e.g., public order, police, public health).
  • Concurrent List (List III): Shared fields where both Parliament and State Legislatures can pass laws (e.g., education, criminal law, contracts).
  • It establishes a principle of federal supremacy: the Union List takes precedence over the State and Concurrent Lists if overlaps occur.

landmarkCase.citation: State of West Bengal v. Union of India (1963)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court established that the Indian Constitution creates a centralized federal structure, and the distribution of subject matter under Article 246 gives the Union final authority over national issues.

articles.title: Special provisions with respect to goods and services tax
articles.officialText: (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in articles 246 and 254, Parliament, and, subject to clause (2), the Legislature of every State, have power to make laws with respect to goods and services tax imposed by the Union or by such State...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• Inserted by the 101st Amendment in 2016, this article introduces a shared tax track to enable the Goods and Services Tax (GST) framework. It grants simultaneous legislative powers to both Parliament and State Legislatures to levy taxes on goods and services.
  • Clause (2) grants Parliament the exclusive power to levy GST on interstate trade and commerce, overriding the traditional separations of Article 246 to create a unified national market.

landmarkCase.citation: Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. (2022)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that Article 246A gives the Union and States simultaneous, equal powers to legislate on GST, meaning recommendations of the GST Council are persuasive and cannot legally bind sovereign legislatures.

articles.title: Power of Parliament to provide for the establishment of certain additional courts
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding anything in this Chapter, Parliament may by law provide for the establishment of any additional courts for the better administration of laws made by Parliament or of any existing laws with respect to a matter enumerated in the Union List.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article gives Parliament the authority to establish additional courts or judicial tribunals to ensure the effective administration and enforcement of central laws passed under the Union List.
  • This power allows Parliament to build specialized judicial tracks, like special CBI courts or intellectual property tribunals, without relying solely on the state's standard trial court networks.

landmarkCase.citation: In re Special Courts Bill (1979)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court validated the creation of specialized court frameworks under Article 247, holding that creating distinct judicial tracks to quickly process urgent public matters complies with the Constitution.

articles.title: Residuary powers of legislation
articles.officialText: (1) Subject to article 246A, Parliament has exclusive power to make any law with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Concurrent List or State List.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article vests all 'residuary powers' of legislation exclusively in Parliament. This means that if a new technology or unforeseen regulatory issue emerges that is not listed in any of the three legislative lists, the power to pass laws on it belongs solely to the Union.
  • Clause (2) clarifies that this residuary power includes the authority to introduce taxes not mentioned in the State or Concurrent fields, emphasizing the central government's fiscal dominance.

landmarkCase.citation: Union of India v. H.S. Dhillon (1971)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court upheld the validity of a central wealth tax on agricultural land, ruling that if a subject matter is not explicitly listed in the State List, Parliament can legislate on it using its residuary powers under Article 248.

articles.title: Power of Parliament to legislate with respect to a matter in the State List in the national interest
articles.officialText: (1) Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Chapter, if the Council of States has declared by resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest that Parliament should make laws... it shall be lawful for Parliament to make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India with respect to that matter...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article allows Parliament to cross into the State List under normal circumstances if a matter becomes an issue of national interest. This process requires the Rajya Sabha (representing the states) to pass a resolution by a two-thirds majority authorizing the shift.
  • Laws passed under this provision are temporary, remaining in force for a maximum of one year, though the Rajya Sabha can extend the resolution for additional one-year periods as needed.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1978)
landmarkCase.summary: The court noted that Article 249 acts as a flexible federal safety valve, allowing the center to take control of state-level regulatory matters when national security or public interest demands it.

articles.title: Power of Parliament to legislate with respect to any matter in the State List if a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation
articles.officialText: (1) Notwithstanding anything in this Chapter, Parliament shall, while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, have power to make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India with respect to any of the matters enumerated in the State List.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article shifts legislative authority during a declared National Emergency under Article 352, granting Parliament the power to pass laws on any matter within the State List.
  • This temporarily transforms India's federal structure into a unitary system. Any state laws that conflict with parliamentary acts passed under this article are suspended, and the emergency laws expire six months after the emergency proclamation is formally lifted.

landmarkCase.citation: A.D.M. Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976)
landmarkCase.summary: The court reviewed the centralized concentration of powers during emergencies, noting that provisions like Article 250 modify regular federal distributions to ensure a unified national response.

articles.title: Inconsistency between laws made by Parliament under articles 249 and 250 and laws made by the Legislatures of States
articles.officialText: Nothing in articles 249 and 250 shall restrict the power of the Legislature of a State to make any law... but if any provision of a law made by the Legislature of a State is repugnant to any provision of a law made by Parliament... the law made by Parliament... shall prevail...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article clarifies that when Parliament passes laws on State List matters under Article 249 or 250, state legislatures do not lose their power to pass laws on those same subjects.
  • However, it reinforces federal supremacy: if a state law conflicts with a parliamentary law passed under these emergency or national interest provisions, the state law becomes inoperative to the extent of the conflict while the central law remains active.

landmarkCase.citation: Hoechst Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. State of Bihar (1983)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court noted that Article 251 acts as a rules engine for resolving statutory conflicts, establishing that state legislative powers continue but must yield to central laws during authorized interventions.

articles.title: Power of Parliament to legislate for two or more States by consent and adoption of such legislation by any other State
articles.officialText: (1) If it appears to the Legislatures of two or more States to be desirable that any of the matters with respect to which Parliament has no power to make laws for the States... should be regulated in such States by Parliament by law, and if resolutions to that effect are passed by all the Houses... it shall be lawful for Parliament to pass an Act for regulating that matter accordingly...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• This article provides a cooperative federal pathway where two or more states can voluntarily yield their legislative authority over a State List matter to Parliament. The process requires these states to pass resolutions requesting the central government to legislate on the matter.
  • The resulting Act of Parliament applies strictly to the consenting states, though other states can adopt it later by passing similar resolutions. Crucially, once a state delegates this power, it cannot amend or repeal the central law on its own; amendments can only be made by Parliament.

landmarkCase.citation: Union of India v. Valiuri Basavaiah (1979)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court ruled that when states pass resolutions under Article 252, they completely surrender their legislative authority over that specific subject area to Parliament, rendering any subsequent state laws on the matter void.

articles.title: Inconsistency between laws made by Parliament and laws made by the Legislatures of States
articles.officialText: (1) If any provision of a law made by the Legislature of a State is repugnant to any provision of a law made by Parliament which Parliament is competent to enact, or to any provision of an existing law with respect to one of the matters enumerated in the Concurrent List, then, subject to the provisions of clause (2), the law made by Parliament, whether passed before or after the law made by the Legislature of such State, or, as the case may be, the existing law, shall prevail and the law made by the Legislature of the State shall, to the extent of the repugnancy, be void. (2) Where a law made by the Legislature of a State with respect to one of the matters enumerated in the Concurrent List contains any provision repugnant to the provisions of an earlier law made by Parliament or an existing law with respect to that matter, then, the law so made by the Legislature of such State shall, if it has been reserved for the consideration of the President and has received his assent, prevail in that State: Provided that nothing in this clause shall prevent Parliament from enacting at any time any law with respect to the same matter including a law adding to, amending, varying or repealing the law so made by the Legislature of the State.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• Doctrine of Repugnancy: This article deals with operational conflicts between Central and State laws on subjects listed under the Concurrent List (List III). When a state provision directly clashes with a central provision, a situation of 'repugnancy' arises.
  • Federal Supremacy: Clause (1) establishes that under normal circumstances, Central legislation will automatically override and invalidate conflicting State legislation to the extent of the inconsistency, regardless of whether the Central law was passed before or after the State law.
  • The Constitutional Exception: Clause (2) provides a vital federal escape hatch. If a State law is repugnant to a Central law on a Concurrent subject, the State can save its law by reserving the Bill for the consideration of the President under Article 200. If it successfully receives Presidential assent, the State law will prevail over the Central law strictly within that specific State's borders.
  • Parliament's Ultimate Veto: The final proviso guards Central supremacy by declaring that even after a State law receives Presidential assent, Parliament can still step in at any time and pass a fresh law to amend, vary, or completely repeal that specific State legislation.

landmarkCase.citation: M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India (1979)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court laid down the definitive conditions for determining repugnancy under Article 254. It established that for repugnancy to exist: there must be a direct and irreconcilable conflict between the two acts, they must operate in the exact same field, and compliance with one must necessarily result in a violation of the other. If they can stand together without a direct collision, the doctrine will not apply.

articles.title: Requirements as to recommendations and previous sanctions to be regarded as matters of procedure only
articles.officialText: No Act of Parliament or of the Legislature of a State, and no provision in any such Act, shall be invalid by reason only that some recommendation or previous sanction required by this Constitution was not given, if assent to that Act was given— (a) where the recommendation required was that of the Governor, either by the Governor or by the President; (b) where the recommendation required was that of the President, by the President.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• Procedural Protection: Certain articles of the Constitution require that a Bill must have the prior 'recommendation' or 'previous sanction' of the President or Governor before being introduced in the legislature (e.g., money bills or bills restricting trade under Article 304). This article acts as a procedural safeguard to ensure legislation is not struck down by courts over purely formal, technical oversights.
  • Curing Procedural Defects: It establishes that if a Bill was mistakenly introduced and passed without this required prior sanction, the error is legally cured the moment the final Act receives the official assent of the respective Governor or President.
  • Substance Over Form: The framework prioritizes the collective political will of the legislature and the formal sign-off by the executive head over rigid, initial procedural technicalities.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1978)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court confirmed that the complete absence of a prior executive recommendation at the introduction stage of a Bill is an internal procedural defect only. It cannot invalidate a fully enacted statute if the final presidential or gubernatorial assent has been secured, as Article 255 fully insulates such laws from structural technical challenges.

articles.title: Obligation of States and the Union
articles.officialText: The executive power of every State shall be so exercised as to ensure compliance with the laws made by Parliament and any existing laws which apply in that State, and the executive power of the Union shall extend to the giving of such directions to a State as may appear to the Government of India to be necessary for that purpose.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• Administrative Coordination: This article marks the transition from legislative to administrative relations in Part XI. It establishes a binding constitutional obligation on every State executive to ensure that its local machinery actively implements and complies with laws passed by Parliament.
  • Union Directives: To maintain national uniformity and prevent local administrative resistance, it explicitly empowers the Central Government to issue binding administrative directions to a State if it notices a failure to execute Central statutes.
  • Federal Enforcement: It sets up a hierarchical dynamic, ensuring that while States retain regional executive autonomy, their machinery remains structurally aligned with the sovereign legislative policies of the Union.

landmarkCase.citation: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court examined the scope of Article 256 in the context of federal commands. The court noted that a persistent, deliberate refusal by a State to comply with valid administrative directions issued by the Union under this article can be construed as a failure of constitutional machinery, potentially triggering sanctions under Article 365 and invoking Article 356.

articles.title: Control of the Union over States in certain cases
articles.officialText: (1) The executive power of every State shall be so exercised as not to impede or prejudice the exercise of the executive power of the Union, and the executive power of the Union shall extend to the giving of such directions to a State as may appear to the Government of India to be necessary for that purpose... (2) The executive power of the Union shall also extend to the giving of directions to a State as to the construction and maintenance of means of communication declared in the direction to be of national or military importance...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
This article expands the Union's administrative oversight, focusing on national strategic interests within State territories.

  • Non-Interference Rule: Clause (1) mandates that a State must ensure its executive actions never impede, obstruct, or prejudice the operational executive powers of the Central Government.
  • Strategic Communications: Clause (2) gives the Union explicit power to issue directions to States to construct, maintain, or protect key lines of communication that carry military or national importance (such as national highways or strategic rail routes).
  • Railway Protection: Clause (3) allows the Union to issue directives regarding the deployment and measures necessary to protect railways passing through a State's territory.
  • Financial Compensation: Clause (4) balances this central intervention by requiring the Government of India to pay the State for any extra administrative expenses incurred while complying with these custom infrastructure or protection commands.

landmarkCase.citation: Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006)
landmarkCase.summary: The court highlighted that Article 257 provides clear, textually bounded scenarios where Union supremacy overrides State executive discretion. It ensures that critical national assets like railways and military communications remain secure and operational, preventing regional political administrations from disrupting essential national services.

articles.title: Power of the Union to confer powers, etc., on States in certain cases
articles.officialText: (1) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the President may, with the consent of the Government of a State, entrust either conditionally or unconditionally to that Government or to its officers functions in relation to any matter to which the executive power of the Union extends...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• Cooperative Federalism: This article enables a flexible administrative mechanism known as 'delegation of powers.' It allows the Central Government to utilize the existing administrative machinery of State governments to execute Central policies.
  • Presidential Entrustment: Under Clause (1), the President can, with the explicit consent of a State government, delegate executive functions concerning Union List matters to that State's officers.
  • Statutory Delegation: Clause (2) allows Parliament to directly use Central laws to bypass the need for prior state consent, imposing statutory executive duties directly onto State officials for matters within its legislative competence.
  • Funding the Machinery: Clause (3) ensures that when State officers act as agents for the Union, the Central Government must pay the State for the extra cost of the administrative and labor overhead, preventing the Union from placing unfair financial burdens on local budgets.

landmarkCase.citation: Jayantilal Amratlal Shodhan v. F.N. Rana (1964)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court clarified the nature of presidential delegation under Article 258(1). It held that the power to entrust Union functions to State officers is a distinct constitutional authority that can include both executive actions and quasi-legislative tasks like issuing notifications, emphasizing the high level of administrative flexibility permitted between federal tiers.

articles.title: Power of the States to entrust functions to the Union
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the Governor of a State may, with the consent of the Government of India, entrust either conditionally or unconditionally to that Government or to its officers functions in relation to any matter to which the executive power of the State extends.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• Reciprocal Delegation: Inserted by the 7th Constitutional Amendment in 1956, this article provides a mirror track to Article 258, enabling a bottom-up administrative delegation.
  • State to Union: It empowers the Governor of a State, acting with the explicit consent of the Government of India, to delegate State-level executive functions (from the State List or Concurrent List) to Central officers.
  • Administrative Convergence: This tool is highly effective when a State requires specialized Central technical skills, logistical support, or infrastructure management that its local civil service lacks, reinforcing a model of mutual cooperation within the federal structure.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Punjab v. Sukhjit Singh (1993)
landmarkCase.summary: The court observed that Article 258A underscores the fluid, non-rigid layout of Indian federalism. It establishes that as long as mutual executive consent is secured, administrative powers can move seamlessly between State and Union tiers to achieve practical governance solutions.

articles.title: Armed Forces in States in Part B of the First Schedule
articles.officialText: [Repealed by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956.]
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• Historical Reorganization: This article originally permitted specific 'Part B' States (which were former princely states like Hyderabad or Mysore) to maintain their own localized military forces alongside the standard Indian Armed Forces.
  • Formal Repeal: It was completely repealed by the 7th Constitutional Amendment in 1956. This reform abolished historical category divisions among states, integrated princely forces into the regular military structure, and established a uniform defense system across the country.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951)
landmarkCase.summary: Early litigation touching upon Part B states noted that these transitional provisions were temporary adjustments designed to protect local administrative structures during integration, and their final removal normalized federal defense control.

articles.title: Jurisdiction of the Union in relation to territories outside India
articles.officialText: The Government of India may by agreement with the Government of any territory not being part of the territory of India undertake any executive, legislative or judicial functions vested in the Government of such territory, but every such agreement shall be subject to, and governed by, any law relating to the exercise of foreign jurisdiction for the time being in force.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• Extra-Territorial Administration: This article outlines the Union's authority to expand its administrative footprint beyond the physical borders of India. It allows the Government of India to enter into bilateral agreements with foreign territories to assume executive, legislative, or judicial control over those regions.
  • Foreign Jurisdiction: This power is frequently used to administer small enclaves, leased territories, or nearby regions during transitions, or to manage cross-border administrative arrangements.
  • Statutory Control: It mandates that all such international administrative arrangements must strictly follow the Foreign Jurisdiction Act and any relevant laws passed by Parliament.

landmarkCase.citation: GVK Industries Ltd. v. Income Tax Officer (2011)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court noted that while Article 245 defines the regular boundaries for legislation, Articles like 260 demonstrate that the sovereign power of the Union can extend extra-territorial functions whenever foreign treaties or geopolitical agreements demand it.

articles.title: Public acts, records and judicial proceedings
articles.officialText: (1) Full faith and credit shall be given throughout the territory of India to public acts, records and judicial proceedings of the Union and of every State. (2) The manner in which and the conditions under which the acts, records and proceedings... shall be proved and the effect thereof determined shall be as provided by law made by Parliament. (3) Final judgments or orders delivered or passed by civil courts in any part of the territory of India shall be capable of execution anywhere within that territory according to law.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• Full Faith and Credit Clause: To prevent interstate chaos and ensure the legal system operates smoothly across the country, Clause (1) mandates that all public acts, official records, and judicial decrees issued in one State must be fully recognized and respected by all other States across India.
  • Uniform Standards: Clause (2) gives Parliament the exclusive authority to pass laws defining how these official public records are to be proven and verified across state borders.
  • Interstate Execution: Clause (3) provides a critical legal guarantee: a final judgment or order delivered by a civil court in any part of India is fully enforceable anywhere else in the country without requiring a fresh trial, creating a unified legal ecosystem.

landmarkCase.citation: Narhari Shivram Shet Shet v. James Fernandes (1976)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that decrees passed by courts within Indian territory must be executed across state borders without facing regional technical barriers. It ruled that Article 261 establishes a unified legal system that binds the entire country together under a single rule of law.

articles.title: Adjudication of disputes relating to waters of inter-State rivers or river valleys
articles.officialText: (1) Parliament may by law provide for the adjudication of any dispute or complaint with respect to the use, distribution or control of the waters of any inter-State river or river valley. (2) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may by law provide that neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall exercise jurisdiction in respect of any such dispute or complaint as is referred to in clause (1).
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• Interstate Water Conflicts: Recognizing that water sharing can trigger intense regional disputes, this article provides a specialized mechanism for managing conflicts over interstate rivers and river valleys.
  • Tribunal System: Clause (1) gives Parliament the exclusive power to pass laws to set up independent tribunals to adjudicate interstate water complaints, leading to the Inter-State Water Disputes Act.
  • Exclusion of Courts: Clause (2) contains an exceptional constitutional tool: it allows Parliament to strip all courts—including the Supreme Court under its original jurisdiction in Article 131—of their authority to hear or intervene in these water disputes once a tribunal track is activated.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Karnataka v. State of Tamil Nadu (Cauvery Water Dispute) (2018)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court clarified that while Article 262 allows Parliament to bar courts from directly adjudicating water disputes, the final award delivered by an Interstate Water Tribunal is still subject to the Supreme Court's appellate oversight under Article 136 to prevent gross violations of fundamental equity or constitutional rights.

articles.title: Provisions with respect to an inter-State Council
articles.officialText: If at any time it appears to the President that the public interests would be served by the establishment of a Council charged with the duty of— (a) inquiring into and advising upon disputes which may have arisen between States; (b) investigating and discussing subjects in which some or all of the States, or the Union and one or more of the States, have a common interest... it shall be lawful for the President by order to establish such a Council...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation:
• Inter-State Council Framework: This article provides a constitutional platform for managing federal conflicts through consultation. It empowers the President to establish an Inter-State Council (ISC) if they determine that doing so will serve the public interest.
  • Investigating Common Interests: The Council is tasked with exploring disputes between states, investigating shared policy challenges, and recommending steps to improve policy coordination between the Union and the States.
  • Cooperative Resolution: Instead of relying on long litigation or central commands, the ISC acts as an open forum where Chief Ministers and Union Cabinet Ministers can meet to resolve differences through negotiation.

landmarkCase.citation: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court emphasized the underutilized role of the Inter-State Council under Article 263. The court noted that major structural disputes regarding federal balances or the dismissal of state governments should ideally be discussed and reviewed within consultative bodies like the ISC to strengthen federal trust.

articles.title: Interpretation
articles.officialText: In this Part, 'Finance Commission' means a Finance Commission constituted under article 280.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This is the opening definition clause of Part XII. It clarifies that wherever the expression 'Finance Commission' appears in this Part, it refers exclusively to the body constituted by the President under Article 280. The purpose is to avoid repetitive definitions and to anchor all fiscal federalism provisions to a single constitutional authority.

landmarkCase.citation: Not directly litigated; interpreted in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
landmarkCase.summary: While Article 264 itself is definitional, the Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati emphasized that fiscal federalism and the Finance Commission mechanism form part of the constitutional scheme of cooperative federalism, which is part of the basic structure.

articles.title: Taxes not to be imposed save by authority of law
articles.officialText: No tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article is the cornerstone of taxation in India. It mandates that neither the Union nor the States can levy or collect any tax unless backed by a valid law enacted by a competent legislature. Executive orders, circulars, or administrative instructions cannot impose taxes. The word 'law' here means a statute passed by Parliament or State Legislature, not delegated legislation alone unless authorized.

landmarkCase.citation: Tata Iron & Steel Co. v. State of Bihar (1958)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that any tax levied without legislative sanction is unconstitutional. The case reinforced that 'authority of law' under Article 265 requires both a valid charging provision and a competent legislature. Mere executive instructions cannot validate tax collection, and any amount collected without authority must be refunded.

articles.title: Consolidated Funds and public accounts of India and of the States
articles.officialText: All revenues received by the Government of India, all loans raised by that Government by the issue of treasury bills, loans or ways and means advances and all moneys received by that Government in repayment of loans shall form one consolidated fund to be entitled 'the Consolidated Fund of India'...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article establishes two key financial repositories: (1) the Consolidated Fund of India/States — into which all government revenues, loans raised, and loan repayments flow, and from which no money can be withdrawn without parliamentary/legislative appropriation; and (2) the Public Account — which holds money received in trust (provident funds, deposits) where the government acts as a banker. The Consolidated Fund is the primary operating account of the government.

landmarkCase.citation: Bhim Singh v. Union of India (2010)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court scrutinized the MPLAD Scheme and clarified that withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund require strict appropriation by Parliament. The judgment reinforced that Article 266 creates a constitutional safeguard against arbitrary executive spending, ensuring legislative control over public money.

articles.title: Contingency Fund
articles.officialText: Parliament may by law establish a Contingency Fund in the nature of an imprest to be entitled 'the Contingency Fund of India' into which shall be paid from time to time such sums as may be determined by such law...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: The Contingency Fund is an emergency reserve placed at the disposal of the President (for the Union) or Governor (for the State) to meet unforeseen expenditure pending parliamentary/legislative authorization. It operates as an 'imprest' — money advanced is later recouped through supplementary appropriations. The fund ensures government continuity during sudden crises like natural disasters without waiting for legislative procedures.

landmarkCase.citation: Re: Special Reference No. 1 of 2002 (Gujarat Assembly Election Case)
landmarkCase.summary: Though primarily about election timing, the Court touched upon emergency expenditure mechanisms, affirming that the Contingency Fund is a constitutional device for executive flexibility, but its use must be ratified by the legislature subsequently, preserving the principle of legislative financial control.

articles.title: Duties levied by the Union but collected and appropriated by the States
articles.officialText: Such stamp duties as are mentioned in the Union List shall be levied by the Government of India but shall be collected — (a) in the case where such duties are leviable within any Union territory, by the Government of India, and (b) in other cases, by the States within which such duties are respectively leviable.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article creates a unique fiscal arrangement: certain duties (like stamp duties on bills of exchange, cheques, promissory notes) are imposed by the Union to maintain uniformity, but collected and retained by the States. The proceeds do not form part of the Consolidated Fund of India. This reflects cooperative federalism — Union ensures rate uniformity while States benefit from revenue.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1977)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court examined the division of fiscal powers and held that the scheme under Articles 268-281 reflects a careful balance between Union and States. The distribution mechanism cannot be unilaterally altered by either level of government, reinforcing fiscal federalism.

articles.title: Service tax levied by Union and collected and appropriated by the Union and the States (Omitted)
articles.officialText: Omitted by the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016. [Previously: Taxes on services shall be levied by the Government of India and such tax shall be collected and appropriated by the Government of India and the States...]
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article, inserted by the 88th Amendment (2003), authorized the Union to levy service tax with shared collection and appropriation between Union and States. It was omitted by the 101st Amendment Act, 2016 when the Goods and Services Tax (GST) regime subsumed service tax. The omission reflects the constitutional shift to a unified indirect tax structure under Articles 246A, 269A, and 279A.

landmarkCase.citation: All India Federation of Tax Practitioners v. Union of India (2007)
landmarkCase.summary: Before its omission, the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of service tax under this framework, holding that services are a distinct subject of taxation. The judgment laid groundwork for the eventual transition to GST by recognizing services as a taxable economic activity.

articles.title: Taxes levied and collected by the Union but assigned to the States
articles.officialText: Taxes on the sale or purchase of goods and taxes on the consignment of goods shall be levied and collected by the Government of India but shall be assigned and shall be deemed to have been assigned to the States...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article covers taxes (like inter-State sales tax and consignment tax) that are levied and collected by the Union but whose entire proceeds are assigned to the States. The Union acts merely as a collecting agency. The principles of distribution among States are formulated by Parliament. This ensures uniform rates across India while channeling revenue to consuming/producing States.

landmarkCase.citation: India Cement Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu (1990)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court analyzed the boundaries between Union and State taxing powers, holding that overlapping or duplicate taxation violates the constitutional scheme. The judgment clarified that Article 269 creates exclusive Union legislative competence with mandatory assignment of proceeds to States.

articles.title: Levy and collection of goods and services tax in course of inter-State trade or commerce
articles.officialText: Goods and services tax on supplies in the course of inter-State trade or commerce shall be levied and collected by the Government of India and such tax shall be apportioned between the Union and the States in the manner as may be provided by Parliament by law on the recommendations of the Goods and Services Tax Council.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Inserted by the 101st Amendment (2016), this article governs Integrated GST (IGST) on inter-State supplies and imports. The Union levies and collects IGST, but proceeds are apportioned between Union and destination State based on GST Council recommendations. This is the bedrock of the 'destination-based consumption tax' principle of GST and ensures seamless credit flow across State borders.

landmarkCase.citation: Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. (2022)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that GST Council recommendations are not binding on Union and States but only persuasive. The Court emphasized that Article 246A and 269A confer simultaneous taxing power, and federalism under GST is based on dialogue and cooperation, not subordination.

articles.title: Taxes levied and distributed between the Union and the States
articles.officialText: All taxes and duties referred to in the Union List, except the duties and taxes referred to in articles 268, 269 and 269A, respectively, surcharge on taxes and duties referred to in article 271 and any cess levied for specific purposes... shall be levied and collected by the Government of India and shall be distributed between the Union and the States in the manner provided in clause (2).
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This is the central revenue-sharing provision. Taxes like income tax (except corporate tax pre-2000) and central GST are levied and collected by the Union, but a portion of the net proceeds is distributed to States as per the Finance Commission's recommendations. Surcharges and cesses are explicitly excluded — they remain wholly with the Union, which has been a source of recent federal tension.

landmarkCase.citation: T.N. State Transport Corporation v. State of Tamil Nadu (1995)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court reiterated that the constitutional scheme requires sharing of divisible pool taxes with States as per Finance Commission formulas. Any attempt to keep shareable revenues outside the divisible pool through reclassification as cess or surcharge undermines the cooperative federal structure.

articles.title: Surcharge on certain duties and taxes for purposes of the Union
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding anything in articles 269 and 270, Parliament may at any time increase any of the duties or taxes referred to in those articles except the goods and services tax under article 246A, by a surcharge for purposes of the Union and the whole proceeds of any such surcharge shall form part of the Consolidated Fund of India.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Parliament can levy surcharges on Union taxes, and the entire proceeds belong exclusively to the Union — not shared with States. The 2016 amendment excluded GST from surcharge powers to protect the GST structure. Critics argue extensive use of surcharges/cesses erodes the States' share in the divisible pool, raising federalism concerns.

landmarkCase.citation: Jaora Sugar Mills v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1966)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court distinguished between tax, fee, surcharge, and cess. It held that a surcharge is essentially an enhancement of an existing tax and Parliament's power under Article 271 is plenary, but it cannot be used as a colorable device to defeat the constitutional revenue-sharing scheme.

articles.title: Taxes which are levied and collected by the Union and may be distributed between the Union and the States (Omitted)
articles.officialText: Omitted by the Constitution (Eightieth Amendment) Act, 2000. [Previously dealt with Union excise duties shareable with States.]
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article previously distinguished mandatorily shared taxes (income tax under Art. 270) from optionally shared Union excise duties. The 80th Amendment (2000), based on the 10th Finance Commission's 'Alternative Scheme of Devolution', merged all Union taxes into a single divisible pool under a revised Article 270. This simplified fiscal federalism and gave States a predictable share of all Union taxes.

landmarkCase.citation: Recommendations of the Tenth Finance Commission (Constitutionalised by 80th Amendment)
landmarkCase.summary: Though not a judicial case, the 80th Amendment, judicially recognized in subsequent federalism cases, marked a paradigm shift. The Supreme Court in later cases acknowledged that the unified divisible pool strengthened fiscal federalism by ensuring States receive a stable, formula-based share of all Union tax revenues.

articles.title: Grants in lieu of export duty on jute and jute products
articles.officialText: There shall be charged on the Consolidated Fund of India in each year as grants-in-aid of the revenues of the States of Assam, Bihar, Orissa and West Bengal, in lieu of assignment of any share of the net proceeds in each year of export duty on jute and jute products to those States, such sums as may be prescribed.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This transitional provision compensates four jute-producing States (Assam, Bihar, Orissa, West Bengal) for the loss of revenue from export duty on jute, which is a Union subject. The grant continues for ten years from commencement or such other period as Parliament may decide. It illustrates how the Constitution provides protective fiscal arrangements for States economically dependent on specific commodities.

landmarkCase.citation: State of West Bengal v. Union of India (1963)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court, in addressing Centre-State fiscal relations, acknowledged that special grants under Article 273 reflect the framers' sensitivity to regional economic dependencies. The Union's obligation to provide such grants is constitutional, not discretionary, during the operative period.

articles.title: Prior recommendation of President required to Bills affecting taxation in which States are interested
articles.officialText: No Bill or amendment which imposes or varies any tax or duty in which States are interested, or which varies the meaning of the expression 'agricultural income' as defined for the purposes of the enactments relating to Indian income-tax, or which affects the principles on which moneys are or may be distributable to States... shall be introduced or moved in either House of Parliament except on the recommendation of the President.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article acts as a federal safeguard. Any parliamentary Bill that affects taxes shared with States, modifies the definition of 'agricultural income' (a State subject), or alters revenue distribution principles requires prior Presidential recommendation. This ensures the Union does not unilaterally alter the financial interests of States and the matter is examined by the executive (which considers federal implications) before legislative debate.

landmarkCase.citation: Atiabari Tea Co. v. State of Assam (1961)
landmarkCase.summary: While primarily about freedom of trade, the Court emphasized the constitutional protections built into Centre-State financial relations. Article 274's requirement of Presidential recommendation was recognized as a procedural safeguard ensuring federal balance in fiscal legislation.

articles.title: Grants from the Union to certain States
articles.officialText: Such sums as Parliament may by law provide shall be charged on the Consolidated Fund of India in each year as grants-in-aid of the revenues of such States as Parliament may determine to be in need of assistance, and different sums may be fixed for different States...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article empowers Parliament to provide statutory grants-in-aid to States needing financial assistance. Unlike Article 282 (discretionary grants), Article 275 grants are charged on the Consolidated Fund and based on Finance Commission recommendations. It includes special provisions for promoting welfare of Scheduled Tribes and raising administration of Scheduled Areas, reflecting commitment to equitable development.

landmarkCase.citation: Bhim Singh v. Union of India (2010)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court distinguished between statutory grants under Article 275 (Finance Commission-based) and discretionary grants under Article 282. It held that the Union's discretionary grant-making power cannot become a parallel route to bypass Finance Commission recommendations and fiscal federalism principles.

articles.title: Taxes on professions, trades, callings and employments
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding anything in article 246, no law of the Legislature of a State relating to taxes for the benefit of the State or of a municipality, district board, local board or other local authority therein in respect of professions, trades, callings or employments shall be invalid on the ground that it relates to a tax on income. The total amount payable in respect of any one person to the State or to any one municipality... shall not exceed two thousand and five hundred rupees per annum.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article empowers States to levy 'profession tax' on professions, trades, callings, and employments without conflicting with the Union's exclusive power to tax income. The constitutional ceiling was originally ₹250, raised to ₹2,500 per annum by the 60th Amendment (1988). Parliament can further enhance this limit. It is a significant revenue source for State governments and local bodies.

landmarkCase.citation: Kamta Prasad Aggarwal v. Executive Officer, Ballabhgarh (1974)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court upheld the validity of State-levied profession tax, ruling that Article 276 carves out a special exception to the Union's exclusive jurisdiction over income tax. The State's power is constitutionally protected even though the tax has elements relating to income, as long as it stays within the prescribed monetary ceiling.

articles.title: Savings
articles.officialText: Any taxes, duties, cesses or fees which, immediately before the commencement of this Constitution, were being lawfully levied by the Government of any State or by any municipality or other local authority or body for the purposes of the State, municipality, district or other local area may, notwithstanding that those taxes, duties, cesses or fees are mentioned in the Union List, continue to be levied...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This is a savings clause protecting pre-Constitutional taxation arrangements. Taxes lawfully levied by States or local bodies before 26 January 1950, even if those subjects later fell in the Union List, may continue until Parliament legislates otherwise. This provided fiscal continuity during the transition from British India to the Republic and prevented sudden disruption of local revenues.

landmarkCase.citation: Union of India v. R.C. Jain (1981)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court clarified the scope of Article 277, holding that the savings clause protects only existing taxes and does not permit States to levy new taxes on Union List subjects. The protection is conditional and ceases when Parliament makes a contrary provision.

articles.title: Agreement with States in Part B of the First Schedule (Omitted)
articles.officialText: Omitted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article originally dealt with financial agreements between the Union and former princely States (Part B States) regarding federal taxes, duties, and grants. With the 7th Amendment (1956) reorganizing States on linguistic lines and abolishing the A/B/C/D classification, this provision became redundant and was omitted. It reflects the constitutional evolution from the post-independence transitional federalism to a more uniform federal structure.

landmarkCase.citation: States Reorganisation Commission Report (1955) — constitutionalised by 7th Amendment
landmarkCase.summary: Though not a judicial case, the reorganization process recognized in subsequent federalism cases marked the end of the dual federalism for princely States. The Supreme Court has consistently held that the post-1956 federal structure is uniform across all States.

articles.title: Calculation of 'net proceeds', etc.
articles.officialText: In the foregoing provisions of this Chapter, 'net proceeds' means in relation to any tax or duty the proceeds thereof reduced by the cost of collection, and for the purposes of those provisions the net proceeds of any tax or duty, or of any part of any tax or duty, in or attributable to any area shall be ascertained and certified by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, whose certificate shall be final.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article defines 'net proceeds' as gross tax collections minus collection costs. The Comptroller and Auditor-General (CAG) certifies the net proceeds, and the certificate is final and non-justiciable. This ensures an independent constitutional authority determines the divisible pool for States, preventing manipulation by either Union or States and lending credibility to fiscal transfers.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1977)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court recognized the CAG's role under Article 279 as a constitutional check on executive financial reporting. The Court emphasized that CAG certification of net proceeds is a safeguard ensuring transparent and accurate revenue sharing between Union and States.

articles.title: Goods and Services Tax Council
articles.officialText: The President shall, within sixty days from the date of commencement of the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, by order, constitute a Council to be called the Goods and Services Tax Council. The Goods and Services Tax Council shall consist of — (a) the Union Finance Minister as Chairperson; (b) the Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance; (c) the Minister in charge of Finance or Taxation or any other Minister nominated by each State Government...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Inserted by the 101st Amendment (2016), this article establishes the GST Council — a constitutional body for cooperative federalism in indirect taxation. It comprises the Union Finance Minister (Chair), Union MoS Finance, and one Minister from each State. Decisions require a 3/4th majority, with the Union having 1/3rd weightage and all States together having 2/3rd. The Council recommends on rates, exemptions, model laws, and dispute resolution.

landmarkCase.citation: Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. (2022)
landmarkCase.summary: The landmark 'GST Council judgment' held that recommendations of the GST Council are not binding on Union and States — they are persuasive. The Supreme Court emphasized that Indian federalism under GST is based on 'cooperative dialogue' and both Union and State legislatures have simultaneous power under Article 246A. This judgment redefined the contours of GST federalism.

articles.title: Finance Commission
articles.officialText: The President shall, within two years from the commencement of this Constitution and thereafter at the expiration of every fifth year or at such earlier time as the President considers necessary, by order constitute a Finance Commission which shall consist of a Chairman and four other members to be appointed by the President.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article establishes the Finance Commission — a quasi-judicial constitutional body constituted every five years. It comprises a Chairman and four members appointed by the President. Its duties include recommending: (a) distribution of net tax proceeds between Union and States; (b) principles governing grants-in-aid; (c) measures to augment State Consolidated Funds for Panchayats and Municipalities; and (d) any other fiscal matter referred by the President. It is the keystone of Indian fiscal federalism.

landmarkCase.citation: Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2006)
landmarkCase.summary: While addressing federalism broadly, the Supreme Court recognized the Finance Commission as a vital constitutional mechanism for federal fiscal balance. The Court emphasized that the Commission's recommendations, though technically advisory, command strong constitutional weight, and any deviation by the Union must be justified before Parliament.

articles.title: Recommendations of the Finance Commission
articles.officialText: The President shall cause every recommendation made by the Finance Commission under the provisions of this Constitution together with an explanatory memorandum as to the action taken thereon to be laid before each House of Parliament.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article ensures parliamentary scrutiny of Finance Commission recommendations. The President must lay before both Houses every recommendation along with an Action Taken Report (ATR) explaining acceptance or rejection. This creates political accountability — while recommendations are not legally binding, the Union must publicly justify any departure, creating strong moral and political pressure to comply.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Andhra Pradesh v. Union of India (Cited in fiscal federalism jurisprudence)
landmarkCase.summary: Courts have consistently held that while Finance Commission recommendations are not strictly binding, the constitutional mandate of Article 281 creates a presumption of acceptance. Departures must be reasoned and laid before Parliament, ensuring transparency in Union-State fiscal relations.

articles.title: Expenditure defrayable by the Union or a State out of its revenues
articles.officialText: The Union or a State may make any grants for any public purpose, notwithstanding that the purpose is not one with respect to which Parliament or the Legislature of the State, as the case may be, may make laws.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article empowers the Union and States to make grants for 'any public purpose' beyond their legislative competence. Originally intended for special grants during emergencies, the Union has used Article 282 extensively for Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) on State subjects like health, education, and agriculture. Critics argue this dilutes federalism by allowing the Union to influence State subjects through conditional grants.

landmarkCase.citation: Bhim Singh v. Union of India (2010) — MPLAD Scheme Case
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of MPLADS under Article 282, holding that the Union's grant-making power for 'public purpose' is wide. However, the Court cautioned that Article 282 must not become a route to bypass Article 275 and Finance Commission mechanisms, and discretionary grants must serve genuine public purposes.

articles.title: Custody, etc., of Consolidated Funds, Contingency Funds and moneys credited to the public accounts
articles.officialText: The custody of the Consolidated Fund of India and the Contingency Fund of India, the payment of moneys into such Funds, the withdrawal of moneys therefrom, the custody of public moneys other than those credited to such Funds received by or on behalf of the Government of India... shall be regulated by law made by Parliament...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article empowers Parliament (for Union) and State Legislatures (for States) to regulate the custody, payment into, and withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund, and Public Account. Until such laws are made, the President/Governor regulates by rules. This ensures legislative control over the entire money management apparatus of the government, reinforcing the principle of 'no taxation or expenditure without representation'.

landmarkCase.citation: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
landmarkCase.summary: While primarily on Article 356, the Court emphasized that legislative control over public finances, including custody and withdrawal protocols under Article 283, is essential to constitutional governance. Any executive bypass of these procedures undermines democratic accountability.

articles.title: Custody of suitors' deposits and other moneys received by public servants and courts
articles.officialText: All moneys received by or deposited with — (a) any officer employed in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State in his capacity as such, other than revenues or public moneys raised or received by the Government of India or the Government of the State, as the case may be, or (b) any court within the territory of India to the credit of any cause, matter, account or persons, shall be paid into the public account of India or the public account of State, as the case may be.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article deals with money received by public servants (like court fees, deposits in litigation, bail moneys) or courts in trust. Such moneys must be credited to the Public Account (not Consolidated Fund) since the government is holding them as a trustee, not as owner. This distinction is crucial — these funds can be withdrawn without parliamentary appropriation as they belong to private parties.

landmarkCase.citation: Sundarjas Kanyalal Bhathija v. Collector, Thane (1989)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court clarified the distinction between Consolidated Fund and Public Account, holding that money held in trust under Article 284 cannot be appropriated by the government for its own use. The fiduciary character of such deposits must be respected, and they must be returned to rightful claimants on demand.

articles.title: Exemption of property of the Union from State taxation
articles.officialText: The property of the Union shall, save in so far as Parliament may by law otherwise provide, be exempt from all taxes imposed by a State or by any authority within a State.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article grants the Union immunity from State taxation on its properties (buildings, lands, vehicles). The doctrine, borrowed from American constitutional law (McCulloch v. Maryland), prevents States from taxing the instrumentalities of the Union. However, Parliament may by law allow such taxation. Pre-Constitutional taxes continue until Parliament provides otherwise — this exception led to extensive litigation between municipalities and Union entities like Railways.

landmarkCase.citation: Union of India v. City Municipal Council, Bellary (1978)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that Union property is broadly exempt from State and local taxation under Article 285, but pre-Constitutional taxes survive under the proviso. The judgment clarified the scope of 'property' and reinforced the federal principle that one government cannot tax another's instrumentalities.

articles.title: Restrictions as to imposition of tax on the sale or purchase of goods
articles.officialText: No law of a State shall impose, or authorise the imposition of, a tax on the supply of goods or of services or both, where such supply takes place — (a) outside the State; or (b) in the course of the import of the goods or services or both into, or export of the goods or services or both out of, the territory of India.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article restricts States' power to tax supplies that occur outside the State or in the course of import/export. Post-101st Amendment, the language was adapted to GST. The purpose is to maintain the integrity of the Indian common market and prevent multiple States from taxing the same transaction. Parliament has exclusive power to formulate principles determining when a supply occurs 'outside' or 'in the course of' inter-State trade.

landmarkCase.citation: Bengal Immunity Co. v. State of Bihar (1955)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court interpreted the pre-amendment Article 286 to prevent multiple taxation of inter-State sales. The Court evolved the 'nexus theory' for determining the situs of sale. This judgment laid the foundation for India's modern indirect tax structure, ultimately leading to CST and then GST.

articles.title: Exemption from taxes on electricity
articles.officialText: Save in so far as Parliament may by law otherwise provide, no law of a State shall impose, or authorise the imposition of, a tax on the consumption or sale of electricity (whether produced by a Government or other persons) which is — (a) consumed by the Government of India, or sold to the Government of India for consumption by that Government; or (b) consumed in the construction, maintenance or operation of any railway by the Government of India...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article exempts electricity consumed by the Union Government and Indian Railways from State taxation, unless Parliament permits otherwise. It is a specific application of the inter-governmental tax immunity principle. The provision ensures that essential Union functions (defense, railways, central administration) are not burdened by varying State electricity duties, promoting uniformity and operational efficiency.

landmarkCase.citation: Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board v. Andhra Pradesh Electricity Regulatory Commission (2003)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court analyzed the scope of inter-governmental tax immunities in electricity. It held that Article 287's exemption is strictly limited to specified Union purposes, and States retain plenary power to tax electricity consumption by all other consumers, including private and commercial entities.

articles.title: Exemption from taxation by States in respect of water or electricity in certain cases
articles.officialText: Save in so far as the President may by order otherwise provide, no law of a State in force immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall impose, or authorise the imposition of, a tax in respect of any water or electricity stored, generated, consumed, distributed or sold by any authority established by any existing law or any law made by Parliament for regulating or developing any inter-State river or river-valley.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article protects inter-State river valley authorities (like the Damodar Valley Corporation, Bhakra Beas Management Board) from State taxation on water and electricity. Such authorities serve multiple States, and unilateral State taxation would disrupt the joint federal project. States can tax such authorities only with prior Presidential assent and Parliamentary law, ensuring central oversight of inter-State resource sharing.

landmarkCase.citation: Damodar Valley Corporation v. State of Bihar (1976)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court upheld the immunity of DVC from State taxation on its electricity generation, holding that Article 288 creates a constitutional shield for inter-State river valley projects. The Court reinforced that such joint federal enterprises require protection from unilateral State action to function effectively.

articles.title: Exemption of property and income of a State from Union taxation
articles.officialText: The property and income of a State shall be exempt from Union taxation. Nothing in clause (1) shall prevent the Union from imposing, or authorising the imposition of, any tax to such extent, if any, as Parliament may by law provide in respect of a trade or business of any kind carried on by, or on behalf of, the Government of a State, or any operations connected therewith, or any property used or occupied for the purposes of such trade or business, or any income accruing or arising in connection therewith.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article is the reciprocal of Article 285 — State property and income are exempt from Union taxation. However, when States engage in commercial 'trade or business' (like running hotels, transport corporations), Parliament can tax such activities to ensure level playing field with private operators. The distinction between 'governmental functions' (exempt) and 'commercial functions' (taxable) is a key constitutional question.

landmarkCase.citation: In Re: Sea Customs Act (1963)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court evolved the doctrine that immunity under Articles 285 and 289 applies to direct taxes, not indirect taxes (customs, excise) which are essentially on goods, not property. The Court distinguished between sovereign and commercial functions of governments and laid down the framework for inter-governmental tax immunities in India.

articles.title: Adjustment in respect of certain expenses and pensions
articles.officialText: Where under the provisions of this Constitution the expenses of any court or Commission, or the pension payable to or in respect of a person who has served before the commencement of this Constitution under the Crown in India or after such commencement in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State, are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India or the Consolidated Fund of a State, then, if — (a) in the case of a charge on the Consolidated Fund of India, the court or Commission serves any of the separate needs of a State... an appropriate contribution... shall be made.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article ensures equitable cost-sharing for expenses and pensions that serve multiple governments. For example, if a High Court serves multiple States (like Punjab and Haryana HC), or a Commission serves Union and States, the costs and pensions are apportioned. The President/Governor or independent arbitrators determine the apportionment, ensuring no government bears the burden of facilities used by others.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Haryana v. State of Punjab (Reorganization Cases)
landmarkCase.summary: Following State reorganizations, the Supreme Court has dealt with cost-sharing disputes between successor States. The Court has consistently applied Article 290's principles of equitable apportionment, ensuring constitutional bodies serving multiple States receive proportionate funding from each.

articles.title: Annual payment to certain Devaswom Funds
articles.officialText: A sum of forty-six lakhs and fifty thousand rupees shall be charged on, and paid out of, the Consolidated Fund of the State of Kerala every year to the Travancore Devaswom Fund; and a sum of thirteen lakhs and fifty thousand rupees shall be charged on, and paid out of, the Consolidated Fund of the State of Tamil Nadu every year to the Devaswom Fund established in that State for the maintenance of Hindu temples and shrines in the territories transferred to that State on the 1st day of November, 1956, from the State of Travancore-Cochin.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Inserted by the 7th Amendment (1956) during States Reorganization, this article ensures perpetual funding for Hindu temple administration in Kerala (Travancore Devaswom) and Tamil Nadu (areas transferred from Travancore-Cochin). It is a unique constitutional provision honoring pre-existing royal commitments to temple maintenance, preserving religious heritage despite political reorganization. The amounts are fixed and charged on State Consolidated Funds.

landmarkCase.citation: Sabarimala Case — Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (2018)
landmarkCase.summary: While primarily on women's entry rights, the Supreme Court discussed the Travancore Devaswom Board's constitutional status under Article 290A. The Court recognized the Board as a statutory authority funded under constitutional mandate, subject to constitutional principles of equality and non-discrimination.

articles.title: Privy purse sums of Rulers (Omitted)
articles.officialText: Omitted by the Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1971.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article originally guaranteed 'privy purses' — annual tax-free payments to rulers of former princely States who acceded to India. After Independence, these payments were a contractual commitment in instruments of accession. The 26th Amendment (1971) abolished privy purses and princely privileges, deeming them inconsistent with republican equality. The Supreme Court had earlier struck down executive de-recognition, leading to this constitutional amendment.

landmarkCase.citation: Madhav Rao Scindia v. Union of India (1971)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court struck down the Presidential Order de-recognizing rulers and abolishing privy purses as unconstitutional. This led to the 26th Amendment formally abolishing privy purses. The case is a landmark on the limits of executive power and the use of constitutional amendments to override judicial decisions, foreshadowing the basic structure doctrine.

articles.title: Borrowing by the Government of India
articles.officialText: The executive power of the Union extends to borrowing upon the security of the Consolidated Fund of India within such limits, if any, as may from time to time be fixed by Parliament by law and to the giving of guarantees within such limits, if any, as may be so fixed.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article empowers the Union Government to borrow domestically or internationally on the security of the Consolidated Fund and to give guarantees. Parliament may impose statutory ceilings on such borrowing. The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003 provides such limits. This article is crucial for managing public debt and ensuring fiscal sustainability of the Union.

landmarkCase.citation: Public Interest cases on Fiscal Responsibility
landmarkCase.summary: Courts have generally treated borrowing decisions as matters of executive and legislative policy, with limited judicial review. However, the FRBM framework under Article 292 has been recognized as a self-imposed legislative check, and the constitutional scheme requires transparency in public debt management.

articles.title: Borrowing by States
articles.officialText: Subject to the provisions of this article, the executive power of a State extends to borrowing within the territory of India upon the security of the Consolidated Fund of the State within such limits, if any, as may from time to time be fixed by the Legislature of such State by law and to the giving of guarantees within such limits, if any, as may be so fixed.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: States can borrow within India on the security of their Consolidated Fund, subject to State legislative limits. Crucially, if a State has an outstanding loan from the Union (or guaranteed by it), it cannot borrow further without the Union's consent. This gives the Union significant leverage over State finances. The Union can impose conditions while granting consent, which has been a source of Centre-State friction, especially regarding off-budget borrowings.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Kerala v. Union of India (2024)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court examined the Union's power under Article 293(3) to impose borrowing limits on States. The case raised significant questions on fiscal federalism, off-budget borrowings, and whether Union conditions on State borrowing violate State autonomy. The judgment is shaping modern Centre-State fiscal relations.

articles.title: Succession to property, assets, rights, liabilities and obligations in certain cases
articles.officialText: As from the commencement of this Constitution — (a) all property and assets which immediately before such commencement were vested in His Majesty for the purposes of the Government of the Dominion of India and all property and assets which immediately before such commencement were vested in His Majesty for the purposes of the Government of each Governor's Province shall vest respectively in the Union and the corresponding State...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This is a transitional provision ensuring legal continuity from British rule to the Republic. All property, assets, rights, and liabilities of the pre-Constitutional governments (Dominion of India and Governor's Provinces) automatically vested in the Union and corresponding States respectively.
