This prevented legal vacuum and ensured the new Republic inherited the functional apparatus of the colonial state without disruption.

landmarkCase.citation: Union of India v. Ladulal Jain (1963)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court applied Article 294 to determine succession of pre-Constitutional contractual liabilities. The Court held that the Union and States automatically succeeded to all rights and liabilities of their predecessor governments, ensuring continuity of legal relationships and contractual obligations across the constitutional transition.

articles.title: Succession to property, assets, rights, liabilities and obligations in other cases
articles.officialText: As from the commencement of this Constitution — (a) all property and assets which immediately before such commencement were vested in any Indian State corresponding to a State specified in Part B of the First Schedule shall vest in the Union, if the purposes for which such property and assets were held immediately before such commencement will thereafter be purposes of the Union relating to any of the matters enumerated in the Union List...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article governs succession of property and obligations from the former princely States (Part B States) to the Union or States, based on the nature of the asset's use. Assets used for Union List purposes vest in the Union; those for State List purposes vest in the State. This provision integrated the assets of integrated princely States into the Indian Union, completing the territorial and administrative integration post-Independence.

landmarkCase.citation: Maharaja Pravir Chandra Bhanj Deo v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1965)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court interpreted Article 295 in disputes over princely State assets, holding that the article ensures functional succession — assets follow their constitutional purpose. The judgment clarified that erstwhile princely State properties became Union or State assets based on the subject matter to which they related under the Seventh Schedule.

articles.title: Property accruing by escheat or lapse or as bona vacantia
articles.officialText: Subject as hereinafter provided, any property in the territory of India which, if this Constitution had not come into operation, would have accrued to His Majesty or, as the case may be, to the Ruler of an Indian State by escheat or lapse, or as bona vacantia for want of a rightful owner, shall, if it is property situate in a State, vest in such State, and shall, in any other case, vest in the Union.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article codifies the common law doctrines of 'escheat' (property reverting on death without heirs), 'lapse' (failure of succession), and 'bona vacantia' (ownerless property) for the Indian Republic. Such property vests in the State if located within a State, otherwise in the Union. The article replaces the sovereign's prerogative under British law with constitutional inheritance — the State as the ultimate heir to abandoned/ownerless property.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Bihar v. Radha Krishna Singh (1983)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the State's right to bona vacantia under Article 296 is not automatic — it must be established that no rightful heir exists. The Court emphasized that escheat and bona vacantia are claims of last resort, and the State cannot use them to defeat genuine succession rights.

articles.title: Things of value within territorial waters or continental shelf and resources of the exclusive economic zone to vest in the Union
articles.officialText: All lands, minerals and other things of value underlying the ocean within the territorial waters, or the continental shelf, or the exclusive economic zone, of India shall vest in the Union and be held for the purposes of the Union. All other resources of the exclusive economic zone of India shall also vest in the Union and be held for the purposes of the Union.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article vests all maritime resources — within territorial waters (12 nautical miles), continental shelf, and Exclusive Economic Zone (200 nautical miles) — in the Union. This includes minerals, oil, gas, fisheries, and seabed resources. Originally narrower, the article was expanded by the 40th Amendment (1976) reflecting UNCLOS principles. Parliament's law (Maritime Zones Act, 1976) operationalizes these limits.

landmarkCase.citation: Reliance Natural Resources Ltd. v. Reliance Industries Ltd. (2010) — Krishna-Godavari Gas Case
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that natural gas from offshore basins vests in the Union under Article 297, making it a national resource. The Court ruled that gas pricing and allocation are matters of national policy under the public trust doctrine, and private agreements cannot override the Union's constitutional ownership of maritime resources.

articles.title: Power to carry on trade, etc.
articles.officialText: The executive power of the Union and of each State shall extend to the carrying on of any trade or business and to the acquisition, holding and disposal of property and the making of contracts for any purpose: Provided that — (a) the said executive power of the Union shall, in so far as such trade or business or such purpose is not one with respect to which Parliament may make laws, be subject in each State to legislation by the State; and (b) the said executive power of each State shall, in so far as such trade or business or such purpose is not one with respect to which the State Legislature may make laws, be subject to legislation by Parliament.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article empowers the Union and States to carry on trade or business, acquire property, and enter contracts — even on subjects outside their legislative competence. However, when operating outside their legislative domain, they are subject to the other's legislative control. This article forms the constitutional basis for Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) and government commercial activities, recognizing the State's role as a commercial actor.

landmarkCase.citation: Khazan Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1974)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court upheld State trading monopolies under Article 298, holding that the State can engage in commerce even on subjects outside its Legislative List, subject to the other government's legislative power. The judgment recognized the State's evolving role as an economic actor and provided the constitutional foundation for State-led economic development.

articles.title: Contracts
articles.officialText: All contracts made in the exercise of the executive power of the Union or of a State shall be expressed to be made by the President, or by the Governor of the State, as the case may be, and all such contracts and all assurances of property made in the exercise of that power shall be executed on behalf of the President or the Governor by such persons and in such manner as he may direct or authorise.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article prescribes the formal requirements for valid government contracts: (1) expressed to be made by the President/Governor; (2) executed on their behalf by authorized persons; and (3) in the prescribed manner. Non-compliance renders the contract unenforceable against the government. The article protects public funds from unauthorized commitments while ensuring contractual certainty in government dealings. The President/Governor is not personally liable.

landmarkCase.citation: K.P. Chowdhry v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1967)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that strict compliance with Article 299 is mandatory — contracts not in the prescribed form are void and unenforceable against the government. However, the Court evolved doctrines of restitution and unjust enrichment to provide some relief to parties who supplied goods/services in good faith. The judgment shapes all government contracting in India.

articles.title: Suits and proceedings
articles.officialText: The Government of India may sue or be sued by the name of the Union of India and the Government of a State may sue or be sued by the name of the State and may, subject to any provisions which may be made by Act of Parliament or of the Legislature of such State enacted by virtue of powers conferred by this Constitution, sue or be sued in relation to their respective affairs in the like cases as the Dominion of India and the corresponding Provinces or the corresponding Indian States might have sued or been sued if this Constitution had not been enacted.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article enables the Union and States to sue and be sued in their own names. It preserves the pre-Constitutional position on government liability until Parliament/Legislature enacts a comprehensive law. The vexed question of distinction between 'sovereign' and 'non-sovereign' functions for tortious liability flows from this article. Despite Law Commission recommendations, no comprehensive Government Liability Act has been enacted, leaving the law judge-made.

landmarkCase.citation: Kasturilal v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1965) and N. Nagendra Rao v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1994)
landmarkCase.summary: In Kasturilal, the Court applied the sovereign immunity doctrine, denying liability for police negligence. In N. Nagendra Rao, the Court substantially narrowed sovereign immunity, holding that in a welfare State, government liability is the rule and immunity is the exception. Modern jurisprudence under Article 300 increasingly favors government accountability for wrongful acts.

articles.title: Persons not to be deprived of property save by authority of law
articles.officialText: No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Inserted by the 44th Amendment (1978), this article replaced the fundamental right to property (Articles 19(1)(f) and 31) with a constitutional right. While no longer a fundamental right enforceable under Article 32, deprivation of property requires 'authority of law' — meaning valid legislation, fair procedure, and a public purpose. Compensation, though not constitutionally mandated, must generally be just and fair under modern jurisprudence.

landmarkCase.citation: K.T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka (2011)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that Article 300A, though not a fundamental right, is a 'constitutional right' and a 'human right'. Deprivation of property requires (1) a valid law, (2) public purpose, and (3) payment of compensation that is not illusory. The judgment significantly strengthened property rights protection despite their demotion from Part III, embedding fair compensation as a constitutional requirement.

partTitle: Trade, Commerce and Intercourse within the Territory of India (Articles 301-307)

articles.title: Freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse
articles.officialText: Subject to the other provisions of this Part, trade, commerce and intercourse throughout the territory of India shall be free.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article guarantees free movement of trade, commerce, and intercourse across India — making India a single economic unit. It prohibits arbitrary State barriers that impede inter-State trade. However, this freedom is not absolute and is subject to reasonable restrictions under Articles 302-305. This article is the foundation of India's common market and complements the GST framework.

landmarkCase.citation: Atiabari Tea Co. v. State of Assam (1961) and Automobile Transport v. State of Rajasthan (1962)
landmarkCase.summary: In Atiabari, the Court held that taxes which directly and immediately restrict trade violate Article 301. In Automobile Transport, the Court refined this with the 'compensatory tax' doctrine — taxes that facilitate trade (like road tolls) are not violations. These twin judgments shape India's inter-State trade jurisprudence.

articles.title: Power of Parliament to impose restrictions on trade, commerce and intercourse
articles.officialText: Parliament may by law impose such restrictions on the freedom of trade, commerce or intercourse between one State and another or within any part of the territory of India as may be required in the public interest.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Parliament can restrict the freedom under Article 301 if 'public interest' so requires. Unlike States (Article 304), Parliament's power is not subject to Presidential sanction or non-discrimination requirements. This allows the Union to manage essential commodities, control inter-State trade in scarce resources, and respond to national economic challenges.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Mysore v. Sanjeeviah (1967)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that 'public interest' under Article 302 is a broad concept giving Parliament wide latitude to regulate inter-State and intra-State trade. However, the restrictions must have a rational nexus with the stated public interest and cannot be arbitrary or excessive.

articles.title: Restrictions on the legislative powers of the Union and of the States with regard to trade and commerce
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding anything in article 302, neither Parliament nor the Legislature of a State shall have power to make any law giving, or authorising the giving of, any preference to one State over another, or making, or authorising the making of, any discrimination between one State and another, by virtue of any entry relating to trade and commerce in any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article prohibits both Parliament and State Legislatures from enacting laws that discriminate between States in trade and commerce. The exception allows Parliament to declare and act on scarcity of goods in any part of India. This ensures formal equality between States in the national economic space, preventing favoritism that could distort the common market.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Madras v. N.K. Nataraja Mudaliar (1969)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that Article 303 prohibits direct and discriminatory preferences but does not bar reasonable classifications based on objective criteria. Differential treatment based on relevant economic factors does not violate the equality mandate as long as it serves legitimate public purposes.

articles.title: Restrictions on trade, commerce and intercourse among States
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding anything in article 301 or article 303, the Legislature of a State may by law — (a) impose on goods imported from other States or the Union territories any tax to which similar goods manufactured or produced in that State are subject, so, however, as not to discriminate between goods so imported and goods so manufactured or produced; and (b) impose such reasonable restrictions on the freedom of trade, commerce or intercourse with or within that State as may be required in the public interest...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article allows States to: (a) tax imported goods on par with locally produced goods (non-discrimination); and (b) impose reasonable restrictions on trade in public interest, but only with prior Presidential sanction. The non-discrimination principle (304(a)) is the cornerstone of inter-State commerce — States cannot use taxation to protect local industries against goods from other States.

landmarkCase.citation: Jindal Stainless Ltd. v. State of Haryana (2016) — 9-Judge Bench
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court overruled the 'compensatory tax' doctrine and held that taxes per se do not violate Article 301 unless they are discriminatory under Article 304(a). The judgment substantially clarified inter-State trade jurisprudence and upheld State entry taxes that are non-discriminatory. This is the modern leading case on free trade within India.

articles.title: Saving of existing laws and laws providing for State monopolies
articles.officialText: Nothing in articles 301 and 303 shall affect the provisions of any existing law except in so far as the President may by order otherwise direct; and nothing in article 301 shall affect the operation of any law made before the commencement of the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, in so far as it relates to, or prevent Parliament or the Legislature of a State from making any law relating to, any such matter as is referred to in sub-clause (ii) of clause (6) of article 19.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This is a savings provision: (1) Pre-Constitutional laws on trade are protected from Articles 301 and 303 unless the President orders otherwise; and (2) State monopolies (carrying on any trade exclusively) are not subject to Article 301. This protects State commercial enterprises and ensures continuity of pre-Constitutional regulatory frameworks during transition.

landmarkCase.citation: Saghir Ahmad v. State of UP (1954)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court analyzed State monopolies and their interaction with free trade under Article 301. The principles laid down were later incorporated into Article 305 by the 4th Amendment (1955), expressly protecting State monopoly laws from challenges under inter-State trade freedom.

articles.title: Power of certain States in Part B of the First Schedule to impose restrictions on trade and commerce (Omitted)
articles.officialText: Omitted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article originally allowed Part B States (former princely States) to continue pre-Constitutional restrictions on trade and commerce, giving them transitional flexibility. The 7th Amendment (1956), which abolished the Part A/B/C/D classification of States during reorganization, made this article obsolete and it was omitted. The provision reflects the constitutional transition from princely autonomy to unified federal structure.

landmarkCase.citation: States Reorganisation Act, 1956 implementation
landmarkCase.summary: Post-1956, the Supreme Court has consistently held that all States stand on equal footing regarding trade and commerce regulations. The omission of Article 306 finalized the transition to uniform federal trade architecture, eliminating any special privileges of former princely States.

articles.title: Appointment of authority for carrying out the purposes of articles 301 to 304
articles.officialText: Parliament may by law appoint such authority as it considers appropriate for carrying out the purposes of articles 301, 302, 303 and 304, and confer on the authority so appointed such powers and such duties as it thinks necessary.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Parliament can establish an authority to oversee inter-State trade and ensure compliance with Articles 301-304. Despite this constitutional provision, no such permanent authority has been created, leaving inter-State trade disputes largely to judicial resolution. The Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions recommended creating such an authority, possibly within the Inter-State Council, but it remains unimplemented.

landmarkCase.citation: Recommendations of Sarkaria Commission on Centre-State Relations (1988)
landmarkCase.summary: While no court case directly relates to Article 307, the Sarkaria Commission noted the constitutional gap created by non-establishment of such an authority. The Supreme Court in inter-State trade cases has effectively performed this function judicially, but expert opinion favors a specialized administrative body.

articles.title: Superintendence, direction and control of elections to be vested in an Election Commission
articles.officialText: The superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of the electoral rolls for, and the conduct of, all elections to Parliament and to the Legislature of every State and of elections to the offices of President and Vice-President held under this Constitution shall be vested in a Commission (referred to in this Constitution as the Election Commission).
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This is the cornerstone of Indian electoral democracy. It vests in the Election Commission of India (ECI) plenary powers of superintendence, direction, and control over all elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President. The ECI is a multi-member body (Chief Election Commissioner + 2 Election Commissioners since 1993). The phrase 'superintendence, direction and control' has been interpreted expansively to include all powers necessary for free and fair elections, including residuary powers where law is silent.

landmarkCase.citation: Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner (1978)
landmarkCase.summary: Justice Krishna Iyer held that Article 324 is a 'reservoir of power' empowering the ECI to take all measures necessary for free and fair elections where existing law is silent. The Court emphasized that the ECI's plenary powers must be exercised consistent with rule of law and natural justice. This judgment established the ECI's vast residuary authority.

articles.title: No person to be ineligible for inclusion in, or to claim to be included in a special, electoral roll on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex
articles.officialText: There shall be one general electoral roll for every territorial constituency for election to either House of Parliament or to the House or either House of the Legislature of a State and no person shall be ineligible for inclusion in any such roll or claim to be included in any special electoral roll for any such constituency on grounds only of religion, race, caste or sex.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article enshrines two foundational principles: (1) ONE general electoral roll for every constituency — abolishing the colonial system of separate electorates based on religion (Muslim, Sikh) that the British had introduced; and (2) NON-DISCRIMINATION — no person can be excluded from the electoral roll or claim inclusion in a 'special' roll based on religion, race, caste, or sex. This article is a powerful affirmation of secular, inclusive democracy and rejects communal electorates that had divided pre-Independence India.

landmarkCase.citation: Indian Union Muslim League v. State of Kerala (Reservation in Local Bodies cases)
landmarkCase.summary: Courts have consistently upheld Article 325's principle of single electoral roll. The Supreme Court has held that any attempt to create religion-based or caste-based separate electorates violates the basic structure of secular democracy. This article was crucial to nation-building by ensuring equal political citizenship.

articles.title: Elections to the House of the People and to the Legislative Assemblies of States to be on the basis of adult suffrage
articles.officialText: The elections to the House of the People and to the Legislative Assembly of every State shall be on the basis of adult suffrage; that is to say, every person who is a citizen of India and who is not less than eighteen years of age on such date as may be fixed in that behalf by or under any law made by the appropriate Legislature and is not otherwise disqualified under this Constitution or any law made by the appropriate Legislature on the ground of non-residence, unsoundness of mind, crime or corrupt or illegal practice, shall be entitled to be registered as a voter at any such election.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article guarantees Universal Adult Suffrage — every Indian citizen aged 18+ has the right to vote in Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly elections. The original voting age was 21, reduced to 18 by the 61st Amendment (1989). Disqualifications are limited to non-residence, unsoundness of mind, crime, or corrupt/illegal electoral practices. India adopted universal adult suffrage from the very beginning — a radical and visionary choice in 1950 when many democracies still restricted franchise based on property, literacy, or gender.

landmarkCase.citation: PUCL v. Union of India (2003) — NOTA and Right to Vote case
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that the right to vote, while statutory in form, has constitutional protection under Article 326. The Court mandated NOTA (None of the Above) option, recognizing the voter's right of negative choice. The judgment strengthened universal adult suffrage by ensuring meaningful electoral participation.

articles.title: Power of Parliament to make provision with respect to elections to Legislatures
articles.officialText: Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, Parliament may from time to time by law make provision with respect to all matters relating to, or in connection with, elections to either House of Parliament or to the House or either House of the Legislature of a State including the preparation of electoral rolls, the delimitation of constituencies and all other matters necessary for securing the due constitution of such House or Houses.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Parliament has the power to legislate on ALL matters relating to elections to Parliament and State Legislatures — including electoral rolls, delimitation, conduct of elections, election offences, and election disputes. The Representation of People Acts, 1950 and 1951 are enacted under this article. Parliament's power is plenary but subject to the Constitution itself, particularly Article 324 (ECI's powers) and fundamental rights.

landmarkCase.citation: Kanhiya Lal Omar v. R.K. Trivedi (1985)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court interpreted Article 327, holding that Parliament's plenary power must coexist with the ECI's plenary power under Article 324. Where Parliament has not legislated, the ECI's directions under Article 324 fill the gap. This established the constitutional balance between parliamentary lawmaking and Election Commission's executive authority.

articles.title: Power of Legislature of a State to make provision with respect to elections to such Legislature
articles.officialText: Subject to the provisions of this Constitution and in so far as provision in that behalf is not made by Parliament, the Legislature of a State may from time to time by law make provision with respect to all matters relating to, or in connection with, the elections to the House or either House of the Legislature of the State including the preparation of electoral rolls and all other matters necessary for securing the due constitution of such House or Houses.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: State Legislatures have residual power to legislate on State elections — but only on matters NOT covered by Parliament. Parliament's power under Article 327 takes precedence. In practice, since Parliament has comprehensively covered State elections through the RP Acts, the scope for State legislation is limited. This reflects the constitutional preference for national uniformity in electoral matters.

landmarkCase.citation: Election Commission of India v. State of Tamil Nadu (1995)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that State Legislatures cannot legislate on matters already covered by parliamentary law on elections. Article 328 operates only in the legislative space left vacant by Parliament. This judgment reinforced the supremacy of central electoral legislation and the unified national framework for elections.

articles.title: Bar to interference by courts in electoral matters
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution — (a) the validity of any law relating to the delimitation of constituencies or the allotment of seats to such constituencies, made or purporting to be made under article 327 or article 328, shall not be called in question in any court; (b) no election to either House of Parliament or to the House or either House of the Legislature of a State shall be called in question except by an election petition presented to such authority and in such manner as may be provided for by or under any law made by the appropriate Legislature.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article bars judicial interference in two areas: (1) delimitation laws cannot be challenged in any court; and (2) elections can only be challenged through 'election petitions' filed before specified tribunals (High Courts under the RP Act, 1951). This ensures elections are completed without judicial disruption — challenges come AFTER the election. The word 'election' here covers the entire process from notification to declaration of results.

landmarkCase.citation: Mohinder Singh Gill v. CEC (1978) and N.P. Ponnuswami v. Returning Officer (1952)
landmarkCase.summary: In Ponnuswami, the Supreme Court held that 'election' is a continuous process and any intermediate challenge is barred by Article 329(b). In Mohinder Singh Gill, the Court clarified that the bar applies only to the actual election process; pre-notification or post-election administrative actions can be challenged under Article 226. These cases shape Indian election dispute jurisprudence.

articles.title: Special provision as to elections to Parliament in the case of Prime Minister and Speaker (Omitted)
articles.officialText: Omitted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This notorious article was inserted by the 39th Amendment (1975) during Emergency to immunize the Prime Minister's election from judicial review. It was a direct response to the Allahabad High Court setting aside Indira Gandhi's election. The Supreme Court in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) struck it down as violating the basic structure (rule of law, free elections, judicial review). The 44th Amendment (1978) formally omitted it. This article and its judicial fate are central to the basic structure doctrine.

landmarkCase.citation: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court struck down clause (4) of Article 329A as violating the basic structure — specifically the principles of free and fair elections, rule of law, and judicial review. This was the FIRST application of the basic structure doctrine after Kesavananda Bharati. The case affirmed that even constitutional amendments cannot immunize specific persons from electoral accountability. A foundational basic structure case.

partTitle: Special Provisions Relating to Certain Classes (Articles 330-342A) — Key Articles

articles.title: Reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the House of the People
articles.officialText: Seats shall be reserved in the House of the People for — (a) the Scheduled Castes; (b) the Scheduled Tribes except the Scheduled Tribes in the autonomous districts of Assam; and (c) the Scheduled Tribes in the autonomous districts of Assam.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article reserves Lok Sabha seats for SCs and STs proportional to their population. Reservations were originally for 10 years but have been extended periodically — most recently by the 104th Amendment (2020) extending till 2030. Reservation operates on rotation among constituencies. This is a measure of substantive equality, ensuring political representation of historically marginalized communities in the national legislature.

landmarkCase.citation: Krishna Chandra Gangopadhyaya v. Union of India (1975)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court upheld SC/ST reservations in legislative bodies as a constitutional mandate for inclusive democracy. The Court emphasized that political reservation under Article 330 is essential for substantive equality and does not violate the equality clause but actively promotes it through compensatory representation.

articles.title: Representation of the Anglo-Indian community in the House of the People (Effectively ceased)
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding anything in article 81, the President may, if he is of opinion that the Anglo-Indian community is not adequately represented in the House of the People, nominate not more than two members of that community to the House of the People. [Discontinued by 104th Amendment, 2020]
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article allowed the President to nominate up to 2 Anglo-Indians to Lok Sabha for adequate representation. The 104th Amendment (2020) discontinued this provision, citing the small community size based on the 2011 census. The provision reflected constitutional sensitivity to minority representation but was discontinued through proper constitutional process.

landmarkCase.citation: 104th Constitutional Amendment Debates (2020)
landmarkCase.summary: While no major judicial case challenged the discontinuation, the parliamentary debates emphasized that nomination was meant as a transitional protection. The community had been adequately integrated into mainstream politics, and the provision had outlived its constitutional purpose.

articles.title: Reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Legislative Assemblies of the States
articles.officialText: Seats shall be reserved for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes, except the Scheduled Tribes in the autonomous districts of Assam, in the Legislative Assembly of every State.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article mirrors Article 330 for State Legislative Assemblies — reserving seats for SCs and STs proportional to their State population. Special provisions exist for tribal areas of Assam and certain northeastern States. Combined with Articles 243D and 243T (panchayat/municipality reservations), this creates a comprehensive system of political reservation at all levels of Indian federalism.

landmarkCase.citation: K. Krishna Murthy v. Union of India (2010)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court upheld political reservations for SCs/STs at all levels as constitutionally mandated. The Court distinguished political reservation from job/education reservation, holding that the 50% ceiling does not apply to political reservation, which has its own constitutional logic of inclusive democracy.

articles.title: Representation of the Anglo-Indian community in the Legislative Assemblies of the States (Effectively ceased)
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding anything in article 170, the Governor of a State may, if he is of opinion that the Anglo-Indian community needs representation in the Legislative Assembly of the State and is not adequately represented therein, nominate one member of that community to the Assembly. [Discontinued by 104th Amendment, 2020]
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Parallel to Article 331, this allowed Governor nomination of 1 Anglo-Indian to State Legislative Assemblies. Discontinued by 104th Amendment (2020). The provision was used in States with historical Anglo-Indian populations like Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and West Bengal.

landmarkCase.citation: Anglo-Indian Representation Debates (104th Amendment)
landmarkCase.summary: No major judicial pronouncement, but the discontinuation reflected demographic changes and integration of the community. The constitutional principle of adequate minority representation was preserved through other mechanisms.

articles.title: Reservation of seats and special representation to cease after certain period
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Part, the provisions of this Constitution relating to — (a) the reservation of seats for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes in the House of the People and in the Legislative Assemblies of the States; and (b) the representation of the Anglo-Indian community in the House of the People and in the Legislative Assemblies of the States by nomination, shall cease to have effect on the expiration of a period of eighty years from the commencement of this Constitution. [Extended periodically; SC/ST reservation till 2030 by 104th Amendment]
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This is the 'sunset clause' for political reservations. Originally for 10 years, it has been extended every decade — 8 times so far. The 104th Amendment (2020) extended SC/ST reservation till 25 January 2030 (80 years from Constitution's commencement) and discontinued Anglo-Indian nomination. The repeated extensions reflect the unfinished agenda of substantive political equality, though some argue for permanent reservation.

landmarkCase.citation: Ashoka Kumar Thakur v. Union of India (2008)
landmarkCase.summary: While addressing OBC reservations, the Supreme Court discussed the constitutional rationale for reservations including political reservations under Article 334. The Court emphasized that the periodic extension reflects ongoing social realities, but reservations cannot be perpetual; they must be reviewed against changing socio-economic conditions.

articles.title: Claims of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes to services and posts
articles.officialText: The claims of the members of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes shall be taken into consideration, consistently with the maintenance of efficiency of administration, in the making of appointments to services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State: Provided that nothing in this article shall prevent in making of any provision in favour of the members of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes for relaxation in qualifying marks in any examination or lowering the standards of evaluation, for reservation in matters of promotion to any class or classes of services or posts in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article mandates consideration of SC/ST claims in public employment 'consistent with efficiency of administration'. The proviso, added by the 82nd Amendment (2000), expressly permits relaxation in qualifying marks and standards for SC/STs, overcoming earlier judicial concerns. This article is the constitutional basis for reservations in government jobs and promotions, balancing affirmative action with administrative efficiency.

landmarkCase.citation: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) — Mandal Case
landmarkCase.summary: The 9-judge bench upheld reservations under Article 335 but capped them at 50%, excluded creamy layer, and prohibited reservation in promotions (later overturned by 77th Amendment). The judgment balanced Article 335's efficiency clause with substantive equality and remains the foundational case on reservation jurisprudence.

articles.title: Special provision for Anglo-Indian community in certain services (Effectively spent)
articles.officialText: During the first two years after the commencement of this Constitution, appointments of members of the Anglo-Indian community to posts in the railway, customs, postal and telegraph services of the Union shall be made on the same basis as immediately before the fifteenth day of August, 1947...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This was a transitional provision protecting Anglo-Indian employment in colonial-era services (railways, customs, posts, telegraph) immediately after independence. The protections phased out over 10 years, with reservations reducing by 10% every 2 years. This article reflects the constitutional commitment to gradual transition rather than abrupt disruption for communities dependent on specific occupations.

landmarkCase.citation: Anglo-Indian Employment Transition Cases
landmarkCase.summary: Courts upheld the gradual phase-out as a reasonable transitional mechanism. The provision is now spent, but it stands as a constitutional model for managing community-specific employment transitions sensitively.

articles.title: Special provision with respect to educational grants for the benefit of Anglo-Indian community (Spent)
articles.officialText: During the first three financial years after the commencement of this Constitution, the same grants, if any, shall be made by the Union and by each State for the benefit of the Anglo-Indian community in respect of education as were made in the financial year ending on the thirty-first day of March, 1948. During every succeeding period of three years the grants may be less by ten per cent than those for the immediately preceding period of three years...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article protected educational grants to Anglo-Indian schools, reducing 10% every 3 years till 1960. It recognized the community's distinctive educational institutions (many missionary and English-medium schools) and provided gradual transition. The provision has long since become spent, but the educational institutions continue under general constitutional protections for minority educational rights (Article 30).

landmarkCase.citation: T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002)
landmarkCase.summary: While not directly on Article 337, the Supreme Court's principles on minority educational institutions inform the legacy of this provision. Anglo-Indian schools now operate under Article 30 protections as religious or linguistic minority institutions.

articles.title: National Commission for Scheduled Castes
articles.officialText: There shall be a Commission for the Scheduled Castes to be known as the National Commission for the Scheduled Castes. Subject to the provisions of any law made in this behalf by Parliament, the Commission shall consist of a Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and three other Members and the conditions of service and tenure of office of the Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and other Members so appointed shall be such as the President may by rule determine.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article establishes the National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC) as a constitutional body. Originally a joint commission for SC/ST, separated by the 89th Amendment (2003). The NCSC investigates safeguards for SCs, inquires into complaints, advises on welfare planning, and reports to the President. Its powers include those of a civil court for inquiries. The Commission is a watchdog ensuring constitutional and legal safeguards for SCs are effectively implemented.

landmarkCase.citation: All India Backward Class Federation v. Union of India
landmarkCase.summary: Courts have recognized NCSC's constitutional status and broad investigative powers. The Supreme Court has held that the Commission's recommendations carry significant weight and the government must give them serious consideration, though they are not strictly binding.

articles.title: National Commission for Scheduled Tribes
articles.officialText: There shall be a Commission for the Scheduled Tribes to be known as the National Commission for the Scheduled Tribes. Subject to the provisions of any law made in this behalf by Parliament, the Commission shall consist of a Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and three other Members and the conditions of service and tenure of office of the Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and other Members so appointed shall be such as the President may by rule determine.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Inserted by the 89th Amendment (2003), this article establishes the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) as a separate constitutional body. Previously, ST matters were handled by the combined SC/ST Commission. Separation recognized that ST issues — land alienation, forest rights, Fifth and Sixth Schedule areas, displacement — are qualitatively different and require dedicated focus.

landmarkCase.citation: Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997)
landmarkCase.summary: Though decided before Article 338A's enactment, this case established the constitutional protection of tribal lands in Scheduled Areas. The judgment informed the rationale for creating a dedicated NCST to monitor tribal rights, including land, forest, and self-governance protections under the Fifth and Sixth Schedules.

articles.title: National Commission for Backward Classes
articles.officialText: There shall be a Commission for the socially and educationally backward classes to be known as the National Commission for Backward Classes. Subject to the provisions of any law made in this behalf by Parliament, the Commission shall consist of a Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and three other Members and the conditions of service and tenure of office of the Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and other Members so appointed shall be such as the President may by rule determine.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Inserted by the 102nd Amendment (2018), this article gave constitutional status to the NCBC (previously a statutory body). The Commission examines complaints regarding rights of socially and educationally backward classes, monitors welfare measures, and tenders advice on inclusion/exclusion from the OBC list. The 102nd Amendment also empowered the President to notify the Central OBC List under Article 342A.

landmarkCase.citation: Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v. Chief Minister of Maharashtra (2021) — Maratha Reservation Case
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court interpreted the 102nd Amendment and held that after its enactment, only the President could notify a community as SEBC in the Central List, denying States this power. This was later modified by the 105th Amendment (2021) which restored States' power to identify their own OBC lists, illustrating the dynamic federalism around OBC identification.

articles.title: Control of the Union over the administration of Scheduled Areas and the welfare of Scheduled Tribes
articles.officialText: The President may at any time and shall, at the expiration of ten years from the commencement of this Constitution by order appoint a Commission to report on the administration of the Scheduled Areas and the welfare of the Scheduled Tribes in the States. The executive power of the Union shall extend to the giving of directions to a State as to the drawing up and execution of schemes specified in the direction to be essential for the welfare of the Scheduled Tribes in the State.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article empowers the President to appoint Commissions to report on Scheduled Areas administration and tribal welfare. The Union can give directions to States on essential tribal welfare schemes — a rare instance of Union directive power over States on a State subject. The Bhuria Commission (1995) and Xaxa Committee (2014) are examples. This recognizes that tribal welfare is a national concern transcending State boundaries.

landmarkCase.citation: Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court emphasized the special constitutional protections for tribal areas and the Union's role under Article 339 in safeguarding tribal interests. The judgment reinforced that tribal welfare creates a constitutional obligation that overrides ordinary federal divisions of power.

articles.title: Appointment of a Commission to investigate the conditions of backward classes
articles.officialText: The President may by order appoint a Commission consisting of such persons as he thinks fit to investigate the conditions of socially and educationally backward classes within the territory of India and the difficulties under which they labour and to make recommendations as to the steps that should be taken by the Union or any State to remove such difficulties and to improve their condition and as to the grants that should be made for the purpose by the Union or any State...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article empowers the President to appoint Commissions to investigate backward classes' conditions. The two most famous such Commissions are: (1) Kaka Kalelkar Commission (1953) — first OBC commission, whose report was shelved; and (2) Mandal Commission (1979) — recommended 27% OBC reservation, eventually implemented in 1990 amid massive controversy. This article is the constitutional foundation of OBC identification and welfare in India.

landmarkCase.citation: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) — Mandal Case
landmarkCase.summary: The 9-judge bench validated the Mandal Commission's recommendations under Article 340. The Court upheld OBC reservations subject to: (1) 50% overall ceiling; (2) creamy layer exclusion; (3) no reservation in promotions; and (4) reservation only in initial appointments. This is THE foundational case on OBC reservations and the Article 340 framework.

articles.title: Scheduled Castes
articles.officialText: The President may with respect to any State or Union territory, and where it is a State, after consultation with the Governor thereof, by public notification, specify the castes, races or tribes or parts of or groups within castes, races or tribes which shall for the purposes of this Constitution be deemed to be Scheduled Castes in relation to that State or Union territory, as the case may be. Parliament may by law include in or exclude from the list of Scheduled Castes specified in a notification issued under clause (1) any caste, race or tribe...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article empowers the President to notify the list of Scheduled Castes for each State/UT after consulting the Governor. Once notified, only Parliament can modify the list — States and the President cannot. The Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950 is the foundational notification. Sub-classification within SCs has been a major issue, recently addressed by the Supreme Court in the 7-judge Davinder Singh judgment (2024) allowing State sub-classification.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024) — 7-Judge Bench
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court, overruling E.V. Chinnaiah (2005), held that States can sub-classify Scheduled Castes for reservation purposes to ensure benefits reach the most disadvantaged sub-groups. The Court recognized that SCs are not a homogenous group, and intra-group inequalities require sub-classification. A landmark judgment redefining SC reservation jurisprudence under Article 341.

articles.title: Scheduled Tribes
articles.officialText: The President may with respect to any State or Union territory, and where it is a State, after consultation with the Governor thereof, by public notification, specify the tribes or tribal communities or parts of or groups within tribes or tribal communities which shall for the purposes of this Constitution be deemed to be Scheduled Tribes in relation to that State or Union territory, as the case may be. Parliament may by law include in or exclude from the list of Scheduled Tribes specified in a notification issued under clause (1) any tribe or tribal community...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Parallel to Article 341, this article governs the notification of Scheduled Tribes. The President notifies after consulting the Governor; only Parliament can amend. The Lokur Committee (1965) developed criteria for ST identification: indigeneity, distinctive culture, geographical isolation, shyness of contact, and backwardness. The ST list has expanded over time as communities seek protections; some demands (like the Jat ST demand) have been controversial.

landmarkCase.citation: State of Maharashtra v. Milind (2001)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that no court, tribunal, or authority can hold any community to be a Scheduled Tribe if not notified under Article 342. Modification of ST list is exclusively Parliament's prerogative. This established the rigid constitutional process for ST identification, preventing judicial or executive expansion of the list.

articles.title: Socially and educationally backward classes
articles.officialText: The President may with respect to any State or Union territory, and where it is a State, after consultation with the Governor thereof, by public notification, specify the socially and educationally backward classes in the Central List which shall for the purposes of the Central Government be deemed to be socially and educationally backward classes in relation to that State or Union territory, as the case may be. Every State or Union territory may, by law, prepare and maintain, for its own purposes, a list of socially and educationally backward classes...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Inserted by the 102nd Amendment (2018) and substantively modified by the 105th Amendment (2021), this article governs OBC identification. The 105th Amendment restored States' power to maintain their own SEBC lists for State purposes, while the Central List remains with the President/Parliament. This bifurcated system recognizes federal diversity in backwardness identification while maintaining a unified Central framework.

landmarkCase.citation: Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v. Chief Minister of Maharashtra (2021)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court interpreted the 102nd Amendment to give exclusive OBC identification power to the Centre, triggering the 105th Amendment which restored State power. The case is pivotal in understanding the dynamic constitutional evolution around OBC reservations and the role of constitutional amendments in shaping federal-state relations on social justice issues.

articles.title: Official language of the Union
articles.officialText: The official language of the Union shall be Hindi in Devanagari script. The form of numerals to be used for the official purposes of the Union shall be the international form of Indian numerals. Notwithstanding anything in clause (1), for a period of fifteen years from the commencement of this Constitution, the English language shall continue to be used for all the official purposes of the Union for which it was being used immediately before such commencement...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article declares Hindi in Devanagari script as the official language of the Union and prescribes international Indian numerals. English was to be replaced after 15 years (1965), but the Official Languages Act, 1963 (amended 1967) allowed continued use of English indefinitely alongside Hindi, following anti-Hindi protests in non-Hindi States. India thus has a bilingual official language regime — a pragmatic compromise reflecting linguistic diversity.

landmarkCase.citation: U.P. Hindi Sahitya Sammelan v. State of UP (2014)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court emphasized that Hindi as the official language must coexist with regional languages and English. The constitutional vision under Article 343 is pluralistic, not monolingual. Government must facilitate Hindi's growth while respecting linguistic diversity protected under other constitutional provisions.

articles.title: Directive for development of the Hindi language
articles.officialText: It shall be the duty of the Union to promote the spread of the Hindi language, to develop it so that it may serve as a medium of expression for all the elements of the composite culture of India and to secure its enrichment by assimilating without interfering with its genius, the forms, style and expressions used in Hindustani and in the other languages of India specified in the Eighth Schedule, and by drawing, wherever necessary or desirable, for its vocabulary, primarily on Sanskrit and secondarily on other languages.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This is a directive principle to the Union to develop Hindi as a composite, enriched language. The vision is of an inclusive Hindi that absorbs vocabulary from Sanskrit, Hindustani, and the 22 Eighth Schedule languages — not an imposed, Sanskritized Hindi. This article reflects nation-building through language enrichment, balancing Hindi promotion with linguistic federalism.

landmarkCase.citation: Santosh Kumar v. Secretary, Ministry of Human Resource Development (1994)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court emphasized that promotion of Hindi under Article 351 must be consistent with respecting other Indian languages. The directive must be implemented in a manner that enriches, not displaces, India's linguistic plurality, especially the languages listed in the Eighth Schedule.

articles.title: Proclamation of Emergency
articles.officialText: If the President is satisfied that a grave emergency exists whereby the security of India or of any part of the territory thereof is threatened, whether by war or external aggression or armed rebellion, he may, by Proclamation, make a declaration to that effect in respect of the whole of India or of such part of the territory thereof as may be specified in the Proclamation. Explanation: A Proclamation of Emergency declaring that the security of India or any part of the territory thereof is threatened by war or by external aggression or by armed rebellion may be made before the actual occurrence of war or of any such aggression or rebellion, if the President is satisfied that there is imminent danger thereof.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This is the National Emergency provision. The President can proclaim Emergency on three grounds: (1) WAR; (2) EXTERNAL AGGRESSION; or (3) ARMED REBELLION (originally 'internal disturbance', changed by the 44th Amendment, 1978). Post-44th Amendment safeguards: (a) written Cabinet recommendation required; (b) Parliament must approve within 1 month by 2/3rd special majority of each House; (c) approval continues Emergency for 6 months at a time. Emergencies have been proclaimed thrice: 1962 (China war), 1971 (Bangladesh war), and 1975 (internal disturbance — Indira Gandhi's controversial declaration).

landmarkCase.citation: Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that Proclamation of Emergency is subject to judicial review. The Court rejected the view that Emergency proclamation is a non-justiciable political question. The judgment, building on the safeguards of the 44th Amendment, ensures that even Emergency powers operate within constitutional limits and judicial oversight, preventing repetition of the 1975-77 Emergency abuses.

articles.title: Effect of Proclamation of Emergency
articles.officialText: While a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, then — (a) notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the executive power of the Union shall extend to the giving of directions to any State as to the manner in which the executive power thereof is to be exercised; (b) the power of Parliament to make laws with respect to any matter shall include power to make laws conferring powers and imposing duties, or authorising the conferring of powers and the imposition of duties, upon the Union or officers and authorities of the Union as respects that matter, notwithstanding that it is one which is not enumerated in the Union List.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: During National Emergency, the federal balance shifts dramatically toward the Union: (1) Union can direct States on the exercise of their executive power — converting federal structure to near-unitary; (2) Parliament can legislate on State List subjects — overriding the Seventh Schedule's division of powers. This transformation reflects the framers' recognition that national security demands centralized response, but the 44th Amendment safeguards ensure it cannot be misused.

landmarkCase.citation: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
landmarkCase.summary: While primarily on Article 356, the Court extensively discussed emergency provisions and held that federal structure is part of basic structure. Even during Emergency, the constitutional transformation under Article 353 is temporary and reversible. The unitary tilt cannot become permanent or destroy federalism, which would violate the basic structure.

articles.title: Application of provisions relating to distribution of revenues while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation
articles.officialText: The President may, while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, by order direct that all or any of the provisions of articles 268 to 279 shall for such period, not extending in any case beyond the expiration of the financial year in which such Proclamation ceases to operate, have effect subject to such exceptions or modifications as he thinks fit.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: During Emergency, the President can modify the constitutional revenue-sharing arrangements between Union and States. The Union can redirect funds away from States to meet emergency expenditure. Such orders must be laid before Parliament. The financial federalism architecture (Articles 268-279) can be temporarily suspended or modified, reflecting that emergencies justify reordering even economic relationships between Union and States.

landmarkCase.citation: Bhuvneshwar Prasad Sinha v. Union of India (Emergency-era cases)
landmarkCase.summary: Courts have held that financial modifications under Article 354 are extraordinary measures requiring strict Parliamentary oversight. The temporary nature is critical — once Emergency ends, normal revenue-sharing must resume. The provision cannot be used to permanently alter fiscal federalism.

articles.title: Duty of the Union to protect States against external aggression and internal disturbance
articles.officialText: It shall be the duty of the Union to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance and to ensure that the government of every State is carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article imposes a constitutional duty on the Union to: (1) protect States from external aggression and internal disturbance; and (2) ensure constitutional governance in every State. This is not a power but a duty. It is often invoked as the basis for Union action under Articles 356 and 365. The article reflects the unitary feature within federalism — ultimate responsibility for constitutional governance rests with the Union.

landmarkCase.citation: Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India (2005)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court invoked Article 355 to strike down the IMDT Act, holding that the Union's duty to protect States from external aggression (including illegal migration) is a constitutional obligation. The judgment expanded the scope of 'external aggression' to include large-scale illegal infiltration affecting demographic balance.

articles.title: Provisions in case of failure of constitutional machinery in States
articles.officialText: If the President, on receipt of a report from the Governor of a State or otherwise, is satisfied that a situation has arisen in which the government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution, the President may by Proclamation — (a) assume to himself all or any of the functions of the Government of the State and all or any of the powers vested in or exercisable by the Governor or any body or authority in the State other than the Legislature of the State; (b) declare that the powers of the Legislature of the State shall be exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament; (c) make such incidental and consequential provisions as appear to the President to be necessary or desirable for giving effect to the objects of the Proclamation...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This is the infamous 'President's Rule' provision. When constitutional machinery fails in a State, the President can: (a) take over State government functions; (b) dissolve or suspend State Assembly and have Parliament legislate for the State; and (c) make other consequential provisions. Imposed over 130 times since 1950, often controversially. Safeguards: Parliamentary approval within 2 months, 6-month duration extendable to maximum 3 years (with stricter conditions for second year onwards). The most abused emergency provision until Bommai disciplined its use.

landmarkCase.citation: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
landmarkCase.summary: The 9-judge bench landmark judgment imposed strict judicial review on Article 356: (1) President's satisfaction is justiciable; (2) Floor test is the sole valid mechanism to determine majority; (3) Assembly should be suspended, not dissolved, until Parliament approves; (4) Courts can restore dismissed governments if Proclamation is malafide; (5) Federalism, secularism, democracy are basic structure. The most important judgment on State emergency, dramatically curtailing Centre's abuse of Article 356.

articles.title: Exercise of legislative powers under Proclamation issued under article 356
articles.officialText: Where by a Proclamation issued under clause (1) of article 356, it has been declared that the powers of the Legislature of the State shall be exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament, it shall be competent — (a) for Parliament to confer on the President the power of the Legislature of the State to make laws, and to authorise the President to delegate, subject to such conditions as he may think fit to impose, the power so conferred to any other authority to be specified by him in that behalf; (b) for Parliament, or for the President or other authority in whom such power to make laws is vested under sub-clause (a), to make laws conferring powers and imposing duties, or authorising the conferring of powers and the imposition of duties, upon the Union or officers and authorities thereof...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article details the legislative arrangements during President's Rule. Parliament can: (a) make laws for the State or delegate this to the President, who can sub-delegate; (b) authorize Union officers to perform State functions; and (c) sanction expenditure from State Consolidated Fund. Laws made during President's Rule continue after its revocation until repealed or amended by the State Legislature. This ensures legislative continuity even during constitutional disruption.

landmarkCase.citation: T. Venkata Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1985)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court clarified the validity of laws made during President's Rule under Article 357. Such laws are constitutionally valid and continue after restoration of State government. The judgment ensures stability of legal frameworks created during constitutional emergencies.

articles.title: Suspension of provisions of article 19 during emergencies
articles.officialText: While a Proclamation of Emergency declaring that the security of India or any part of the territory thereof is threatened by war or by external aggression is in operation, nothing in article 19 shall restrict the power of the State as defined in Part III to make any law or to take any executive action which the State would but for the provisions contained in that Part be competent to make or to take, but any law so made shall, to the extent of the incompetency, cease to have effect as soon as the Proclamation ceases to operate, except as respects things done or omitted to be done before the law so ceases to have effect...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: During Emergency due to WAR or EXTERNAL AGGRESSION (NOT armed rebellion, post-44th Amendment), Article 19 (freedoms) is AUTOMATICALLY suspended. The State can pass laws restricting these freedoms without challenge under Article 19. Such laws lapse when Emergency ends, except for acts already done. The 44th Amendment narrowed this — armed rebellion emergencies do NOT suspend Article 19, a critical safeguard against domestic political misuse like in 1975.

landmarkCase.citation: Makhan Singh v. State of Punjab (1964) and post-44th Amendment jurisprudence
landmarkCase.summary: Pre-44th Amendment cases held Article 358's automatic suspension absolute. Post-44th Amendment, the Supreme Court has clarified that suspension applies only to war/external aggression emergencies, not armed rebellion. The 44th Amendment was specifically designed to prevent recurrence of 1975 Emergency abuses where Article 19 freedoms were summarily suspended.

articles.title: Suspension of the enforcement of the rights conferred by Part III during emergencies
articles.officialText: Where a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, the President may by order declare that the right to move any court for the enforcement of such of the rights conferred by Part III (except articles 20 and 21) as may be mentioned in the order and all proceedings pending in any court for the enforcement of the rights so mentioned shall remain suspended for the period during which the Proclamation is in force or for such shorter period as may be specified in the order...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: During Emergency, the President can suspend the ENFORCEMENT (not the rights themselves) of fundamental rights by court order. After the 44th Amendment, Articles 20 (protection in respect of conviction) and 21 (life and liberty) CANNOT be suspended under any circumstances — addressing the dark legacy of ADM Jabalpur (1976). The order specifies which rights and for what duration. This is different from Article 358 which auto-suspends Article 19 only.

landmarkCase.citation: ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976) — Habeas Corpus Case (overruled)
landmarkCase.summary: The infamous 4-1 majority held that even Article 21 could be suspended during Emergency, denying habeas corpus to detainees. Justice H.R. Khanna's lone dissent — that Article 21 reflects natural law inalienable rights — was vindicated by the 44th Amendment (1978) which made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable. The judgment was formally overruled in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017). One of the darkest chapters in Indian constitutional history.

articles.title: Provisions as to financial emergency
articles.officialText: If the President is satisfied that a situation has arisen whereby the financial stability or credit of India or of any part of the territory thereof is threatened, he may by a Proclamation make a declaration to that effect. A Proclamation issued under clause (1) — (a) may be revoked or varied by a subsequent Proclamation; (b) shall be laid before each House of Parliament; (c) shall cease to operate at the expiration of two months, unless before the expiration of that period it has been approved by resolutions of both Houses of Parliament...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This is the Financial Emergency provision — NEVER invoked in India's history. The President can declare it if 'financial stability or credit of India' is threatened. During Financial Emergency: (1) Union can direct States on financial matters; (2) Salaries and allowances of all government servants (including judges) can be reduced; (3) All money bills passed by State Legislatures can be reserved for Presidential consideration. The 2018 demand for Financial Emergency due to economic concerns was rejected; the provision is reserved for extreme economic crises.

landmarkCase.citation: No direct case (never invoked); academic discussion in fiscal federalism cases
landmarkCase.summary: Since Financial Emergency has never been invoked, there is no direct jurisprudence. However, in fiscal federalism cases, courts have noted that Article 360 represents an extreme measure requiring genuine financial crisis. The very threshold of 'financial stability or credit of India' being threatened sets a high bar, and courts would subject any such proclamation to strict judicial scrutiny under Bommai principles.

articles.title: Protection of President and Governors and Rajpramukhs
articles.officialText: The President, or the Governor or Rajpramukh of a State, shall not be answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of his office or for any act done or purporting to be done by him in the exercise and performance of those powers and duties: Provided that the conduct of the President may be brought under review by any court, tribunal or body appointed or designated by either House of Parliament for the investigation of a charge under article 61...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article grants the President and Governors personal immunity: (1) Not answerable to any court for performance of official duties; (2) No criminal proceedings during term of office; (3) No civil proceedings without 2 months' notice for personal acts. The immunity is from courts, not from constitutional accountability — the President can be impeached under Article 61, and gubernatorial acts can be judicially reviewed (though Governor cannot be personally prosecuted). The immunity preserves the dignity and functioning of these high offices.

landmarkCase.citation: Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that while the Governor enjoys personal immunity under Article 361, the Governor's actions are subject to judicial review. The Court can strike down unconstitutional gubernatorial acts (like recommending President's Rule on malafide grounds) without holding the Governor personally liable. This balances personal protection with constitutional accountability.

articles.title: Protection of publication of proceedings of Parliament and State Legislatures
articles.officialText: No person shall be liable to any proceedings, civil or criminal, in any court in respect of the publication in a newspaper of a substantially true report of any proceedings of either House of Parliament or the Legislative Assembly, or, as the case may be, either House of the Legislature of a State, unless the publication is proved to have been made with malice...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Inserted by the 44th Amendment (1978), this article protects media freedom by immunizing newspapers (and by extension other media) from civil/criminal proceedings for fair and substantially true reports of legislative proceedings, unless made with malice. Secret sittings are excluded. This reverses the British common law position and aligns with parliamentary privilege protections. A crucial press freedom provision strengthening democratic transparency.

landmarkCase.citation: Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court has consistently held that press freedom to report legislative proceedings is essential to democracy. Article 361A's protection complements Article 19(1)(a)'s freedom of speech and expression. The judgment recognized that informed citizens are essential for democracy, requiring robust protection for journalists reporting on legislative business.

articles.title: Rights and privileges of Rulers of Indian States (Omitted)
articles.officialText: Omitted by the Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1971.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article originally guaranteed personal rights, privileges, and dignities of former princely State rulers. Omitted by the 26th Amendment (1971) alongside the abolition of privy purses (Article 291). The constitutional rationale was the inconsistency of hereditary privileges with republican equality. The amendment was challenged in Raghunathrao Ganpatrao v. Union of India (1993) but upheld as not violating the basic structure.

landmarkCase.citation: Raghunathrao Ganpatrao v. Union of India (1993)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court upheld the 26th Amendment as not violating the basic structure. The Court reasoned that hereditary privileges of former rulers were antithetical to republican democracy and equality. The judgment validated the constitutional transition from princely India to a fully republican State.

articles.title: Bar to interference by courts in disputes arising out of certain treaties, agreements, etc.
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution but subject to the provisions of article 143, neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall have jurisdiction in any dispute arising out of any provision of a treaty, agreement, covenant, engagement, sanad or other similar instrument which was entered into or executed before the commencement of this Constitution by any Ruler of an Indian State and to which the Government of the Dominion of India or any of its predecessor Governments was a party and which has or has been continued in operation after such commencement, or in any dispute in respect of any right accruing under or any liability or obligation arising out of any of the provisions of this Constitution relating to any such treaty, agreement, covenant, engagement, sanad or other similar instrument.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article bars judicial jurisdiction over disputes arising from pre-Constitutional treaties/agreements with princely rulers (Instruments of Accession, Standstill Agreements). The rationale is that integration of princely States was a political process — judicial interference could destabilize the carefully negotiated settlement. The bar is absolute except for Presidential reference under Article 143.

landmarkCase.citation: Madhav Rao Scindia v. Union of India (1971)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court navigated Article 363 in the privy purse case, distinguishing between executive action under treaties (barred from review) and constitutional amendments affecting treaty rights (reviewable). The case led to the 26th Amendment, illustrating the complex interplay between Article 363's jurisdictional bar and constitutional change.

articles.title: Recognition granted to Rulers of Indian States to cease and privy purses to be abolished
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution or in any law for the time being in force — (a) the Prince, Chief or other person who, at any time before the commencement of the Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1971, was recognised by the President as the Ruler of an Indian State or any person who, at any time before such commencement, was recognised by the President as the successor of such Ruler shall, on and from such commencement, cease to be recognised as such Ruler or the successor of such Ruler; (b) on and from the commencement of the Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1971, privy purse is abolished and all rights, liabilities and obligations in respect of privy purse are extinguished and accordingly the Ruler or, as the case may be, the successor of such Ruler...shall not be paid any sum as privy purse.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Inserted by the 26th Amendment (1971), this article formalized the abolition of: (1) recognition of princely rulers and their successors; and (2) privy purses (annual payments). This completed the constitutional integration of princely States into republican India. The amendment was the legislative response to the Supreme Court's striking down of the executive de-recognition order in Madhav Rao Scindia case.

landmarkCase.citation: Raghunathrao Ganpatrao v. Union of India (1993)
landmarkCase.summary: The 5-judge bench upheld Article 363A, holding that abolition of princely titles and privy purses does not violate the basic structure. The Court emphasized that republican equality is a basic feature of the Constitution, and special privileges of former rulers are inconsistent with constitutional principles of equal citizenship.

articles.title: Special provisions as to major ports and aerodromes
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the President may by public notification direct that as from such date as may be specified in the notification — (a) any law made by Parliament or by the Legislature of a State shall not apply to any major port or aerodrome or shall apply thereto subject to such exceptions or modifications as may be specified in the notification, or (b) any existing law shall cease to have effect in any major port or aerodrome except as respects things done or omitted to be done before the said date, or shall in its application to such port or aerodrome have effect subject to such exceptions or modifications as may be specified in the notification.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article empowers the President to selectively apply or exempt central or State laws from major ports and aerodromes, with modifications as necessary. The rationale is that ports and airports require specialized regulatory regimes given their strategic importance for trade and defense.
