This flexibility allows tailored legal frameworks for these critical infrastructure facilities.

landmarkCase.citation: Mumbai Port Trust v. Premier Automobiles (1981)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court interpreted the special status of major ports under Article 364, holding that selective application of laws to ports is a recognized constitutional flexibility. The judgment upheld the President's authority to modify legal applicability for ports while maintaining constitutional standards of equality and due process.

articles.title: Effect of failure to comply with, or to give effect to, directions given by the Union
articles.officialText: Where any State has failed to comply with, or to give effect to, any directions given in the exercise of the executive power of the Union under any of the provisions of this Constitution, it shall be lawful for the President to hold that a situation has arisen in which the Government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article links Union directives with Article 356. If a State fails to comply with Union directions issued under any constitutional provision (Articles 256, 257, 339(2), 353, etc.), the President can deem this as 'failure of constitutional machinery' triggering President's Rule. This is a powerful Union enforcement mechanism, though Bommai principles require any such finding to be objectively justifiable and judicially reviewable.

landmarkCase.citation: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court held that Article 365 cannot be used mechanically to justify President's Rule. The Union directive must be constitutionally valid, the State's failure must be substantial, and the deeming clause is subject to judicial review. The Bommai principles apply to any Article 356 action invoking Article 365, preventing its misuse.

articles.title: Definitions
articles.officialText: In this Constitution, unless the context otherwise requires, the following expressions have the meanings hereby respectively assigned to them, that is to say — (1) 'agricultural income' means agricultural income as defined for the purposes of the enactments relating to Indian income-tax; (2) 'an Anglo-Indian' means a person whose father or any of whose other male progenitors in the male line is or was of European descent but who is domiciled within the territory of India... (12A) 'goods and services tax' means any tax on supply of goods, or services or both except taxes on the supply of the alcoholic liquor for human consumption...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This is the master definitions article of the Constitution. It contains 30+ definitions of key terms used throughout — from 'Anglo-Indian' to 'Foreign State' to 'Goods and Services Tax' (added by 101st Amendment). These definitions are binding interpretations unless the context requires otherwise. The article ensures consistency and clarity across the entire constitutional text, preventing interpretive ambiguities on fundamental concepts.

landmarkCase.citation: Builders Association of India v. Union of India (2007)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court repeatedly relies on Article 366 definitions to resolve constitutional interpretation disputes. The definitions act as the constitutional dictionary, and courts have held that these are binding unless explicit contextual displacement is shown. Many landmark cases on taxation, federalism, and fundamental rights turn on Article 366 definitions.

articles.title: Interpretation
articles.officialText: Unless the context otherwise requires, the General Clauses Act, 1897, shall, subject to any adaptations and modifications that may be made therein under article 372, apply for the interpretation of this Constitution as it applies for the interpretation of an Act of the Legislature of the Dominion of India. Any reference in this Constitution to Acts or laws of, or made by, Parliament, or to Acts or laws of, or made by, the Legislature of a State, shall be construed as including a reference to an Ordinance made by the President or, to an Ordinance made by a Governor, as the case may be...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article provides interpretive rules: (1) The General Clauses Act, 1897 applies to constitutional interpretation; (2) References to laws include Ordinances; (3) References to rulers include successors and Governors as the case may be; (4) The expression 'foreign State' is defined. This article ensures interpretive continuity with pre-Constitutional legal principles while adapting them to the new constitutional framework. The infamous 2019 abrogation of Article 370 used Article 367 modification — a constitutionally controversial route.

landmarkCase.citation: In Re: Article 370 Abrogation Case — Article 370 Petitions (2023)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court examined the use of Article 367 to modify references in Article 370 during the 2019 abrogation. While the Court upheld the abrogation, it acknowledged that using Article 367 to amend Article 370 raised constitutional questions about whether interpretive provisions can substantively amend other provisions. A landmark case on the limits of Article 367's interpretive use.

articles.title: Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and procedure therefor
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may in exercise of its constituent power amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision of this Constitution in accordance with the procedure laid down in this article. An amendment of this Constitution may be initiated only by the introduction of a Bill for the purpose in either House of Parliament, and when the Bill is passed in each House by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting, it shall be presented to the President who shall give his assent to the Bill and thereupon the Constitution shall stand amended in accordance with the terms of the Bill: Provided that if such amendment seeks to make any change in — (a) article 54, article 55, article 73, article 162, article 241 or article 279A; or (b) Chapter IV of Part V, Chapter V of Part VI, or Chapter I of Part XI; or (c) any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule; or (d) the representation of States in Parliament; or (e) the provisions of this article, the amendment shall also require to be ratified by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States by resolutions to that effect passed by those Legislatures before the Bill making provision for such amendment is presented to the President for assent.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This is the heart of constitutional change. Three amendment procedures: (1) SIMPLE MAJORITY — for provisions in Articles 4, 169, etc. (not strictly under Article 368); (2) SPECIAL MAJORITY — 2/3rd present and voting + majority of total membership of each House (default under Article 368); and (3) SPECIAL MAJORITY + STATE RATIFICATION — for federal provisions listed in the proviso (President's election, executive/judicial powers, Seventh Schedule, State representation, Article 368 itself), requiring ratification by at least half the State Legislatures. The Constitution has been amended 106 times. The BASIC STRUCTURE DOCTRINE (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) holds that even Article 368 cannot destroy the basic features of the Constitution — the most important limitation on constituent power.

landmarkCase.citation: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) — 13-Judge Bench
landmarkCase.summary: The MOST IMPORTANT case in Indian constitutional history. The 13-judge bench (7-6 majority) held that Parliament's power to amend under Article 368 is plenary but NOT unlimited — it cannot alter the 'basic structure' of the Constitution. The basic structure includes supremacy of the Constitution, rule of law, separation of powers, federalism, secularism, democracy, judicial review, and fundamental rights. This doctrine has been applied to strike down constitutional amendments in Indira Gandhi (1975), Minerva Mills (1980), Waman Rao (1981), I.R. Coelho (2007), and NJAC (2015). The basic structure doctrine is India's unique contribution to global constitutional jurisprudence, preserving the soul of the Constitution against majoritarian amendment.

partTitle: Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions (Articles 369-392) — Key Articles

articles.title: Temporary provisions with respect to the State of Jammu and Kashmir (Abrogated in operative effect, 2019)
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding anything contained in this Constitution — (a) the provisions of article 238 shall not apply now in relation to the State of Jammu and Kashmir; (b) the power of Parliament to make laws for the said State shall be limited to — (i) those matters in the Union List and the Concurrent List which, in consultation with the Government of the State, are declared by the President to correspond to matters specified in the Instrument of Accession governing the accession of the State to the Dominion of India... [Effectively abrogated by Presidential Order C.O. 272 and 273 of 2019]
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article granted special autonomous status to Jammu & Kashmir, recognizing the unique circumstances of its accession to India. J&K had its own Constitution, flag, and laws on most subjects except Defense, External Affairs, and Communications. On 5 August 2019, the President issued Constitutional Order 272 (applying all Constitution provisions to J&K) and Order 273 (making Article 370 'inoperative'). Simultaneously, the J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019 bifurcated the State into UTs of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh. The constitutional validity of this process was a major controversy resolved by the Supreme Court in 2023.

landmarkCase.citation: In Re: Article 370 of the Constitution (2023) — 5-Judge Constitution Bench
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court unanimously upheld the abrogation of Article 370, holding: (1) Article 370 was always intended as a temporary provision; (2) J&K had no internal sovereignty distinct from other States after accession; (3) The President had power under Article 370(3) to declare it inoperative; (4) The use of Article 367 to modify references was scrutinized but upheld in this context; (5) The bifurcation into UTs was constitutional, though the Court directed restoration of statehood to J&K and conducting elections by September 2024. A landmark judgment defining the constitutional integration of J&K with the Indian Union.

articles.title: Special provision with respect to the States of Maharashtra and Gujarat
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the President may by order made with respect to the State of Maharashtra or Gujarat, provide for any special responsibility of the Governor for — (a) the establishment of separate development boards for Vidarbha, Marathwada, and the rest of Maharashtra or, as the case may be, Saurashtra, Kutch and the rest of Gujarat with the provision that a report on the working of each of these boards will be placed each year before the State Legislative Assembly...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article and Articles 371A-371J provide special provisions for various States addressing their unique historical, regional, or developmental circumstances. Article 371 itself empowers the Governors of Maharashtra and Gujarat to set up development boards for Vidarbha, Marathwada, Saurashtra, Kutch to address regional development imbalances. This reflects asymmetric federalism — different States having different constitutional arrangements based on their specific needs.

landmarkCase.citation: Vidarbha Development Board v. State of Maharashtra (Various)
landmarkCase.summary: Courts have upheld the constitutional validity of regional development boards under Article 371, recognizing them as legitimate mechanisms for addressing intra-State developmental disparities. The Governor's role is constitutionally protected and serves the federal goal of equitable development.

articles.title: Special provisions for various States (Nagaland, Assam, Manipur, Andhra Pradesh, Sikkim, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Karnataka)
articles.officialText: Articles 371A (Nagaland), 371B (Assam), 371C (Manipur), 371D & 371E (Andhra Pradesh/Telangana), 371F (Sikkim), 371G (Mizoram), 371H (Arunachal Pradesh), 371I (Goa), 371J (Karnataka — Hyderabad-Karnataka region). [Each contains state-specific special provisions]
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: These articles provide asymmetric federal arrangements for States with special circumstances: (1) 371A — Nagaland: protection of Naga customary law, religious/social practices, ownership of land; (2) 371F — Sikkim: special provisions on accession; (3) 371G — Mizoram: protection of Mizo culture, land; (4) 371J — Karnataka: special status for Hyderabad-Karnataka region in education and employment. These provisions recognize India's diversity and prevent 'one-size-fits-all' federalism, accommodating regional, tribal, and cultural specificities within the federal framework.

landmarkCase.citation: Naga People's Movement of Human Rights v. Union of India (1998)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court has consistently upheld the special provisions under Articles 371A-371J as constitutional accommodations of India's diversity. The Court has emphasized that these provisions are essential to preserving the cultural, social, and developmental identities of specific regions while maintaining constitutional unity. Asymmetric federalism is a recognized feature of Indian constitutional design.

articles.title: Continuance in force of existing laws and their adaptation
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding the repeal by this Constitution of the enactments referred to in article 395 but subject to the other provisions of this Constitution, all the law in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall continue in force therein until altered or repealed or amended by a competent Legislature or other competent authority.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This is the crucial continuity provision. ALL pre-Constitutional laws continue in force until altered by competent legislatures, subject to constitutional consistency. This prevented a legal vacuum on 26 January 1950 — IPC (1860), CrPC (1898), Indian Contract Act (1872), etc. all continued. Courts can adapt them to constitutional requirements. Article 13 simultaneously voids pre-Constitutional laws inconsistent with fundamental rights, creating a process of constitutional reconciliation of inherited law.

landmarkCase.citation: Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court evolved the doctrine of 'eclipse' under Article 372 read with Article 13: pre-Constitutional laws inconsistent with fundamental rights are 'eclipsed' (not void), and revive automatically if the inconsistency is removed by constitutional amendment. This nuanced approach preserved the maximum continuity of inherited legal system while enforcing constitutional supremacy.

articles.title: Power of President to make order in respect of persons under preventive detention in certain cases
articles.officialText: Until provision is made by Parliament under clause (7) of article 22, or until the expiration of one year from the commencement of this Constitution, whichever is earlier, the said article shall have effect as if for any reference to Parliament in clauses (4) and (7) thereof there were substituted a reference to the President and for any reference to any law made by Parliament in those clauses there were substituted a reference to an order made by the President.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This transitional provision empowered the President to make orders on preventive detention until Parliament enacted laws under Article 22(7). This filled an immediate post-Constitutional gap in personal liberty jurisprudence, as preventive detention was being widely used in newly-independent India. The provision became spent once Parliament enacted the Preventive Detention Act, 1950.

landmarkCase.citation: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950)
landmarkCase.summary: The first major preventive detention case decided shortly after Constitution's commencement. The Supreme Court applied the constitutional framework including Article 373's transitional provisions, examining the scope of personal liberty under Article 21. Though the narrow approach was later overruled in Maneka Gandhi (1978), this case established the foundational jurisprudence on detention under the new Constitution.

articles.title: Provisions as to Judges of Federal Court and proceedings pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council
articles.officialText: The Judges of the Federal Court holding office immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, become on such commencement the Judges of the Supreme Court and shall thereupon be entitled to such salaries and allowances and to such rights in respect of leave of absence and pension as are provided for under article 125 in respect of the Judges of the Supreme Court...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article ensured institutional continuity for the judiciary: (1) Federal Court judges became Supreme Court judges; (2) Pending Federal Court proceedings transferred to Supreme Court; (3) Appeals pending before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London either continued there or transferred to Supreme Court as specified. This ensured smooth transition from colonial judicial structure to the new constitutional Supreme Court of India without disrupting pending litigation.

landmarkCase.citation: Federal Court to Supreme Court transition (1950)
landmarkCase.summary: The seamless judicial transition validated by Article 374 ensured that the Supreme Court inherited the institutional credibility and continuity of the Federal Court. The first Chief Justice, H.J. Kania, had been Chief Justice of the Federal Court. The transition reflects the constitutional commitment to institutional continuity in the rule of law.

articles.title: Courts, authorities and officers to continue to function subject to the provisions of the Constitution
articles.officialText: All courts of civil, criminal and revenue jurisdiction, all authorities and all officers, judicial, executive and ministerial, throughout the territory of India, shall continue to exercise their respective functions subject to the provisions of this Constitution.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article ensured continuity of all judicial, executive, and ministerial authorities and officers. All courts (district, sessions, revenue), all government departments, and all officers continued functioning subject to constitutional consistency. This prevented administrative chaos on 26 January 1950 — the State machinery continued operating seamlessly while adapting to constitutional supremacy.

landmarkCase.citation: Administrative Continuity Cases post-1950
landmarkCase.summary: Courts have consistently held that Article 375 ensured uninterrupted governance during constitutional transition. The continuity provided by this article allowed the new Republic to function from day one without recreating the entire administrative apparatus, while progressively constitutionalizing inherited institutions.

articles.title: Provisions as to Judges of High Courts
articles.officialText: Notwithstanding anything in clause (2) of article 217, the Judges of a High Court in any Province holding office immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, become on such commencement the Judges of the High Court in the corresponding State, and shall thereupon be entitled to such salaries and allowances and to such rights in respect of leave of absence and pension as are provided for under clause (1) of article 221 in respect of the Judges of such High Court...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article continued the office of pre-Constitutional High Court judges in the corresponding new High Courts. They became regular High Court judges under the Constitution with all rights and benefits under Article 221. This ensured judicial continuity at the High Court level, paralleling Article 374 for the Supreme Court. The judges retained their expertise and institutional memory while operating under the new constitutional framework.

landmarkCase.citation: High Court Continuity Cases (1950)
landmarkCase.summary: The transition of provincial High Court judges to constitutional High Courts under Article 376 was seamless. Courts have recognized that this continuity preserved judicial expertise and ensured stability in the appellate judicial system during constitutional transition.

articles.title: Provisions as to Comptroller and Auditor-General of India
articles.officialText: The Auditor-General of India holding office immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless he has elected otherwise, become on such commencement the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India and shall thereupon be entitled to such salaries and to such rights in respect of leave of absence and pension as are provided for under clause (3) of article 148 in respect of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article ensured continuity of the Auditor-General as the constitutional Comptroller and Auditor-General (CAG) of India under Article 148. The CAG is a crucial constitutional authority auditing government accounts. The transition preserved the institutional independence and expertise of public auditing in the new Republic.

landmarkCase.citation: CAG v. K.S. Jagannathan (1986)
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court has consistently recognized the constitutional importance and independence of the CAG. The institutional continuity provided by Article 377 ensured the CAG inherited the expertise and credibility necessary to discharge its critical constitutional function of auditing all government expenditure and ensuring financial accountability.

articles.title: Provisions as to Public Service Commissions
articles.officialText: The members of the Public Service Commission for the Dominion of India holding office immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, become on such commencement the members of the Public Service Commission for the Union and shall, notwithstanding anything in clauses (1) and (2) of article 316, continue to hold office until the expiration of their term of office as determined under the rules which were applicable immediately before such commencement to such members...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article continued members of the Public Service Commission of the Dominion of India as members of the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC). It similarly continued provincial PSC members as State PSC members. This ensured continuity of merit-based recruitment to public services through constitutional public service commissions, which are crucial pillars of administrative democracy.

landmarkCase.citation: UPSC Continuity and Independence Cases
landmarkCase.summary: Courts have recognized that institutional continuity of PSCs under Article 378 was essential to maintaining merit-based recruitment in the public service. The constitutional independence of PSCs under Articles 315-323 builds on this foundational continuity, ensuring impartial selection to government positions.

articles.title: Power of the President to remove difficulties
articles.officialText: The President may, for the purpose of removing any difficulties, particularly in relation to the transition from the provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935, to the provisions of this Constitution, by order direct that this Constitution shall, during such period as may be specified in the order, have effect subject to such adaptations, whether by way of modification, addition or omission, as he may deem to be necessary or expedient: Provided that no such order shall be made after the first meeting of Parliament duly constituted under Chapter II of Part V.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This was a transitional provision empowering the President to remove difficulties in the Constitution's implementation, particularly during transition from the Government of India Act, 1935. The power was limited to before the first sitting of Parliament. This 'removal of difficulties' clause allowed practical adjustments during the critical early period of constitutional implementation, preventing technical glitches from derailing the new constitutional order.

landmarkCase.citation: Constitutional Transition Cases (1950)
landmarkCase.summary: The Presidential power under Article 392 was used pragmatically during the constitutional transition. Courts have noted that such transitional powers are essential during constitutional implementation but must be strictly time-bound and limited to genuine difficulties, not used to substantively modify the Constitution.

partTitle: Short Title, Commencement, Authoritative Text in Hindi and Repeals

articles.title: Short title
articles.officialText: This Constitution may be called the Constitution of India.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This brief article officially names the document 'The Constitution of India'. While seemingly procedural, it formally establishes the identity of the supreme law of the land. The name itself carries constitutional significance — it is the Constitution of 'India', the new republic, distinct from any colonial enactment.

landmarkCase.citation: Constitutional Identity Cases
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court has repeatedly emphasized that the 'Constitution of India' represents the sovereign will of 'We, the People of India' as stated in the Preamble. The constitutional identity is a unified concept binding diverse provisions into a coherent supreme law.

articles.title: Commencement
articles.officialText: This article and articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 shall come into force at once, and the remaining provisions of this Constitution shall come into force on the twenty-sixth day of January, 1950, which day is referred to in this Constitution as the commencement of this Constitution.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This article fixes 26 January 1950 as the commencement date — celebrated as Republic Day. Certain articles (citizenship — Articles 5-9, presidential election — Article 60, Election Commission — Article 324, etc.) came into force on 26 November 1949 (Constitution's adoption) to enable the constitutional framework's establishment. The date 26 January was chosen to commemorate the Lahore Congress's 1930 declaration of Purna Swaraj (complete independence) — embedding nationalist memory in the constitutional moment.

landmarkCase.citation: Constitution Commencement Recognition
landmarkCase.summary: The date of constitutional commencement is fundamental to all subsequent constitutional jurisprudence. Article 372 (continuance of existing laws), Article 13 (pre-existing laws and fundamental rights), and numerous other provisions reference this date as the critical constitutional moment from which the Republic was born.

articles.title: Authoritative text in the Hindi language
articles.officialText: The President shall cause to be published under his authority — (a) the translation of this Constitution in the Hindi language, signed by the members of the Constituent Assembly, with such modifications as may be necessary to bring it in conformity with the language, style and terminology adopted in the authoritative texts of Central Acts in the Hindi language, and incorporating therein all the amendments of this Constitution made before such publication; and (b) the translation in the Hindi language of every amendment of this Constitution made in the English language...
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: Inserted by the 58th Amendment (1987), this article empowers the President to publish an authoritative Hindi text of the Constitution. The Hindi version has the same legal force as the English version. In case of difficulty in construing the Hindi version, the President can issue revised translations. This reflects the Constitution's bilingual nature and Hindi's status as official language under Article 343.

landmarkCase.citation: Linguistic Constitutional Interpretation Cases
landmarkCase.summary: Courts generally rely on the English version of the Constitution as the original text, but the Hindi authoritative version under Article 394A has equal legal status. The constitutional bilingualism reflects India's linguistic diversity while ensuring legal certainty and accessibility of the supreme law.

articles.title: Repeals
articles.officialText: The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed.
articles.w3schoolsExplanation: This is the FINAL article of the Constitution. It expressly REPEALS the two foundational colonial-era statutes: (1) the Indian Independence Act, 1947 (which created the Dominions of India and Pakistan); and (2) the Government of India Act, 1935 (the colonial constitution India operated under since 1935 and which served as the structural template for much of our Constitution). The Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949 was preserved as it dealt with the transition of judicial appeals. With this final article, the Constitution decisively breaks from colonial constitutional foundations, establishing India as a fully independent constitutional Republic with its own supreme law. The Constitution stands complete and self-contained from this point onwards.

landmarkCase.citation: Berubari Union Case (1960) and Constitutional Sovereignty Cases
landmarkCase.summary: The Supreme Court has emphasized that with the repeal of colonial enactments under Article 395, India achieved complete constitutional sovereignty. The Constitution is the supreme source of all governmental authority — there is no residual colonial constitutional authority. This article symbolizes the complete constitutional independence of the Indian Republic, where 'We, the People' are the sole source of constitutional legitimacy.
